PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: La siguiente pregunta se basa en los tres documentos a continuación. Analiza cada documento usando el marco HIPP (Contexto histórico, Audiencia prevista, Propósito, Punto de vista). Luego construye un argumento bien organizado en respuesta al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: Usando los tres documentos y tu conocimiento de la Era Dorada, evalúa la siguiente afirmación: "La rápida industrialización de los Estados Unidos entre 1877 y 1900 creó prosperidad para algunos estadounidenses mientras explotaba sistemáticamente a otros, y los mecanismos que los trabajadores y el gobierno usaron para responder fueron fundamentalmente inadecuados para abordar la desigualdad estructural que produjo la industrialización."

Construye un argumento que esté de acuerdo, en desacuerdo o que matice esta afirmación usando evidencia de los tres documentos y al menos dos piezas adicionales de conocimiento histórico externo. Tu respuesta debe abordar las perspectivas de al menos dos grupos — trabajadores industriales, industrialistas o legisladores — y evaluar la efectividad de sus estrategias.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Andrew Carnegie, "El Evangelio de la Riqueza," North American Review, junio de 1889. Disponible en las colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"El hombre que muere así rico muere deshonrado. Tal es, en mi opinión, el verdadero Evangelio sobre la Riqueza, obediente al cual es el deber del hombre de Riqueza: Primero, dar ejemplo de vida modesta y sin ostentación, huyendo del despliegue o la extravagancia; proveer moderadamente para las necesidades legítimas de quienes dependen de él; y después de hacerlo considerar todos los ingresos excedentes que le lleguen simplemente como fondos en fideicomiso."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Samuel Gompers, Informe a la Convención de la Federación Americana del Trabajo, diciembre de 1890. Disponible en la Biblioteca del Congreso, colección American Memory.

"No hay un hombre aquí que no haya sentido la degradación de verse obligado a trabajar más horas de las que la resistencia humana puede soportar bien, y con salarios insuficientes para mantenerse a sí mismo y a su familia en algo parecido a la comodidad y la decencia. La Federación Americana del Trabajo declara que la jornada de ocho horas no es una demanda de ociosidad — es una demanda de vida. No demandamos caridad a los ricos. Demandamos justicia al sistema."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Ley Sherman Antimonopolio, Sección 1, Congreso de los Estados Unidos, 2 de julio de 1890. Disponible en los Archivos Nacionales y Administración de Registros.

"Todo contrato, combinación en forma de trust o de otro modo, o conspiración, en restricción del comercio o industria entre los diversos Estados, o con naciones extranjeras, se declara ilegal. Toda persona que celebre cualquier contrato o participe en cualquier combinación o conspiración aquí declarada ilegal será considerada culpable de un delito menor."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Recuerda: (1) Aplicar el análisis HIPP a cada documento. (2) Construir un argumento claro que responda al enunciado. (3) Usar evidencia de los tres documentos. (4) Incorporar al menos dos hechos históricos externos no mencionados en los documentos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response constructs a qualified argument: industrialization created genuine prosperity measured by national GDP and consumer goods availability, but this prosperity was distributed through a system of structural exploitation that workers and government lacked the tools to effectively challenge in the short term. HIPP analysis of Document 1: Historical context — Carnegie writing amid Gilded Age inequality and labor unrest; Intended audience — middle-class readers of the North American Review; Purpose — to justify concentrated wealth through a philanthropic obligation framework; Point of view — a self-made industrialist who conflates his own success story with a universal social good. Document 2: Historical context — AFL founding period and eight-hour movement; Audience — AFL convention delegates; Purpose — to mobilize workers around a specific, winnable demand; Point of view — craft union leader who rejects socialist revolution in favor of practical gains. Document 3: Historical context — congressional response to Standard Oil and trust formation; Audience — courts and corporations; Purpose — to establish federal authority over interstate commerce monopolies; Point of view — government as regulator, but the vague language ("restraint of trade") would be interpreted by courts to target labor unions as frequently as corporations. Outside knowledge: the Homestead Strike (1892) demonstrates how government power (militia/Pinkerton agents) was turned against workers; Standard Oil's survival of Sherman Act challenges until 1911 shows the law's initial ineffectiveness against capital; the Clayton Act (1914) was needed to close Sherman Act loopholes. Conclusion: worker and government mechanisms were inadequate in the 1890s but laid the institutional groundwork for Progressive Era reform.

SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

6 — Exemplary: Constructs a clear, historically defensible argument (agree, disagree, or qualified) that is responsive to the prompt's specific claim about structural inadequacy. Applies HIPP analysis to all three documents, identifying at least one HIPP element per document (historical context, audience, purpose, or point of view) that directly supports the argument. Incorporates at least two specific outside historical facts not present in the documents (e.g., Homestead Strike, Standard Oil dissolution timeline, Pullman Strike, Haymarket Affair, Clayton Act). Addresses perspectives of at least two groups and evaluates strategy effectiveness. Demonstrates cross-document synthesis — e.g., comparing Carnegie's philanthropic frame with Gompers's structural critique, or noting the Sherman Act's ironic use against labor unions. Response is organized with a clear thesis, body paragraphs, and conclusion.

5 — Advanced: Strong argument with HIPP analysis of all three documents. Two outside facts incorporated. Addresses two groups. Some cross-document synthesis present but less fully developed than exemplary. Minor analytical gaps.

4 — Proficient: Clear argument with HIPP analysis of at least two documents. At least one outside fact. Addresses two groups but evaluation of strategy effectiveness is incomplete. Documents used as evidence but not analyzed beyond surface content.

3 — Adequate: Argument present but may be vague or not fully responsive to the structural inadequacy claim. HIPP applied to one or two documents. One outside fact. One group perspective addressed.

2 — Developing: Attempts an argument but it is largely a summary of the documents. Limited or no HIPP analysis. No outside facts or only a general claim without specifics.

1 — Beginning: Lists information from the documents without constructing an argument. No HIPP analysis. No outside knowledge.

0 — No response or off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS (HIPP):
Document 1 — Carnegie: Historical context: Gilded Age inequality and labor unrest; Audience: educated middle-class readers; Purpose: to legitimate concentrated wealth through a stewardship framework; POV: self-made industrialist conflating personal narrative with social theory — limits reliability as evidence of actual worker conditions.
Document 2 — Gompers: Historical context: AFL founding and the eight-hour movement; Audience: AFL convention delegates seeking to mobilize; Purpose: to justify labor organizing as a civic, not just economic, necessity; POV: craft union leader — may underrepresent unskilled workers and exclude women and immigrants from the AFL frame.
Document 3 — Sherman Act: Historical context: congressional response to trust formation; Audience: courts and corporations; Purpose: to establish federal anti-monopoly authority; POV: federal government — the vague language was a legislative compromise that initially proved more effective against labor than capital.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Homestead Strike (1892) — Carnegie/Frick use of Pinkerton agents and Pennsylvania militia; Pullman Strike (1894) — federal government uses injunction against labor under Sherman Act; Haymarket Affair (1886) — backlash against labor organizing; Standard Oil's continued dominance until 1911 dissolution; Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) closing Sherman Act loopholes; AFL membership growth from 140,000 (1886) to 1.5 million (1904); child labor statistics in steel/textile industries; real wage stagnation for unskilled workers despite GDP growth.

6 — Ejemplar: Construye un argumento claro y históricamente defendible que responde específicamente a la afirmación del enunciado sobre la inadecuación estructural. Aplica el análisis HIPP a los tres documentos, identificando al menos un elemento HIPP por documento que apoya directamente el argumento. Incorpora al menos dos hechos históricos externos específicos no presentes en los documentos. Aborda las perspectivas de al menos dos grupos y evalúa la efectividad de las estrategias. Demuestra síntesis entre documentos.

3 — Adecuado: El argumento está presente pero puede ser vago. HIPP aplicado a uno o dos documentos. Un hecho externo. Se aborda la perspectiva de un grupo.

2 — En desarrollo: Intenta un argumento pero es en gran medida un resumen de los documentos. Análisis HIPP limitado o nulo. Sin hechos externos.

1 — Inicial: Enumera información de los documentos sin construir un argumento.

0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Huelga de Homestead (1892); Huelga Pullman (1894); Asunto Haymarket (1886); dominancia continua de Standard Oil hasta la disolución de 1911; Ley Clayton Antimonopolio (1914); crecimiento de la membresía de la AFL; estadísticas de trabajo infantil; estancamiento de salarios reales para trabajadores no calificados.

DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze each of the following three documents using the HIPP framework. Then construct a well-organized argument that responds to the prompt.

PROMPT: Theodore Roosevelt has been called both "the great trust buster" and "the great trust regulator." Using all three documents and at least two outside historical facts, evaluate which characterization is more historically accurate. In your argument, assess whether the federal government's approach to monopoly between 1890 and 1914 fundamentally changed the relationship between concentrated economic power and democratic governance, or whether it preserved that relationship under new management.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Andrew Carnegie, "The Gospel of Wealth," North American Review, June 1889. Library of Congress digital collections.

"The concentration of business, industrial and commercial, in the hands of a few, and the law of competition between these, is not only beneficial, but essential for the future progress of the race... While the law [of competition] may be sometimes hard for the individual, it is best for the race, because it ensures the survival of the fittest in every department. We accept and welcome, therefore, as conditions to which we must accommodate ourselves, great inequality of environment, the concentration of business, industrial and commercial, in the hands of a few, and the law of competition between these, as being not only beneficial but essential for the future progress of the race."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 2
Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 2, United States Congress, July 2, 1890. National Archives and Records Administration.

"Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and, on conviction thereof, shall be punished by fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or by both said punishments, in the discretion of the court."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 3
Source: Theodore Roosevelt, "The New Nationalism," speech at Osawatomie, Kansas, August 31, 1910. National Archives.

"We are face to face with new conceptions of the relations of property to human welfare, of the relations of the State to the individual... The man who wrongly holds that every human right is secondary to his profit must now give way to the advocate of human welfare, who rightly maintains that every man holds his property subject to the general right of the community to regulate its use to whatever degree the public welfare may require it."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Remember to apply HIPP to each document, construct a clear argument, use all three documents, and incorporate at least two outside historical facts.

PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analiza cada uno de los tres documentos siguientes usando el marco HIPP. Luego construye un argumento bien organizado que responda al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: Theodore Roosevelt ha sido llamado tanto "el gran destructor de trusts" como "el gran regulador de trusts." Usando los tres documentos y al menos dos hechos históricos externos, evalúa cuál caracterización es más históricamente precisa. En tu argumento, evalúa si el enfoque del gobierno federal hacia el monopolio entre 1890 y 1914 cambió fundamentalmente la relación entre el poder económico concentrado y la gobernanza democrática, o si la preservó bajo una nueva gestión.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Andrew Carnegie, "El Evangelio de la Riqueza," North American Review, junio de 1889. Colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"La concentración de los negocios, industriales y comerciales, en manos de unos pocos, y la ley de la competencia entre estos, no solo es beneficiosa, sino esencial para el progreso futuro de la raza... Mientras que la ley [de la competencia] puede ser a veces dura para el individuo, es la mejor para la raza, porque asegura la supervivencia del más apto en cada departamento."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Ley Sherman Antimonopolio, Sección 2, Congreso de los Estados Unidos, 2 de julio de 1890. Archivos Nacionales y Administración de Registros.

"Toda persona que monopolice, o intente monopolizar, o combine o conspire con cualquier otra persona o personas, para monopolizar cualquier parte del comercio o industria entre los varios Estados, o con naciones extranjeras, será considerada culpable de un delito menor."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Theodore Roosevelt, "El Nuevo Nacionalismo," discurso en Osawatomie, Kansas, 31 de agosto de 1910. Archivos Nacionales.

"Nos enfrentamos a nuevas concepciones de las relaciones de la propiedad con el bienestar humano, de las relaciones del Estado con el individuo... El hombre que sostiene erróneamente que cada derecho humano es secundario a su ganancia debe ahora ceder el paso al defensor del bienestar humano, quien mantiene correctamente que cada hombre posee su propiedad sujeta al derecho general de la comunidad de regular su uso hasta el grado que el bienestar público pueda requerirlo."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Recuerda aplicar HIPP a cada documento, construir un argumento claro, usar los tres documentos e incorporar al menos dos hechos históricos externos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that Roosevelt was more accurately a trust regulator than a trust buster: he distinguished between "good" and "bad" trusts and sought to manage rather than dissolve concentrated economic power. HIPP for Document 1: Carnegie provides the ideological baseline against which regulation must be measured — his social Darwinist argument that concentration is "beneficial" and "essential" reveals the intellectual framework that federal regulation challenged. The document's purpose is legitimation, and its point of view is that of someone who directly benefited from the absence of regulation, limiting its reliability. Document 2: The Sherman Act's text reveals both its ambition (criminalizing monopolization) and its limitation — the misdemeanor penalty and vague "restraint of trade" language made enforcement difficult; courts initially applied it more against labor unions than corporations. Document 3: Roosevelt's "subject to the general right of the community" framing is not anti-monopoly but pro-regulation — he wants state oversight, not dissolution. The post-presidency timing (1910) suggests this is a political manifesto, not a record of action. Outside knowledge: Northern Securities dissolution (1902) was TR's signature trust-bust but the company continued operating in modified form; Standard Oil survived until 1911; the Bureau of Corporations monitored rather than dismantled trusts; Wilson's Clayton Act (1914) was considered by many Progressives a more genuinely anti-monopoly instrument than anything Roosevelt accomplished.

SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

6 — Exemplary: Takes a clear, historically defensible position on "trust buster" vs. "trust regulator" and sustains it across the response. Applies HIPP to all three documents with specific analysis of historical context, purpose, and point of view for each. Incorporates two or more outside historical facts. Demonstrates cross-document synthesis (e.g., Carnegie's social Darwinism as the foil against which Roosevelt's regulatory philosophy must be measured; or the gap between Sherman Act's language and its actual judicial application). Addresses the deeper question of whether regulation changed or preserved the power relationship.

5 — Advanced: Clear position with HIPP of all three documents. Two outside facts. Synthesis present. Minor analytical gaps.

4 — Proficient: Clear position with HIPP of two documents. One outside fact. The trust buster vs. regulator distinction is addressed but not fully evaluated.

3 — Adequate: Takes a position but evidence is general. HIPP applied to one document. One outside fact or general knowledge.

2 — Developing: Lists TR's actions without analytical argument. Limited HIPP. No outside knowledge beyond the documents.

1 — Beginning: Summarizes documents without analysis or argument.

0 — No response or off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS (HIPP):
Doc 1 — Carnegie: Historical context: Gilded Age before any federal regulation; the document is written while Carnegie Steel operates without antitrust constraint. Purpose: to construct an ideological defense of concentrated wealth. POV: a direct beneficiary of laissez-faire policy — deeply unreliable as evidence of public benefit.
Doc 2 — Sherman Act: Historical context: congressional response to Standard Oil and railroad trusts; the law's vague language reflects a political compromise. Purpose: establishing federal authority without explicitly targeting specific companies. POV: Congress — the law's initial application against labor unions reveals a bias toward protecting capital.
Doc 3 — Roosevelt New Nationalism: Historical context: post-presidency, contemplating a 1912 run; Roosevelt distinguishing himself from Taft's more aggressive (but court-blocked) antitrust approach. Purpose: political positioning. POV: a Progressive who sees regulation, not dissolution, as the solution.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Northern Securities Company case (1902) — first TR trust bust but limited impact; Standard Oil dissolution (1911) — under Taft, not TR; Bureau of Corporations (1903) — TR's regulatory rather than punitive approach; distinction between "good trusts" (US Steel, which TR chose not to prosecute) and "bad trusts"; Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) under Wilson; the "rule of reason" standard established by the Supreme Court in Standard Oil case (1911); Woodrow Wilson's "New Freedom" as a contrast to TR's New Nationalism.

Demuestra síntesis entre documentos. Aborda la pregunta más profunda de si la regulación cambió o preservó la relación de poder.

2 — En desarrollo: Enumera las acciones de TR sin argumento analítico. HIPP limitado.

1 — Inicial: Resume los documentos sin análisis ni argumento.

0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze each document using the HIPP framework. Then construct a well-organized argument that responds to the prompt.

PROMPT: Some historians argue that the Progressive Era's labor reforms were genuine structural achievements; others argue they were minimal concessions that left the fundamental power imbalance between capital and labor intact. Using all three documents and at least two outside historical facts, evaluate which interpretation is better supported by the historical evidence available from 1890 to 1920. In your argument, assess both what Progressive labor reforms achieved and what they failed to change about the relationship between employers and workers.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Samuel Gompers, Testimony before the U.S. Senate Committee on Education and Labor, 1883. United States Senate Historical Records; also available through the Library of Congress.

"We do not want any class legislation. What we want is fair play, and we do not want interference, either from the government on the one hand or from monopoly on the other. We simply ask that the working people shall have a chance — a fair field and no favor... We are not asking for charity. We are asking for our rights, as men. If men who wish to sell the labor of their hands are free to combine for the purpose of getting the best price for that labor, then capital also has a right to combine. The question is whether, in practice, combination by capital can be made as effective and as free from reprisal as combination by labor."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 2
Source: New York Factory Investigating Commission, Preliminary Report, Volume I, 1912. Available through the New York State Library and the National Archives.

"This Commission finds that the present labor law of the State of New York is inadequate to protect those employed in manufacturing establishments... The Commission recommends the enactment of legislation providing: (1) that all factory buildings shall be fireproof in construction; (2) that all exits, stairways, and fire escapes shall be adequate in number and construction; (3) that a working day of not more than 54 hours per week shall be established for women and minors; (4) that labor inspectors shall have authority to close unsafe premises without judicial approval."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 3
Source: Clayton Antitrust Act, Section 6, United States Congress, October 15, 1914. National Archives and Records Administration.

"The labor of a human being is not a commodity or article of commerce. Nothing contained in the antitrust laws shall be construed to forbid the existence and operation of labor, agricultural, or horticultural organizations, instituted for the purposes of mutual help, and not having capital stock or conducted for profit, or to forbid or restrain individual members of such organizations from lawfully carrying out the legitimate objects thereof; nor shall such organizations, or the members thereof, be held or construed to be illegal combinations or conspiracies in restraint of trade, under the antitrust laws."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Apply HIPP to each document, construct a clear argument, use all three documents as evidence, and incorporate at least two outside historical facts.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analiza cada documento usando el marco HIPP. Luego construye un argumento bien organizado que responda al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: Algunos historiadores argumentan que las reformas laborales de la Era Progresista fueron logros estructurales genuinos; otros argumentan que fueron concesiones mínimas que dejaron intacto el desequilibrio de poder fundamental entre el capital y el trabajo. Usando los tres documentos y al menos dos hechos históricos externos, evalúa cuál interpretación está mejor respaldada por la evidencia histórica disponible de 1890 a 1920. En tu argumento, evalúa tanto lo que lograron las reformas laborales progresistas como lo que no cambiaron sobre la relación entre empleadores y trabajadores.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Samuel Gompers, Testimonio ante el Comité del Senado de los EE.UU. sobre Educación y Trabajo, 1883. Registros Históricos del Senado de los Estados Unidos; también disponible en la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"No queremos ninguna legislación de clase. Lo que queremos es juego limpio, y no queremos interferencia, ni del gobierno por un lado ni del monopolio por el otro. Simplemente pedimos que los trabajadores tengan una oportunidad — un campo justo y sin favoritismos... No pedimos caridad. Pedimos nuestros derechos, como hombres. Si los hombres que desean vender el trabajo de sus manos son libres de combinarse con el propósito de obtener el mejor precio por ese trabajo, entonces el capital también tiene derecho a combinarse."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Comisión de Investigación de Fábricas de Nueva York, Informe Preliminar, Volumen I, 1912. Disponible en la Biblioteca del Estado de Nueva York y los Archivos Nacionales.

"Esta Comisión encuentra que la ley laboral actual del Estado de Nueva York es inadecuada para proteger a los empleados en establecimientos manufactureros... La Comisión recomienda la promulgación de legislación que establezca: (1) que todos los edificios de fábricas sean a prueba de incendios en su construcción; (2) que todas las salidas, escaleras y escaleras de incendios sean adecuadas en número y construcción; (3) que se establezca una jornada laboral de no más de 54 horas por semana para mujeres y menores; (4) que los inspectores laborales tengan autoridad para cerrar locales inseguros sin aprobación judicial."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Ley Clayton Antimonopolio, Sección 6, Congreso de los Estados Unidos, 15 de octubre de 1914. Archivos Nacionales y Administración de Registros.

"El trabajo de un ser humano no es una mercancía o artículo de comercio. Nada contenido en las leyes antimonopolio se interpretará para prohibir la existencia y operación de organizaciones laborales, agrícolas u hortícolas, instituidas con fines de ayuda mutua, y que no tengan capital social ni se conduzcan con fines de lucro, o para prohibir o restringir a los miembros individuales de dichas organizaciones de llevar a cabo lícitamente los objetivos legítimos de las mismas."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Aplica HIPP a cada documento, construye un argumento claro, usa los tres documentos como evidencia e incorpora al menos dos hechos históricos externos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that Progressive labor reforms were meaningful but limited: they established important regulatory precedents and defined the terms of a future labor-government relationship, but they did not alter the fundamental power asymmetry between capital and labor that Gompers identified in 1883. HIPP Document 1 — Gompers: Historical context: pre-Sherman Act, labor unions vulnerable to injunction as criminal conspiracies in restraint of trade; Audience: U.S. Senate — Gompers is making a legal argument for labor's right to organize; Purpose: to establish a philosophical framework for labor rights that does not challenge capitalism itself; POV: a craft union leader who accepted the capitalist framework and sought parity within it rather than structural transformation — this limits how far AFL-led reform could go. Document 2 — NY Factory Commission: Historical context: post-Triangle Shirtwaist fire, public outrage demanding legislative response; Audience: state legislature; Purpose: to produce specific legislative recommendations that translate the fire's moral lesson into law; POV: government investigators with reform mandates — the specific and concrete recommendations show genuine structural intent (fire codes, maximum hours), but the 54-hour maximum for women and minors still allowed 10.8-hour days and excluded adult men entirely. Document 3 — Clayton Act Section 6: Historical context: Progressive peak, AFL lobbying for explicit exemption from antitrust; Audience: courts and employers; Purpose: to establish that labor is not a commodity subject to antitrust law; POV: Congress — the declaration that labor "is not a commodity" was a significant rhetorical achievement, but the Duplex Printing case (1921) showed courts would still find ways to apply antitrust to union activity. Outside knowledge: the Pullman Strike injunction (1894) under the Sherman Act; AFL membership growth 1890-1920; the lack of a federal minimum wage until 1938 as evidence that the fundamental wage relationship remained unaddressed by Progressive reform.

Evaluates both what was achieved and what remained unchanged.

items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response constructs a qualified argument: the industrial economy created structural conditions incompatible with democratic equality — concentrated economic power undermined political self-determination — and Progressive regulation was genuine but limited because it addressed symptoms rather than the accumulation mechanisms that produced inequality. Three or more evidence pieces: (1) Standard Oil's horizontal integration giving Rockefeller control of ~90% of American oil refining — creating economic power that translated directly into political influence over legislatures and courts; (2) the Homestead Strike (1892) in which Carnegie used private armies (Pinkerton agents) and state militia against workers, demonstrating that economic power could mobilize government force against democratic organizing; (3) the Sherman Antitrust Act's initial use against labor unions in the Pullman Strike (1894) rather than against capital — a structural irony that shows how "neutral" law operates in favor of existing power. Progressive response: Northern Securities dissolution (1902) and Clayton Act (1914) as evidence of genuine regulatory achievement, but Standard Oil remained the largest company in America until its 1911 dissolution, and no federal minimum wage, no right to organize, and no progressive income tax existed until after 1913. Synthesis: connects to Reconstruction (the 14th Amendment's due process clause was being used by corporations to claim protection from state regulation — the exact opposite of its Reconstruction-era purpose) or to the New Deal (the Wagner Act 1935 and the progressive income tax finally addressed structural inequality that Progressive reform had only partially touched).

items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that journalism and executive leadership were mutually reinforcing within specific issue areas — food safety, railroad regulation, antitrust — but that their combination was insufficient to achieve structural reforms because it depended on individual leadership rather than institutional transformation. Evidence (1): Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (1906) → Roosevelt ordered independent inspections → Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) — a clear journalism-to-legislation pathway in which executive action was the bridge between public outrage and law. Evidence (2): Ida Tarbell's Standard Oil (1904) → informed public opinion → but took seven years and a Supreme Court case (1911) to produce dissolution, and only under Taft, not TR — showing that journalism without immediate executive commitment could not accelerate reform. Evidence (3): Roosevelt coined the term "muckraker" (1906) as a critique of journalists who went too far — revealing that the journalism-executive relationship was not purely collaborative; TR used and limited investigative journalism to maintain control over reform's pace and scope. Reasoning: the combination worked when journalists exposed issues the public could easily understand (tainted food) and executives found politically advantageous to address; it failed when the structural remedy required challenging entrenched corporate political power (labor rights, minimum wage). Synthesis: connects to the abolitionist press (Garrison's Liberator, 1831-1865) — the same dynamic of moral journalism failing to achieve structural change without executive (Lincoln) leadership and ultimately a constitutional amendment; OR connects to the New Deal — FDR's fireside chats and use of radio as a media instrument shows how the journalism-executive power relationship evolved into direct executive communication with the public.

¿Quiénes fueron los principales beneficiarios de la reforma de la Era Progresista, y en qué medida el movimiento progresista cumplió o traicionó sus ideales democráticos para los afroamericanos y las mujeres?

En tu respuesta:
- Establece un ARGUMENTO claro que tome una posición defendible sobre la pregunta de quién se benefició de la reforma progresista y el alcance de la traición o el cumplimiento democrático.
- Proporciona al menos TRES piezas específicas de EVIDENCIA de tu conocimiento sobre el liderazgo afroamericano (US.17), el sufragio femenino (US.16) y la economía industrial (US.08) que apoyen tu argumento.

items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response makes a qualified argument: the primary beneficiaries of Progressive reform were middle-class and upper-class white Americans — both men (who gained cleaner government, regulated business, and consumer protection) and women (who gained the vote and expanded civic roles) — while African Americans and working-class immigrant men received marginal or no benefit from most Progressive reforms. Evidence (1): The 19th Amendment (1920) gave white women the vote, a genuine democratic achievement — but Black women in Southern states remained disenfranchised through Jim Crow mechanisms, and NAWSA had deliberately excluded Black women to secure Southern white women's support, revealing the racial compromise at the center of the suffrage movement. Evidence (2): Booker T. Washington's Tuskegee Institute demonstrated that Black Americans could achieve industrial education and economic advancement on Washington's terms, but the documented failures Du Bois enumerated — disfranchisement, legal inferiority, withdrawal of educational funding — occurred simultaneously with Progressive reforms that included everyone but Black Americans. Evidence (3): Progressive regulatory reforms (Sherman Act, Clayton Act, food safety laws) benefited middle-class consumers and legitimate businesses but did not address the sharecropping system, convict leasing, or the structural poverty of Black agricultural workers in the South. Reasoning: Progressive reform was selective by design — it sought to rationalize capitalism, protect white consumers, and integrate white women into civic life, not to dismantle racial hierarchies or redistribute economic power. Synthesis: connects to Reconstruction — which had attempted a more expansive democratic project through the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments and the Freedmen's Bureau, only to be dismantled through the Compromise of 1877 and subsequent Jim Crow laws — showing that the Progressive Era inherited and reinforced Reconstruction's failure rather than completing its promises; OR to the Civil Rights Movement, which had to accomplish through the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) what the Progressive Era's selective democracy had refused to address.

items.stem: The 19th Amendment changed the Constitution by:

items.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, barred the United States and the states from denying the vote on account of sex, extending suffrage to women in federal and state elections. Choice A is wrong because prohibition of alcohol came from the Eighteenth Amendment. Choice C is wrong because the federal income tax came from the Sixteenth Amendment. Ratification followed roughly seventy years of organized campaigning that began at Seneca Falls in 1848.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The 1898 cartoon shows Uncle Sam rolling up his sleeves in preparation for military action. It reflects the interventionist argument that it was America's 'duty' to act in Cuba and the Philippines.

Which factor most directly triggered the United States' entry into the Spanish-American War in 1898?

choices.text: The Zimmermann Telegram, in which Spain proposed a military alliance with Mexico against the United States
Cuba's declaration of independence, which Spain refused to recognize and violently suppressed
The Platt Amendment, which gave the United States the right to intervene in Cuban affairs
The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor, which was blamed on Spain and inflamed American public opinion

items.explanation: D is correct: The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor in February 1898, killing 266 sailors, was used by yellow journalists and interventionists to build public support for war with Spain. 'Remember the Maine!' became a rallying cry. Though the cause of the explosion was never definitively determined, American newspapers blamed Spain, and the outrage helped push Congress to declare war. A is incorrect: the Zimmermann Telegram involved Mexico and Germany during WWI, not the Spanish-American War. B is incorrect: Cuba was not yet independent; it was under Spanish colonial rule. C is incorrect: the Platt Amendment came after the war and governed U.S.-Cuba relations.

The war made the United States a colonial power in the Caribbean and the Pacific.
items.explanationEs: La Guerra Hispano-Estadounidense (1898) fue impulsada por el sensacionalismo de la prensa amarilla (Hearst, Pulitzer), la explosión del USS Maine en el puerto de La Habana (15 de febrero de 1898) y los intereses económicos y estratégicos de EE. UU. en Cuba. La Enmienda Teller renunció a la anexión de Cuba; el Tratado de París transfirió Puerto Rico, Guam y Filipinas. (Fuente: history.state.gov — Guerra Hispano-Estadounidense.)

items.stem: The Platt Amendment had which effect on U.S.-Cuban relations?

choices.text: It allowed the United States to intervene in Cuban affairs and limited Cuban sovereignty
It granted Cuba complete independence from American influence
It made Cuba an official U.S. state
It returned Cuba to Spanish colonial rule

items.explanation: The Platt Amendment (1901) set the conditions for withdrawing U.S. troops from Cuba: Cuba could not make treaties impairing its independence, had to allow the United States to intervene to preserve order, and had to lease naval stations, which produced the base at Guantanamo Bay. Choice B is wrong because the terms restricted Cuban sovereignty rather than granting full independence. Choice C is wrong because Cuba was never a state. The amendment shows how the United States exercised control without formal annexation.
items.explanationEs: El imperialismo estadounidense de finales del siglo XIX se justificó con una mezcla de motivos económicos (mercados, materias primas), estratégicos (bases navales, la tesis del poder marítimo de Mahan), ideología darwinista social y de jerarquía racial, y impulsos misioneros. La Liga Antiimperialista (1898), liderada por figuras como Mark Twain y Andrew Carnegie, se opuso a la anexión por motivos republicanos y morales. (Fuente: history.state.gov — Anexión de Hawái; LOC — Imperialismo estadounidense.)

items.stem: Wilson framed U.S. entry into World War I primarily as a fight to:

choices.text: Acquire new overseas colonies for the United States
Defend democracy and self-government internationally
Punish Mexico for the Zimmermann Telegram
Establish American economic dominance over Europe

items.explanation: Wilson cast the war as a defense of democratic self-government rather than a contest for territory or advantage, asking Congress for a war to make the world safe for democracy. Choice A is wrong because Wilson explicitly disclaimed territorial gain. Choice C is wrong because the Zimmermann Telegram was evidence of German hostility, not the object of the war. That framing carried into the Fourteen Points and his push for a League of Nations.
items.explanationEs: El sistema europeo de alianzas previo a la Primera Guerra Mundial unió a las grandes potencias en dos bloques opuestos: la Triple Alianza (Alemania, Austria-Hungría, Italia) y la Triple Entente (Gran Bretaña, Francia, Rusia). Cuando Austria-Hungría declaró la guerra a Serbia tras el asesinato de Francisco Fernando, las obligaciones de alianza desencadenaron una guerra continental en cuestión de semanas. (Fuente: LOC — Guía de investigación sobre la Primera Guerra Mundial.)

items.stem: Which economic motivation most directly drove the United States to pursue an imperial foreign policy in the late 19th century?

choices.text: The need to find new markets and sources of raw materials for American industrial production
The desire to establish military alliances with European colonial powers in Asia
The goal of providing land for American farmers who had lost their homesteads
The effort to reduce immigration by expanding American territory abroad

items.explanation: American industrialization created surplus goods and capital that required new overseas markets; simultaneously, industries needed raw materials not available domestically. These economic pressures were primary engines of late 19th-century imperialism alongside ideological motives.

items.stem: How did yellow journalism contribute to the growth of American imperialism in the 1890s?

choices.text: It provided factual reporting that convinced Congress to pass formal declarations of war against colonial powers
It inflamed public opinion by using sensationalized stories to build popular support for overseas intervention
It educated Americans about the economic benefits of free trade with Latin American nations
It persuaded business leaders to invest in domestic infrastructure rather than foreign territories

items.explanation: Yellow journalism, exemplified by Hearst and Pulitzer, used dramatic and often exaggerated reporting — particularly about Spanish atrocities in Cuba — to whip up public sentiment in favor of US military intervention, directly fueling imperialist momentum.

items.stem: Which belief best explains why many Americans in the late 1800s argued that the United States had a moral duty to expand its influence abroad?

choices.text: Americans believed foreign nations had already consented to US governance through trade agreements
Americans felt obligated to repay debts owed to European nations through territorial concessions
Americans were convinced that spreading democracy and civilization was a righteous responsibility of a superior nation
Americans wanted to prevent the spread of European socialism by building competing colonies

items.explanation: Influenced by Social Darwinism, the 'White Man's Burden' ideology, and thinkers like Alfred Thayer Mahan, many Americans believed the US had a divine or racial responsibility to spread democracy and civilization — a key ideological pillar of American imperialism.

items.stem: Which argument was most commonly used by non-interventionists to oppose American overseas expansion in the late 1800s and early 1900s?

choices.text: Foreign territories would drain military resources needed to defend the US mainland from invasion
Acquiring overseas colonies contradicted American democratic principles and the consent of the governed
Expanding into foreign markets would cause inflation that would hurt American consumers
Building a strong navy was unnecessary because the US had natural oceanic defenses

items.explanation: The core anti-imperialist argument, advanced by figures like Mark Twain and the Anti-Imperialist League, held that governing foreign peoples without their consent violated the foundational American principle of self-determination established in the Declaration of Independence.

items.stem: How did interventionists justify the acquisition of Pacific territories such as the Philippines in the 1890s?

choices.text: They argued Pacific territories were needed as coaling stations and strategic bases to project naval power in Asia
They claimed the Philippines had formally requested annexation through a popular vote of its citizens
They insisted that Pacific territories were necessary to prevent the spread of communism in Asia
They argued the US needed Pacific islands to resolve overcrowding in American cities

items.explanation: Alfred Thayer Mahan's sea power theory, widely embraced by interventionists, argued that Pacific island bases were strategically essential for refueling and resupplying naval vessels enabling the US to compete commercially and militarily in Asia.

items.stem: Which factor best explains why interventionist arguments gained more public support than non-interventionist arguments in the United States during the 1890s?

choices.text: Non-interventionists failed to organize any formal political opposition to imperialist policies
Non-interventionists were discredited after foreign powers invaded US territories in the Pacific
Most Americans believed non-interventionists were unpatriotic because they refused to support the military
Interventionists had the support of yellow journalism, economic interests, and popular ideas about national greatness

items.explanation: The combination of sensationalized press coverage, business community pressure for new markets, Social Darwinist ideology, and naval expansion arguments by Mahan gave interventionists a multi-front advantage in the public debate over expansion.

items.stem: How did the outcome of the Spanish-American War change the relationship between the United States and Latin America?

choices.text: The US withdrew from Latin American affairs and adopted a strict policy of non-interference
The US established itself as the dominant power in the Caribbean and asserted the right to intervene in the region
The US transferred control of Cuba and Puerto Rico to newly formed independent governments without conditions
The US formed a military alliance with Spain to jointly manage Caribbean territories

items.explanation: The Spanish-American War resulted in the US acquiring Puerto Rico and establishing the Platt Amendment over Cuba, positioning the US as the dominant Caribbean power and setting the stage for the Roosevelt Corollary's interventionist doctrine.

items.stem: Why was the construction of the Panama Canal significant for American foreign policy at the beginning of the 20th century?

choices.text: It allowed the US to avoid maintaining a naval presence in the Pacific Ocean
It reduced the need for overseas coaling stations by shortening transoceanic shipping distances
It gave the US a strategic shortcut connecting the Atlantic and Pacific, enabling rapid naval deployment and expanding commercial reach
It resolved the border dispute between Colombia and Panama without US military involvement

items.explanation: The Panama Canal was central to US strategic planning: it cut the sailing distance between US coasts by over 7,000 miles, allowing the Navy to move rapidly between oceans and strengthening US commercial and military power across both hemispheres.

items.stem: How did the Philippine Insurrection reveal a tension in American foreign policy following the Spanish-American War?

choices.text: It showed that the US lacked the military capacity to govern territories outside the Western Hemisphere
It revealed that yellow journalism had exaggerated the popularity of American rule in the Philippines
It proved that the US Senate was unwilling to fund overseas military operations for more than one year
It demonstrated a contradiction between American democratic ideals and the reality of suppressing a population seeking independence

items.explanation: Filipino resistance under Emilio Aguinaldo directly contradicted US claims of liberating the Philippines from Spain; the brutal suppression of the insurrection exposed the gap between American democratic rhetoric and colonial practice, energizing the Anti-Imperialist League.

items.stem: How did President Theodore Roosevelt's Big Stick diplomacy differ from President William Howard Taft's Dollar Diplomacy in its primary method of influencing other nations?

choices.text: Big Stick diplomacy relied primarily on military threats and force, while Dollar Diplomacy used American investment to secure US interests
Big Stick diplomacy focused on economic partnerships, while Dollar Diplomacy relied on moral persuasion and democratic ideals
Big Stick diplomacy was limited to Europe, while Dollar Diplomacy was applied exclusively in Asia
Big Stick diplomacy required congressional approval for each action, while Dollar Diplomacy operated through executive agreements

items.explanation: Roosevelt's Big Stick policy used the threat or use of military power to enforce US interests (e.g., Roosevelt Corollary interventions), while Taft's Dollar Diplomacy pursued US objectives by encouraging and protecting American financial investment in Latin America and Asia.

items.stem: Which characteristic best describes President Woodrow Wilson's Moral Diplomacy compared to the foreign policies of his predecessors Roosevelt and Taft?

choices.text: Wilson's approach relied entirely on trade sanctions to pressure foreign governments into reform
Wilson's approach prioritized military intervention over diplomatic negotiation in all foreign disputes
Wilson's approach emphasized withholding US recognition and support from governments that did not uphold democratic and moral principles
Wilson's approach sought to avoid any US involvement in Latin American affairs

items.explanation: Moral Diplomacy held that the US should only support governments that were democratic and morally aligned with American ideals, withholding recognition from authoritarian regimes — a contrast with Taft's financial approach and Roosevelt's power-based approach.

items.stem: A historian studying early 20th-century US foreign policy argues that all three diplomatic approaches — Big Stick, Dollar, and Moral — shared a common underlying goal. Which goal best supports this argument?

choices.text: All three policies sought to reduce US military spending by avoiding direct conflict
All three policies were designed to transfer governance of unstable nations to the United Nations
All three policies prioritized building formal military alliances with European democracies
All three policies aimed to extend and protect US influence and interests in Latin America and beyond

items.explanation: Despite their different methods — coercion, investment, and moral suasion — all three doctrines shared the underlying purpose of extending and protecting US strategic and economic influence, particularly in the Western Hemisphere.

items.stem: Which long-term cause of World War I best explains how a regional conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia rapidly expanded to involve most of Europe?

choices.text: Democratic governments across Europe were pressured by public opinion into declaring war within days of the crisis beginning
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand directly destroyed the peace treaties that had kept Europe stable for decades
Economic competition over African colonies had already brought European powers to the edge of war, making conflict inevitable
The system of interlocking alliances meant that a declaration of war by one power automatically drew in its treaty partners

items.explanation: The alliance system — Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) — created a chain reaction in which Austria-Hungary's declaration against Serbia triggered Russian mobilization, which activated German obligations, which drew in France and Britain.

items.stem: Why did the United States initially declare neutrality when World War I broke out in Europe in 1914?

choices.text: President Wilson believed the US military was too weak to participate effectively in a European war
The US had signed a formal neutrality treaty with both the Allied and Central Powers before the war began
The US had a strong tradition of avoiding entanglement in European conflicts, and Americans were divided in their loyalties due to diverse immigrant populations
Congress passed a constitutional amendment forbidding the president from entering foreign wars without a national referendum

items.explanation: US neutrality in 1914 reflected the Washington-Jefferson tradition of non-entanglement in European affairs, Wilson's 'peace without victory' idealism, and practical concern that siding with either alliance would alienate the millions of German-Americans, British-Americans, and other immigrants with divided loyalties.

items.stem: How did militarism contribute to the outbreak of World War I?

choices.text: European nations had built large armies and navies, creating an arms race that increased tensions and made military solutions more appealing to leaders
Military leaders in France and Britain organized a preemptive strike against Germany before the alliance system could be activated
The development of new weapons such as poison gas made European nations eager to test them before they became obsolete
Military spending caused economic collapse across Europe, forcing governments to seek resources through territorial conquest

items.explanation: Decades of competitive military build-up — especially the Anglo-German naval arms race — created mutual suspicion, mobilization plans, and a military culture that saw war as both inevitable and manageable, making diplomatic de-escalation in 1914 politically and logistically very difficult.

items.stem: How did trench warfare on the Western Front change the nature of combat compared to earlier 19th-century wars?

choices.text: Trench warfare enabled rapid advances by infantry units and led to the quick resolution of most battles
Trench warfare eliminated the need for artillery by providing soldiers with protected positions from which to fight
Trench warfare created a defensive stalemate in which millions of soldiers suffered massive casualties for minimal territorial gain
Trench warfare was only used on the Eastern Front and did not affect US soldiers fighting in France

items.explanation: Unlike the mobile warfare of 19th-century conflicts, WWI's Western Front settled into years of entrenched stalemate in which machine guns, barbed wire, and artillery combined to make offensive advances catastrophically costly with negligible territorial gains.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Harlem Hell Fighters' service in World War I?

choices.text: They were the first African American unit granted full officer commissions in the US Army during the war
They were formed as a result of a congressional mandate requiring racial integration of all combat units
They were assigned exclusively to supply and support roles because the US military doubted their combat ability
They served under French command, fought with distinction, and challenged the racial segregation that limited African American soldiers in the American military

items.explanation: The 369th Infantry Regiment served 191 days in combat under French command (longer than any other American unit), won numerous Croix de Guerre medals, and became a symbol of African American patriotism and the injustice of segregation in their own nation's military.

items.stem: How did new weapons technology introduced during World War I change the experience of soldiers on the battlefield?

choices.text: New weapons, including poison gas, tanks, and aircraft, increased the lethality of combat and made traditional cavalry charges obsolete
New weapons technology allowed soldiers to communicate more effectively and reduced the overall number of battlefield casualties
The introduction of the machine gun was the only significant technological change from previous wars
New weapons technology allowed infantry to advance rapidly across open ground without the need for artillery support

items.explanation: WWI introduced poison gas (chlorine, mustard gas), tanks, aircraft, long-range artillery, and the dominant machine gun into large-scale combat, making open-field infantry charges suicidal and rendering horse cavalry essentially obsolete as a tactical force.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The 1898 cartoon 'The Duty of the Hour' shows Uncle Sam rolling up his sleeves, preparing for military action. The cartoon reflects expansionist sentiment arguing it was America's duty to intervene in Cuba and the Philippines during the Spanish-American War.

The phrase 'Duty of the Hour' in the cartoon's title most directly reflects which justification for American intervention in 1898?

choices.text: American businesses needed the U.S. military to protect their financial investments in Cuba
The United States had a moral obligation to liberate oppressed peoples from European colonial rule
Spain had directly attacked American territory, making U.S. military response a matter of national defense
The United States wanted to end the practice of slavery in Spanish-controlled territories

items.explanation: B is correct: The 'duty' framing reflects the idea of humanitarian or moral obligation — that the United States had a responsibility to liberate Cuba from Spanish oppression (and later to 'civilize' the Philippines). This moral justification, combined with expansionist ideology like Manifest Destiny extended overseas, was a key argument used by interventionists in 1898. A is incorrect: while economic interests were a factor, the 'duty' language specifically frames intervention in moral and humanitarian terms. C is incorrect: the cartoon reflects enthusiasm for intervention, not reluctant defense. D is incorrect: the Spanish-American War was not primarily about slavery but about colonial control and national independence movements.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows Theodore Roosevelt and the Rough Riders in Cuba, 1898.

(Photograph, 1898. Public Domain.)

How did the Spanish-American War, in which the soldiers shown in this photograph fought, change the role of the United States in world affairs?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo cambió la Guerra Hispanoamericana el papel de Estados Unidos en los asuntos mundiales?

choices.text: The United States emerged as an imperial power with overseas territories including Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines
The war ended American involvement in foreign affairs for the next two decades
Spain gained control of additional territories in the Caribbean as a result of the war
The war had no significant impact on American foreign policy

items.explanation: The Spanish-American War (1898) marked the emergence of the United States as a world power. Victory gave the U.S. control of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and established American influence over Cuba. The war signaled a shift from continental expansion to overseas imperialism.
items.explanationEs: La Guerra Hispanoamericana marcó la emergencia de EE.UU. como potencia mundial con territorios ultramarinos.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows Panama Canal construction, c. 1910.

(Photograph, c. 1910. Public Domain.)

How did the construction of the Panama Canal, shown in this photograph, serve the strategic and economic interests of the United States?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo sirvió la construcción del Canal de Panamá a los intereses estratégicos y económicos de EE.UU.?

choices.text: It allowed the U.S. to control all trade routes between Europe and Asia
It was built primarily to benefit the people of Panama and Central America
It dramatically reduced naval transit times between the Atlantic and Pacific and lowered shipping costs for American commerce
It replaced the need for a strong American navy in the Western Hemisphere

items.explanation: The Panama Canal cut the maritime journey between the Atlantic and Pacific from approximately 13,000 miles (around Cape Horn) to about 50 miles through the canal. This reduced naval response times, lowered commercial shipping costs, and strengthened U.S. economic and military dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
items.explanationEs: El canal redujo drásticamente los tiempos de tránsito naval y costos de envío, fortaleciendo el dominio estadounidense.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows workers on the Ford assembly line at Highland Park Plant, c. 1913.

(Photograph, c. 1913. Public Domain.)

How did the manufacturing method shown in this photograph transform the American economy in the early twentieth century?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo transformó el método de fabricación mostrado en esta fotografía la economía estadounidense?

choices.text: It decreased production because workers moved more slowly at fixed stations
It lowered production costs, made consumer goods affordable to the middle class, and expanded industrial employment
It benefited only wealthy factory owners while wages for workers declined significantly
It replaced all factory workers with machines, causing massive unemployment

items.explanation: The assembly line dramatically cut production costs, allowing Ford to reduce the Model T's price from $850 to under $300. This made automobiles and other consumer goods accessible to average Americans, fueling the consumer economy of the 1920s.
items.explanationEs: La línea de ensamblaje redujo costos de producción, haciendo los bienes de consumo accesibles a la clase media.

items.stem: Which of Wilson's Fourteen Points most directly reflected his desire to prevent future wars by giving people the right to determine their own political future?

choices.text: Freedom of the seas
Reduction of armaments among all nations
The principle of self-determination for ethnic and national groups
The establishment of a general association of nations

items.explanation: Self-determination — the principle that ethnic and national groups should have the right to form their own governments — was Wilson's response to the multi-ethnic empires (Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian) that had collapsed during the war and whose forced unity had contributed to instability.

items.stem: Why did the United States Senate reject American membership in the League of Nations following World War I?

choices.text: Senators feared that League membership would require the US to commit troops to future conflicts without a congressional declaration of war
Senators believed the League would give the United States too much control over European nations and their internal affairs
Senators rejected the League because it did not include Germany as a founding member, making it an ineffective peace organization
Senators opposed the League because it required the US to maintain a permanent military base in Geneva, Switzerland

items.explanation: Led by Henry Cabot Lodge, Senate opponents — 'Reservationists' and 'Irreconcilables' — argued that Article X of the League Covenant would obligate the US to defend any League member against aggression, bypassing Congress's constitutional war-making power.

items.stem: Which feature of the Treaty of Versailles conflicted most directly with Wilson's peace vision?
items.stemEs: Which feature of the tratado of Versailles conflicted most directly with Wilson's peace vision?

choices.text: Punitive reparations and war-guilt terms imposed on Germany
choices.textEs: Punitive reparations and war-guilt terms imposed on Germany

choices.text: To build a lasting peace based on open diplomacy and self-determination
choices.textEs: To build a lasting peace based on open diplomacia and self-determination

choices.text: Americans looked overseas for new opportunities and markets
choices.textEs: Americans looked overseas for new opportunities and markets

choices.text: Britain, France, Russia, Italy, and later the United States
choices.textEs: Britain, France, Russia, Italy, and later the United States

items.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles clashed with Wilson's peace vision because it punished Germany with war-guilt language and heavy reparations instead of emphasizing reconciliation and self-determination. Choice B states Wilson's own goal rather than the treaty's conflicting feature, and choice D just lists Allied powers. This conflict showed how the postwar settlement moved away from Wilson's idealism toward revenge and power politics.
items.explanationEs: The tratado of Versailles clashed with Wilson's peace vision because it punished Germany with war-guilt language and heavy reparations instead of emphasizing reconciliation and self-determination. Choice B states Wilson's own goal rather than the tratado's conflicting feature, and choice D just lists Allied powers. This conflict showed how the postwar settlement moved away from Wilson's idealism toward revenge and power politics.

items.stem: Why did many U.S. senators oppose joining the League of Nations?
items.stemEs: ¿Por qué many U.S. senators oppose joining the League of Nations?

choices.text: They feared Article X could commit the U.S. to conflicts without congressional approval
choices.textEs: They feared Article X could commit the U.S. to conflicts without Congresoional approval

choices.text: It weakened collective security by removing a major economic and military power
choices.textEs: It weakened collective security by removing a major economic and military power

choices.text: It reflected a conflict between international cooperation and preserving U.S. foreign-policy autonomy
choices.textEs: It reflected a conflict between international cooperation and preserving U.S. foreign-policy autonomy

choices.text: Practical politics and national interests limited the implementation of Wilson's ideals
choices.textEs: Practical politics and national interests limited the implementation of Wilson's ideals

items.explanation: Many senators opposed the League of Nations because Article X seemed to risk pulling the United States into foreign conflicts without a separate decision by Congress. Choice B describes the effect of rejecting the League, not the reason senators gave, and choice C summarizes the broader debate rather than the specific objection. The fight reflected a lasting tension between international cooperation and American control over foreign policy.
items.explanationEs: Many senators opposed the League of Nations because Article X seemed to risk pulling the United States into foreign conflicts without a separate decision by Congreso. Choice B describes the effect of rejecting the League, not the reason senators gave, and choice C summarizes the broader debate rather than the specific objection. The fight reflected a lasting tension between international cooperation and American control over política exterior.

items.stem: U.S. rejection of the League of Nations contributed to which outcome?
items.stemEs: U.S. rejection of the League of Nations contribuyó a which outcome?

choices.text: European nations forming their own military alliances that led to WWII
choices.textEs: European nations forming their own military alianzas that condujo a WWII

choices.text: Britain and France refusing to cooperate with the United States on economic matters
choices.textEs: Britain and France refusing to cooperate with the United States on economic matters

choices.text: Germany immediately repudiating the Versailles Treaty reparations
choices.textEs: Germany immediately repudiating the Versailles tratado reparations

choices.text: The League's failure to prevent Japanese aggression in Manchuria in 1931
choices.textEs: The League's failure to prevent Japanese aggression in Manchuria in 1931

items.explanation: When the United States stayed out of the League of Nations, it weakened the new organization's credibility and removed a major economic and military power from collective security efforts. Choice B explains why some senators opposed the League, but the question asks about the effect of rejection, not the reason for it. That decision helped push the United States toward a more limited role in postwar international politics.
items.explanationEs: When the United States stayed out of the League of Nations, it weakened the new organization's credibility and removed a major economic and military power from collective security efforts. Choice B explains why some senators opposed the League, but the question asks about the effect of rejection, not the reason for it. That decision helped push the United States toward a more limited role in postwar international politics.

items.stem: How did American imperialism contradict the principles established in the Declaration of Independence?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo contradijo el imperialismo estadounidense los principios establecidos en la Declaración de Independencia?

choices.text: Governing peoples without consent violated core principles
choices.textEs: Gobernar pueblos sin su consentimiento violaba la autodeterminación e igualdad

choices.text: Rulings that territories lacked full constitutional rights
choices.textEs: El imperialismo se alineaba perfectamente con los principios fundacionales estadounidenses

choices.text: Chinese nationalists who opposed foreign influence in China
choices.textEs: La Declaración apoyaba la expansión colonial

choices.text: Colonial administration would be costly and drain resources
choices.textEs: No existía contradicción entre el imperialismo y los valores estadounidenses

items.explanation: Governing peoples without consent violated core principles, and the correct choice matches the main historical idea, event, or policy named in the question. Choice B talks about rulings that territories lacked full constitutional rights, but that describes rulings that territories lacked full constitutional rights, not the main idea in the question; Choice C talks about chinese nationalists who opposed foreign influence in China, but that refers to the Boxer Rebellion in China, not the main idea in the question. This fits the larger story of how World War I reshaped life on the home front and expanded federal power.
items.explanationEs: La Declaración afirmaba que "todos los hombres son creados iguales" con derechos a "vida, libertad y búsqueda de la felicidad". Gobernar colonias sin consentimiento contradecía estos ideales, un punto fuertemente hecho por los anti-imperialistas.

items.stem: How did American imperialism reflect both economic interests and ideological beliefs?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo reflejó el imperialismo estadounidense tanto intereses económicos como creencias ideológicas?

choices.text: A policy ensuring all nations had equal trading access in China
choices.textEs: Solo motivos económicos impulsaron la expansión sin componente ideológico

choices.text: Businesses sought profits while others promoted racial missions
choices.textEs: Las empresas buscaron ganancias mientras los ideólogos promovieron misiones civilizadoras y superioridad racial

choices.text: It provided valuable natural resources and strategic location
choices.textEs: Solo importaba la ideología sin buscar beneficios económicos

choices.text: Promoting democracy and moral principles in foreign relations
choices.textEs: Ni la economía ni la ideología influyeron en el imperialismo

items.explanation: Businesses sought profits while others promoted racial missions, and the correct choice matches the main historical idea, event, or policy named in the question. Choice A talks about a policy ensuring all nations had equal trading access in China, but that is the Open Door Policy, which dealt with trade in China, not the main idea in the question; Choice C talks about it provided valuable natural resources and strategic location, but that describes it provided valuable natural resources and strategic location, not the main idea in the question. This shows how the United States moved from continental expansion to a more active overseas empire at the turn of the 20th century.
items.explanationEs: El imperialismo estadounidense combinó objetivos económicos prácticos (mercados, recursos, bases navales) con justificaciones ideológicas (darwinismo social, "Carga del Hombre Blanco

items.stem: Analyze how the alliance system contributed to the outbreak of World War I:
items.stemEs: Analice cómo el sistema de alianzas contribuyó al estallido de la Primera Guerra Mundial:

choices.text: Take an active role in world affairs to protect American interests
choices.textEs: Las alianzas previnieron la guerra al crear un equilibrio de poder en Europa

choices.text: Mutual defense agreements turned a regional conflict into a world war
choices.textEs: Los acuerdos de defensa mutua convirtieron un conflicto regional en una guerra mundial

choices.text: Violate American democratic principles and lead to foreign entanglements
choices.textEs: Los miembros de las alianzas se negaron a honrar sus obligaciones del tratado

choices.text: It gave the U.S. the right to intervene and maintain a naval base
choices.textEs: El sistema de alianzas no tuvo impacto significativo en el inicio de la guerra

items.explanation: Mutual defense agreements turned a regional conflict into a world war, and the correct choice matches the main historical idea, event, or policy named in the question. Choice A talks about take an active role in world affairs to protect American interests, but that describes a different law or court ruling, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation; Choice C talks about violate American democratic principles and lead to foreign entanglements, but that describes violate American democratic principles and lead to foreign entanglements, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation. This helps explain how a regional crisis in Europe grew into a global war that eventually drew in the United States.
items.explanationEs: La red de alianzas significó que cuando Austria-Hungría declaró la guerra a Serbia, Rusia se movilizó para defender a Serbia, Alemania declaró la guerra a Rusia y Francia, y Gran Bretaña entró para honrar su alianza con Francia y Bélgica.

items.stem: Evaluate the factors that led President Wilson to ask Congress for a declaration of war in 1917:
items.stemEs: Evalúe los factores que llevaron al Presidente Wilson a pedir al Congreso una declaración de guerra en 1917:

choices.text: Roosevelt emphasized military power, Taft focused on economic influence, and Wilson promoted democratic ideals
choices.textEs: Solo la presión pública obligó a Wilson a abandonar su política de neutralidad

choices.text: Long argued the New Deal did too little for the poor; the Court argued it exceeded constitutional authority
choices.textEs: Los gobiernos aliados amenazaron con atacar a Estados Unidos si permanecía neutral

choices.text: One has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, but must accept the legal consequences to demonstrate the injustice
choices.textEs: Las consideraciones económicas fueron el único factor en la decisión de Wilson

choices.text: Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram convinced Wilson that war was necessary
choices.textEs: La reanudación de la guerra submarina sin restricciones por Alemania y el Telegrama Zimmermann convencieron a Wilson de que la guerra era necesaria

items.stem: Explain how the Dust Bowl was both a natural disaster AND a human-caused environmental crisis. Provide specific evidence for each dimension.
items.stemEs: Explique cómo el Dust Bowl fue TANTO un desastre natural COMO una crisis ambiental causada por el ser humano. Proporcione evidencia específica para cada dimensión.
items.correctAnswer: Natural factors: severe drought across the Great Plains in the 1930s, high winds. Human factors: decades of deep plowing destroyed native grassland root systems that held topsoil in place; Homestead Act encouraged farming unsuitable land; mechanized farming amplified soil destruction. The combination turned drought into catastrophe — 2.5 million people displaced.
items.explanation: The Dust Bowl grew out of both nature and human choices: severe drought and high winds struck the Great Plains, but deep plowing had already torn up the native grasses that held the soil in place. A strong answer should separate the natural causes from the human causes and use details like drought, high winds, overplowing, and the loss of grass roots that held topsoil in place. These changes revealed how the 1920s mixed cultural innovation with sharp social conflict and inequality.

choices.textEs: Wilson's Fourteen Points were fully implemented at Versailles and the tratado would have produced lasting peace had the U.S. Senado ratified it

items.explanation: Wilson achieved some goals — the League of Nations, national self-determination for some peoples, open diplomacy — but Allied leaders Clemenceau and Lloyd George used their leverage to impose punitive measures on Germany that violated Wilson's principles, leaving Wilson with a deeply flawed treaty that was neither his vision nor an effective peace, and wilson wanted nations to use collective security so aggression against one member would concern all the others. Choice D talks about wilson's Fourteen Points were fully implemented at Versailles and the treaty would have produced lasting peace had the U.S. Senate ratified it, but that describes Wilson’s Fourteen Points, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation; Choice B talks about wilson substantially failed at Versailles since none of the Fourteen Points were reflected in the final treaty, but that describes Wilson’s Fourteen Points, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation. It also shows how difficult it was to turn wartime ideals into a stable postwar peace.
items.explanationEs: Wilson achieved some goals — the League of Nations, national self-determination for some peoples, open diplomacia — but Allied leaders Clemenceau and Lloyd George used their leverage to impose punitive measures on Germany that violated Wilson's principles, leaving Wilson with a deeply flawed tratado that was neither his vision nor an effective peace, and wilson wanted nations to use collective security so aggression against one member would concern all the others. Choice D talks about wilson's Fourteen Points were fully implemented at Versailles and the tratado would have produced lasting peace had the U.S. Senado ratified it, but that describes Wilson’s Fourteen Points, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation; Choice B talks about wilson substantially failed at Versailles since none of the Fourteen Points were reflected in the final tratado, but that describes Wilson’s Fourteen Points, not the interpretation that best fits the historical situation. It also shows how difficult it was to turn wartime ideals into a stable postwar peace.

items.stem: Design a "New Deal Report Card" that grades THREE specific programs on two criteria: (1) effectiveness in addressing the immediate crisis, and (2) long-term impact on American government and society. For each program, assign a letter grade (A-F) for each criterion and justify your grading with specific historical evidence.
