items.stem: Beveridge's argument in this excerpt is best described as a defense of:

choices.text: American isolationism in foreign affairs
American imperialism and overseas expansion
Free trade with European nations
Reduction of the U.S. military budget

items.explanation: Albert Beveridge argued that the United States had a duty and a destiny to govern overseas territory, using expansion and trade as evidence — a direct defense of American imperialism. Choice A is wrong because isolationism is the position he was arguing against. Choice C is wrong because his subject was territorial and strategic expansion, not tariff policy. Beveridge's speeches are the standard example of the expansionist case that the Anti-Imperialist League opposed.
items.explanationEs: La Política de Puertas Abiertas (1899-1900), articulada por el secretario de Estado John Hay, afirmó el interés de EE. UU. en el acceso comercial igualitario a China para todas las naciones y la oposición a su división en esferas de influencia europeas. Se entiende mejor como una estrategia de imperialismo económico que protegía el comercio estadounidense sin requerir colonización formal. (Fuente: history.state.gov — Hay y la Puerta Abierta en China.)

items.stem: Based on the map, what was a primary strategic and economic benefit of the Panama Canal for the United States?

choices.text: It significantly shortened shipping routes between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts
It opened direct U.S. trade with Africa for the first time
It allowed the United States to claim South American territory
It eliminated the need for a U.S. Navy in the Atlantic Ocean

items.explanation: The canal let ships move between the Atlantic and Pacific without rounding South America, cutting thousands of miles from the voyage and letting the Navy shift fleets between oceans quickly. Choice B is wrong because the canal linked the Americas, not the United States and Africa. Choice D is wrong because a shorter route made the Atlantic fleet more useful, not unnecessary. Speed of naval movement was the strategic argument that made the canal a national priority.
items.explanationEs: La política de Theodore Roosevelt en Panamá combinó el apoyo a la independencia panameña de Colombia (1903), el Tratado Hay-Bunau-Varilla que otorgó a EE. UU. derechos sobre el canal y la afirmación del «gran garrote» del poder hemisférico estadounidense. El canal se abrió al tráfico el 15 de agosto de 1914. (Fuente: history.state.gov — Construcción del Canal de Panamá.)

items.stem: The release of this telegram in February 1917 contributed most directly to which decision?

choices.text: Mexico's declaration of war against the United States
The U.S. decision to enter World War I against Germany
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The passage of the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s

items.explanation: The Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany proposed a Mexican alliance and the recovery of territory lost to the United States, was published in early 1917 and hardened American opinion toward the war Congress declared that April. Choice A is wrong because Mexico declined the proposal and did not declare war. Choice C is wrong because the Treaty of Versailles came in 1919, after the fighting ended. Together with unrestricted submarine warfare, the telegram made continued neutrality untenable.
items.explanationEs: El Corolario Roosevelt (diciembre de 1904) amplió la Doctrina Monroe al afirmar la autoridad de EE. UU. para intervenir en los Estados de América Latina con inestabilidad financiera o política crónica a fin de prevenir la intervención europea. Se utilizó para justificar la administración de aduanas en la República Dominicana (1905) e intervenciones posteriores. (Fuente: history.state.gov — Roosevelt y la Doctrina Monroe.)

items.stem: Following the Spanish-American War, the Supreme Court's Insular Cases (1901) ruled that the Constitution did not automatically apply in full to newly acquired territories like the Philippines and Puerto Rico. How does the Court's creation of 'unincorporated territory' status expose a fundamental tension within American democratic principles?

choices.text: The Supreme Court correctly ruled that all territories eventually incorporated into the United States would receive full constitutional protections, making the unincorporated status a temporary practical arrangement rather than a permanent denial of rights.

The decisions revealed that Congress had overstepped its constitutional authority by acquiring overseas territories without clear authorization, forcing the Court to construct an ad hoc legal framework to manage a fundamentally unconstitutional expansion of American jurisdiction.

By ruling that the Constitution did not automatically follow the flag into unincorporated territories, the Court created a category of people subject to American governance and taxation without the constitutional protections that governance is supposed to guarantee — directly contradicting the founding principle that just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed

The Insular Cases resolved the constitutional question cleanly by treating newly acquired territories as sovereign entities in a special protective relationship with the United States, allowing flexible governance without triggering the full constitutional obligations attached to formal American territories.

items.explanation: The Insular Cases created a constitutionally anomalous situation in which millions of people came under permanent American governmental authority without receiving the full constitutional protections American governance was theoretically founded upon, exposing a contradiction between democratic ideology and imperial governance.

items.stem: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) replaced selection of senators by state legislatures with their direct election by voters, reversing the original constitutional design. Which argument provides the strongest democratic theory justification for this fundamental change in how the upper chamber of Congress was constituted?

choices.text: Direct election was constitutionally necessary because state legislatures had repeatedly failed to fill Senate vacancies in a timely manner, creating governing crises when senators died or resigned mid-term.

Corporate domination of state legislatures had made Senate seats effectively purchasable by concentrated economic interests, and direct election was intended to restore competitive democratic politics by giving ordinary voters a mechanism to challenge entrenched corporate power.

By removing the Senate from state government influence, the Seventeenth Amendment advanced a nationalist constitutional vision in which citizens related directly to federal institutions rather than through state political machines as intermediary layers of accountability.

The original constitutional assumption that state legislatures would reliably represent their constituents had been invalidated by machine politics and corporate corruption, making direct election the only available mechanism for restoring the functional popular sovereignty that republican government requires as its legitimating foundation.

items.explanation: The strongest democratic theory argument for the Seventeenth Amendment was that the original system had lost its functional legitimacy: state legislatures captured by machine politicians and corporate interests were no longer producing senators who represented the will of state citizens, undermining the representative republican principle the original design was meant to serve.

items.stem: The women's suffrage movement employed two parallel strategies by 1910: a state-by-state campaign that had achieved full suffrage in several Western states and a federal amendment campaign. What does the movement's eventual success through the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920 most clearly reveal about the relationship between state-level reform and national constitutional change?

choices.text: State-level victories demonstrated that women's suffrage was politically viable and did not disrupt the social order, building an evidentiary foundation that a federal constitutional amendment could be safely ratified — showing that subnational experimentation can generate the political conditions necessary for national constitutional reform.

The federal strategy succeeded primarily because Progressive-era politicians recognized that women's moral authority was needed to advance Prohibition and other social reform measures, meaning the Nineteenth Amendment was granted instrumentally rather than as a principled recognition of democratic equality.

The state-by-state strategy ultimately failed to produce sufficient momentum for a constitutional amendment, demonstrating that federalist approaches to expanding civil rights are structurally inadequate compared to direct federal intervention when opponents can block progress state by state.

The amendment's ratification demonstrated that constitutional change requires near-unanimous national consensus before succeeding, as the suffrage movement achieved federal victory only after opposition had essentially collapsed in the years immediately following World War I.

items.explanation: Western state experiments with women's suffrage provided crucial empirical evidence that feared social consequences had not materialized, giving federal amendment advocates a powerful practical argument that transformed the debate from speculation about consequences to evaluation of demonstrated outcomes.

items.stem: African American women leaders including Ida B. Wells and Mary Church Terrell supported women's suffrage but faced exclusion and deliberate marginalization from mainstream white suffrage organizations that accommodated Southern racial segregation to maintain political viability. What does this tension within the suffrage movement most clearly reveal about the meaning of 'democracy' and 'equality' in the Progressive Era?

choices.text: The marginalization of Black women proves that the Progressive Era's democratic ideals were entirely and uniformly hypocritical, as white reformers consistently chose racial hierarchy over democratic inclusion every time the two goals came into conflict.

The suffrage movement's racial politics accurately reflected the broader Progressive Era pattern of treating reform as a project that would primarily benefit white Americans, demonstrating that expanding democracy for white women was politically and strategically compatible with maintaining white supremacy as a governing principle.

Because Black women faced both racial and gender discrimination simultaneously, their exclusion reveals that intersectional oppression required distinctly different organizing approaches, which is why Black women founded separate organizations like the National Association of Colored Women rather than fighting for inclusion within majority-white reform institutions.

The suffrage movement's accommodation of Southern racism illustrates that democratic movements operating within a racist society frequently reproduce that society's racial hierarchies — suggesting that formal democratic gains such as the vote can coexist with and even structurally require the exclusion of the most politically marginalized groups.

items.explanation: The exclusion of Black women from mainstream suffrage organizations reveals that 'democracy' in the Progressive Era was a bounded concept: the movement's white leadership treated democratic inclusion as divisible, exposing the degree to which race structured even reform-minded Americans' understanding of who counted as a full democratic participant. Unit 4: The Roaring 20s, 1920–1929 (US.28–US.38)

items.stem: The Red Scare of 1919–1920 most directly illustrates which recurring pattern in American political history?

choices.text: Economic prosperity typically produces political tolerance of radical and dissenting ideas.
Foreign policy crises consistently cause Americans to restrict immigration from all parts of the world equally.
Periods of social and economic anxiety can produce widespread suppression of civil liberties in the name of national security.
Labor strikes are most politically effective when they occur during periods of broad social unrest.

items.explanation: The Palmer Raids, deportation of suspected radicals, and suppression of labor and socialist organizations during the Red Scare demonstrate that anxieties about economic disruption and foreign ideology can rapidly erode civil liberties protections.

items.stem: Which conclusion about the Harlem Renaissance is best supported by its emergence in New York City during the 1920s?

choices.text: African American cultural expression flourished most in regions where state-level racial segregation laws were entirely absent.
The Great Migration created concentrated African American communities in Northern cities that became centers of cultural and intellectual achievement.
African American artists deliberately rejected Southern cultural and musical traditions in favor of European artistic forms.
The economic prosperity of the 1920s provided African Americans equal access to economic opportunity for the first time since Reconstruction.

items.explanation: The Great Migration (1910–1970) relocated hundreds of thousands of African Americans to Northern cities. Harlem became a destination for Black intellectuals, artists, and writers, and its concentrated community enabled the cultural flowering known as the Harlem Renaissance.

items.stem: Which best explains how the expansion of consumer credit in the 1920s contributed to the economic vulnerability that preceded the Great Depression? H Consumer credit allowed workers to purchase goods they could not immediately afford, but created unsustainable household debt that collapsed purchasing power when the economy contracted. B. Consumer credit enabled small businesses to expand rapidly, creating regional monopolies that drove down wages across multiple industries. C. Consumer credit was used primarily by farmers to purchase mechanized equipment, making the agricultural sector disproportionately responsible for the Depression. D. Consumer credit reduced Americans' reliance on savings accounts before the crash, which is why bank failures spread so quickly in 1929. CORRECT ANSWER

choices.text: Consumer credit allowed workers to purchase goods they could not immediately afford, but created unsustainable household debt that collapsed purchasing power when the economy contracted.
Consumer credit enabled small businesses to expand rapidly, creating regional monopolies that drove down wages across multiple industries.
Consumer credit was used primarily by farmers to purchase mechanized equipment, making the agricultural sector disproportionately responsible for the Depression.
Consumer credit reduced Americans' reliance on savings accounts before the crash, which is why bank failures spread so quickly in 1929.

items.explanation: Installment buying allowed American consumers to purchase radios, cars, and appliances on credit. When the economy contracted and unemployment rose, those debts became unpayable, collapsing consumer demand in a destructive cycle.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The 1898 cartoon shows Uncle Sam preparing for military action and frames U.S. intervention as a 'duty.' It was published during the build-up to the Spanish-American War and reflects the expansionist mood of the era.

Historians often argue that yellow journalism played a key role in bringing about the Spanish-American War. Based on the cartoon and your knowledge of the period, which of the following best describes yellow journalism's role in the conflict?

choices.text: It used sensationalized reporting and exaggerated Spanish atrocities to inflame American public opinion and build support for war
It accurately documented Spanish abuses in Cuba while arguing the United States should resolve the conflict through diplomacy
It reported on the USS Maine explosion with careful investigation before concluding Spain was responsible
It persuaded Spain to miscalculate American military strength, causing Spain to make aggressive moves that started the war

items.explanation: A is correct: Yellow journalism, practiced by newspapers like William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal and Joseph Pulitzer's New York World, used sensationalized, often exaggerated or fabricated stories about Spanish atrocities in Cuba to inflame American public opinion and build support for war. Their coverage of events like the USS Maine explosion ('Remember the Maine!') helped create the popular pressure that moved Congress to declare war. B is incorrect: yellow journalists supported intervention; they did not oppose it or favor diplomacy. C is incorrect: yellow journalists were not interested in presenting balanced reporting or calming tensions. D is incorrect: yellow journalism was a domestic phenomenon — it shaped American public opinion, not Spanish military strategy.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows the Rough Riders in Cuba, 1898.

(Photograph, 1898. Public Domain.)

Evaluate the extent to which the Spanish-American War represented a turning point in United States foreign policy.
items.stemEs: Evalúe en qué medida la Guerra Hispanoamericana representó un punto de inflexión en la política exterior de EE.UU.

choices.text: The war was not a turning point because the United States had always been an imperial power with overseas colonies
The war ended American expansionism permanently and led to a policy of strict isolationism
The war only affected relations with Spain and had no broader implications for American foreign policy
The war marked a fundamental shift from continental expansion to overseas imperialism, establishing the U.S. as a global power with strategic territories across the Pacific and Caribbean

items.explanation: The Spanish-American War was a pivotal turning point. Before 1898, U.S. expansion was primarily continental. After the war, the U.S. held overseas territories, built the Panama Canal, asserted the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, and projected military power globally — fundamentally redefining America's role in international affairs.
items.explanationEs: La guerra fue un punto de inflexión de la expansión continental al imperialismo ultramarino.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows the excavation of the Culebra Cut during Panama Canal construction.

(Photograph, c. 1910. Public Domain.)

Analyze how the construction of the Panama Canal reflected the principles of Theodore Roosevelt's approach to foreign policy.
items.stemEs: Analice cómo la construcción del Canal de Panamá reflejó los principios de la política exterior de Theodore Roosevelt.

choices.text: Roosevelt's 'Big Stick' diplomacy combined military readiness with assertive action, as seen in his support for Panamanian independence and unilateral canal construction
Roosevelt preferred diplomatic negotiation over action, as shown by his patient 20-year effort to gain permission from Colombia
The canal project demonstrated Roosevelt's isolationist beliefs and reluctance to engage in foreign affairs
Roosevelt opposed the canal but was overruled by Congress, which funded the project independently

items.explanation: The Panama Canal epitomized Roosevelt's 'Big Stick' diplomacy: he supported Panama's secession from Colombia when Colombia rejected a canal treaty, quickly recognized the new nation, secured canal rights, and deployed American engineers and military resources. This assertive, action-oriented approach defined Roosevelt's foreign policy and expanded American influence throughout the Western Hemisphere via the Roosevelt Corollary.
items.explanationEs: El canal ejemplificó la diplomacia del 'Gran Garrote' de Roosevelt: acción asertiva combinada con preparación militar.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows workers on the Ford assembly line, c. 1913.

(Photograph, c. 1913. Public Domain.)

To what extent did mass production methods like those shown in this photograph create BOTH prosperity and new social challenges in American society?
items.stemEs: ¿En qué medida los métodos de producción en masa crearon TANTO prosperidad como nuevos desafíos sociales?

choices.text: Mass production only benefited consumers and had no negative effects on workers
Mass production destroyed small businesses without creating any new economic opportunities
Mass production was limited to the automobile industry and did not spread to other sectors
Mass production drove economic growth and consumer culture while also creating repetitive, dehumanizing work conditions that fueled labor organizing

items.explanation: Mass production created enormous prosperity — lower prices, more consumer goods, economic growth — but also introduced monotonous, physically demanding assembly line work. This tension fueled labor movements, with workers seeking higher wages and better conditions even as they benefited from cheaper goods.
items.explanationEs: La producción en masa generó prosperidad pero también trabajo repetitivo y deshumanizante que impulsó el movimiento obrero.

items.stem: Lodge's primary objection in this excerpt was that the League of Nations would:

choices.text: Strengthen American isolation from European affairs
Compromise U.S. sovereignty by drawing the country into foreign conflicts
Lower tariffs on European imported goods
Require the United States to abolish its standing army

items.explanation: Henry Cabot Lodge objected that League membership, especially the collective-security obligation in Article X, would draw the United States into foreign conflicts without a decision by Congress, surrendering part of its sovereignty. Choice A is wrong because he argued the League would entangle the country, not isolate it. Choice C is wrong because tariffs were not his objection. Wilson refused to accept Lodge's reservations, and the Senate rejected the treaty.
items.explanationEs: Las reservas del senador Henry Cabot Lodge a la Sociedad de Naciones se centraron en el Artículo X, que según él comprometería a Estados Unidos a una acción militar sin aprobación del Congreso, vulnerando el poder constitucional de declarar la guerra. Las «Reservas» de Lodge habrían preservado la autonomía de EE. UU. en sus compromisos exteriores; Wilson se negó a transigir y el Senado rechazó el tratado en marzo de 1920. (Fuente: LOC — Chronicling America: debate sobre la Sociedad de Naciones.)

items.stem: The Committee on Public Information (1917) used propaganda, voluntary press censorship agreements, and community informant networks to manage American public opinion during World War I. How does the CPI's systematic approach to information control represent a significant departure from traditional American norms regarding free expression and the role of government communication?

choices.text: The CPI's activities were constitutionally permissible as subsequently confirmed by the Supreme Court in Schenck v. United States, demonstrating that free speech protections could be legally suspended during wartime emergencies when expression presented a clear and present danger to national security.

By creating a government apparatus to manufacture consent for the war rather than allowing public opinion to form through open debate among competing viewpoints, the CPI established a precedent that democratic governments could legitimately manage information as a tool of national policy — departing from the liberal assumption that citizens form reasoned opinions through access

The CPI's methods were primarily problematic because they incited mob violence against German Americans and other ethnic minorities, demonstrating that government propaganda produces unintended social harms that undermine the civil order the wartime state claims to be protecting.

The CPI represented a necessary wartime compromise between democratic free expression and the practical demands of mobilizing a diverse and initially reluctant nation for total industrial warfare, justifiable given that Germany was simultaneously deploying sophisticated propaganda campaigns targeting American public opinion.

items.explanation: The CPI marked a qualitative departure from previous American government communication by making the management of public belief a formal state function — rather than presenting information for citizens to evaluate, the CPI's goal was to produce specific emotional and behavioral responses, introducing techniques of psychological manipulation into the relationship between democratic government and its citizens.

items.stem: Wilson's Fourteen Points called for national self-determination, arms reduction, open diplomacy, and a League of Nations, but the Treaty of Versailles imposed crushing reparations and reflected the territorial ambitions of European allied powers. What does the gap between Wilson's proposals and the treaty's actual terms reveal about the structural challenges of translating liberal internationalism into diplomatic reality?

choices.text: Wilson's failure demonstrated that American presidents lack the constitutional authority to make binding international commitments without Senate ratification, making all presidential foreign policy promises inherently unreliable as foundations for multinational peace negotiations.

European allied insistence on punitive terms exposed the fundamental inadequacy of progressive idealism as a foreign policy framework, proving that national interest and power politics will always overcome principled commitments whenever the two conflict in peace negotiations following major wars.

The treaty's harsh terms resulted primarily from Wilson's personal rigidity at the Paris Peace Conference, where his refusal to compromise on specific points antagonized allies who might otherwise have accepted a larger share of his Fourteen Points.

The disjunction between Wilson's vision and the treaty's terms illustrates that liberal internationalist frameworks face structural obstacles in a multipolar diplomatic environment where major powers hold competing territorial claims, divergent war aims, and domestic political pressures that a principled programmatic approach cannot resolve through argument alone.

items.explanation: The Paris Peace Conference demonstrated that even a powerful and idealistic American president could not unilaterally impose a principled framework onto allied powers who had entered the war with specific territorial and security objectives — illustrating the gap between liberal theory and multipolar diplomatic practice.

items.stem:
Document-Based Question: The Foundations and Contradictions of American Imperialism, 1890–1902

Directions: Read the three documents below carefully. Then write a well-organized essay that constructs an argument addressing the following question: To what extent did economic, strategic, and ideological motivations for American imperialism in the 1890s represent a coherent foreign policy, and to what extent did they conflict with one another?

Your essay must:
— Apply HIPP analysis (Historical context, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view) to at least two of the three documents
— Use all three documents as evidence
— Incorporate your own outside knowledge of this period
— Construct a clear, defensible argument supported by evidence from the documents and outside knowledge

---
DOCUMENT 1
Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power Upon History (1890), Chapter I — public domain, Avalon Project, Yale Law School (avalon.law.yale.edu) and Company, Boston:
"Whether they will or no, Americans must now begin to look outward. The growing production of the country demands it. An increasing volume of public sentiment demands it. The position of the United States, between the two great oceans, makes the same claim, which will soon be strengthened by the creation of the new link joining the Atlantic and Pacific. The tendency will be maintained and increased by the growth of the country's in-terests abroad."

---
DOCUMENT 2
Anti-Imperialist League Platform, October 18, 1899 — public domain, Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain:
"We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and tends toward militarism, an evil from which it has been our glory to be free. We regret that it has become necessary in the land of Washington and Lincoln to reaffirm that all men, of whatever race or color, are entitled to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness... We maintain that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. We insist that the subjugation of any people is 'criminal aggression' and open disloyalty to the distinctive principles of our Government."

---
DOCUMENT 3
Senator Albert Beveridge, Congressional Record, January 9, 1900 — public domain:
"The Philippines are ours forever... And just beyond the Philippines are China's illimitable markets. We will not retreat from either... We will not renounce our part in the mission of our race, trustee, under God, of the civilization of the world. And we will move forward to our work, not howling out regrets like slaves whipped to their burdens, but with gratitude for a task worthy of our strength and thanksgiving to Almighty God that He has marked us as His chosen people, henceforth to lead in the regeneration of the world."
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: Los Fundamentos y Contradicciones del Imperialismo Americano, 1890–1902

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos a continuación con detenimiento. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que construya un argumento que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿En qué medida las motivaciones económicas, estratégicas e ideológicas para el imperialismo estadounidense en la década de 1890 representaron una política exterior coherente, y en qué medida se contradijeron entre sí?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis HIPP (Contexto histórico, Audiencia prevista, Propósito, Punto de vista) a al menos dos de los tres documentos
— Utilizar los tres documentos como evidencia
— Incorporar su propio conocimiento externo de este período
— Construir un argumento claro y defendible apoyado por evidencia de los documentos y conocimiento externo

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Alfred Thayer Mahan, La influencia del poder naval en la historia (1890), Capítulo I — dominio público:
"Quieran o no, los americanos deben comenzar ahora a mirar hacia afuera. La creciente producción del país lo exige. Un volumen creciente de sentimiento público lo exige. La posición de los Estados Unidos, entre los dos grandes océanos, plantea la misma exigencia, que pronto se verá fortalecida por la creación del nuevo enlace que une el Atlántico y el Pacífico. La tendencia se mantendrá e incrementará con el crecimiento de los intereses del país en el exterior."

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Plataforma de la Liga Antiimperialista, 18 de octubre de 1899 — dominio público:
"Sostenemos que la política conocida como imperialismo es hostil a la libertad y tiende hacia el militarismo, un mal del cual ha sido nuestra gloria estar libres. Lamentamos que haya sido necesario en la tierra de Washington y Lincoln reafirmar que todos los hombres, de cualquier raza o color, tienen derecho a la vida, la libertad y la búsqueda de la felicidad... Mantenemos que los gobiernos derivan sus justos poderes del consentimiento de los gobernados. Insistimos en que la subyugación de cualquier pueblo es 'agresión criminal' y deslealtad abierta a los principios distintivos de nuestro Gobierno."

---
DOCUMENTO 3
Senador Albert Beveridge, Registro del Congreso, 9 de enero de 1900 — dominio público:
"Las Filipinas son nuestras para siempre... Y justo más allá de las Filipinas están los mercados ilimitables de China. No nos retiraremos de ninguno... No renunciaremos a nuestra parte en la misión de nuestra raza, fideicomisaria, bajo Dios, de la civilización del mundo. Y avanzaremos hacia nuestro trabajo, no llorando arrepentimientos como esclavos azotados hacia sus cargas, sino con gratitud por una tarea digna de nuestra fuerza y acción de gracias al Dios Todopoderoso que nos ha marcado como Su pueblo elegido, en adelante para liderar la regeneración del mundo."
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response: Presents a clear, complex thesis — such as: 'American imperialism was driven by three distinct but interlocking motivations — economic necessity (Mahan, Beveridge), racial-ideological mission (Beveridge), and strategic sea power (Mahan) — but these created an inherent contradiction with American democratic self-determination principles, as the Anti-Imperialist League recognized.' HIPP analysis of at least two documents: Document 1 — Mahan's intended audience is the American political and naval establishment; his purpose is to argue for naval expansion and commercial empire; his point of view reflects Social Darwinist assumptions that national greatness requires outward expansion; historical context is the closing of the frontier (1890 Census) and the need for new markets. Document 3 — Beveridge's intended audience is the U.S. Senate and the American public; his purpose is to justify Philippine annexation; his point of view is explicitly racial (Anglo-Saxon mission) and religious manifest destiny; historical context is the Philippine-American War beginning in February 1899. Document 2 — Anti-Imperialist League argues from the founding documents (consent of the governed), representing figures including Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie, and former President Grover Cleveland; its purpose is to oppose the Treaty of Paris ratification; historical context is the Senate vote on the Treaty of Paris (February 1899, passed 57–27, barely the 2/3 needed). Outside knowledge should include: Spanish-American War outcomes, Philippine-American War costs, Hawaii annexation, Insular Cases. The essay should argue that Mahan's strategic-economic vision and Beveridge's racial mission reinforced each other but both conflicted directly with the Anti-Imperialist position rooted in American founding ideals, making U.S. imperialism structurally contradictory.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.19, US.21 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Complex, defensible thesis that addresses coherence AND contradiction. HIPP analysis applied to all three documents with specific, accurate content. Extensive outside knowledge (e.g., Spanish-American War, Philippine-American War, Hawaii, Insular Cases). Essay is well-organized with clear argument structure. Recognizes nuance — e.g., that Mahan's economic argument and Beveridge's racial argument reinforce each other but differ in kind.
5 - Advanced: Clear thesis addressing both coherence and contradiction. HIPP analysis applied to at least two documents accurately. Solid outside knowledge. Well-organized. May lack the full nuance of a 6 response.
4 - Proficient: Clear thesis. Uses all three documents as evidence. HIPP applied to at least two documents, mostly accurately. Some outside knowledge. Argument is present and mostly coherent.
3 - Adequate: Thesis present but may be simple or partially address the question. Uses two or more documents. Some HIPP elements applied to at least one document. Limited outside knowledge. Argument has some organizational issues.
2 - Developing: Weak or no thesis. Uses one or two documents as evidence without HIPP analysis. Little or no outside knowledge. Response is more descriptive than argumentative.
1 - Beginning: No thesis or off-topic thesis. Minimal or incorrect document use. No HIPP analysis. No outside knowledge.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
— Doc 1 (Mahan): Context = post-frontier industrial economy; Audience = naval/political establishment; Purpose = argue for sea power expansion; POV = strategic-economic nationalist. Note his 'must look outward' as an economic pressure argument.
— Doc 2 (Anti-Imperialist League): Context = Senate Treaty of Paris ratification debate; Audience = U.S. public and Senate; Purpose = oppose annexation; POV = democratic-egalitarian rooted in Declaration of Independence. Note the explicit invocation of Washington and Lincoln.
— Doc 3 (Beveridge): Context = Philippine-American War beginning; Audience = Senate; Purpose = justify annexation and war; POV = racial Anglo-Saxon manifest destiny. Note the religious language ('chosen people') and commercial rationale (Chinese markets) coexisting.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Closing of frontier (1890); Spanish-American War (1898); Treaty of Paris (1898); Philippine-American War (1899–1902); Emilio Aguinaldo; Anti-Imperialist League members (Mark Twain, Carnegie, Cleveland); Hawaii annexation (1898); Insular Cases (1901); Social Darwinism; Josiah Strong 'Our Country' (1885) as ideological context.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: Tesis compleja y defendible que aborda tanto la coherencia como la contradicción. Análisis HIPP aplicado a los tres documentos con contenido específico y preciso. Amplio conocimiento externo. El ensayo está bien organizado con una estructura de argumento clara.
5 - Avanzado: Tesis clara que aborda coherencia y contradicción. Análisis HIPP aplicado con precisión a al menos dos documentos. Sólido conocimiento externo. Bien organizado.
4 - Competente: Tesis clara. Usa los tres documentos como evidencia. HIPP aplicado a al menos dos documentos. Algo de conocimiento externo. Argumento presente y mayormente coherente.
3 - Adecuado: Tesis presente pero puede ser simple. Usa dos o más documentos. Algunos elementos HIPP aplicados a al menos un documento. Conocimiento externo limitado.
2 - En desarrollo: Tesis débil o ausente. Usa uno o dos documentos sin análisis HIPP. Poco o ningún conocimiento externo.
1 - Inicial: Sin tesis o tesis fuera de tema. Uso mínimo o incorrecto de documentos.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Cierre de la frontera (1890); Guerra Hispano-Americana (1898); Tratado de París (1898); Guerra Filipino-Americana (1899–1902); Emilio Aguinaldo; miembros de la Liga Antiimperialista (Mark Twain, Carnegie, Cleveland); anexión de Hawái (1898); Casos Insulares (1901); darwinismo social; 'Our Country' de Josiah Strong (1885).

items.stem:
Document-Based Question: The Spanish-American War and the Question of Empire, 1898

Directions: Read the three documents below. Then write a well-organized essay that constructs an argument addressing the following question: Did the Spanish-American War represent a turning point in American foreign policy, or was it the inevitable product of forces already at work in American society and politics?

Your essay must:
— Apply SOAPS analysis (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Significance) to at least two of the three documents
— Use evidence from all three documents
— Incorporate outside knowledge of the period
— Construct a clear, defensible argument

---
DOCUMENT 1
President William McKinley, War Message to Congress, April 11, 1898 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"The present condition of affairs in Cuba is a constant menace to our peace and entails upon this Government an enormous expense. With such a conflict waged for years in an island so near our border and with which our people have such trade and business relations; when the lives and liberty of our citizens are in constant danger and their property destroyed and themselves ruined; where our trading vessels are liable to seizure and are seized at our very door by warships of a foreign nation — the expedient of enforcing American interests will justify forceful intervention."

---
DOCUMENT 2
Teller Amendment, April 20, 1898, Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain — public domain:
"Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives... That the United States hereby disclaims any disposition or intention to exercise sovereignty, jurisdiction, or control over said Island except for the pacification thereof, and asserts its determination, when that is accomplished, to leave the government and control of the Island to its people."

---
DOCUMENT 3
Platt Amendment, 1901, Statutes at Large of the United States — public domain:
"The government of Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for protecting life, property, and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris on the United States... Cuba will sell or lease to the United States lands necessary for coaling or naval stations at certain specified points to be agreed upon with the President of the United States."
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: La Guerra Hispano-Americana y la Cuestión del Imperio, 1898

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos a continuación. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que construya un argumento que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿Representó la Guerra Hispano-Americana un punto de inflexión en la política exterior estadounidense, o fue el producto inevitable de fuerzas ya en acción en la sociedad y la política estadounidenses?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis SOAPS (Orador, Ocasión, Audiencia, Propósito, Significado) a al menos dos de los tres documentos
— Utilizar evidencia de los tres documentos
— Incorporar conocimiento externo del período
— Construir un argumento claro y defendible

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Presidente William McKinley, Mensaje de Guerra al Congreso, 11 de abril de 1898 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"La presente condición de los asuntos en Cuba es una amenaza constante para nuestra paz y supone para este Gobierno un enorme gasto. Con tal conflicto librado durante años en una isla tan cercana a nuestra frontera y con la que nuestro pueblo tiene tales relaciones comerciales y de negocios; cuando las vidas y la libertad de nuestros ciudadanos están en peligro constante y su propiedad destruida y ellos mismos arruinados; donde nuestros barcos mercantes son susceptibles de incautación y son incautados a nuestra misma puerta por buques de guerra de una nación extranjera — el expediente de hacer cumplir los intereses americanos justificará la intervención forzosa."

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Enmienda Teller, 20 de abril de 1898, Registro del Congreso de EE. UU. — dominio público:
"Resuelto por el Senado y la Cámara de Representantes... Que los Estados Unidos por la presente reniegan de cualquier disposición o intención de ejercer soberanía, jurisdicción o control sobre dicha Isla excepto para la pacificación de la misma, y afirman su determinación, cuando se logre eso, de dejar el gobierno y control de la Isla a su pueblo."

---
DOCUMENTO 3
Enmienda Platt, 1901, Estatutos Generales de los Estados Unidos — dominio público:
"El gobierno de Cuba consiente en que los Estados Unidos puedan ejercer el derecho de intervenir para la preservación de la independencia de Cuba, el mantenimiento de un gobierno adecuado para proteger la vida, la propiedad y la libertad individual, y para cumplir las obligaciones respecto a Cuba impuestas por el Tratado de París a los Estados Unidos... Cuba venderá o arrendará a los Estados Unidos tierras necesarias para estaciones de carbón o navales en ciertos puntos especificados a acordar con el Presidente de los Estados Unidos."
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response presents a complex, defensible thesis — such as: 'The Spanish-American War was both a turning point and an inevitable product of prior forces: it accelerated an imperial trajectory already shaped by Mahan's sea-power theory, economic expansion, and Social Darwinism, but the pivot from the Teller Amendment's anti-annexation promise (Document 2) to the Platt Amendment's protectorate structure (Document 3) represents a genuine and consequential policy turn.' SOAPS analysis for at least two documents: Document 1 (McKinley War Message) — Speaker: sitting president; Occasion: formal request for a declaration of war; Audience: Congress and the American public; Purpose: justify intervention by framing it as defensive of American commercial and citizen interests; Significance: framing of the war as economic/strategic rather than humanitarian reveals the priorities behind the public humanitarian narrative. Document 2 (Teller Amendment) — Speaker: U.S. Congress; Occasion: declaration of war authorization; Audience: American public, Cuba, and Spain; Purpose: preclude accusations of imperial annexation; Significance: its promise was immediately contradicted by post-war policy, revealing the gap between stated intentions and imperial outcomes. Document 3 (Platt Amendment) — Speaker: U.S. Congress, 1901; Occasion: post-war governance of Cuba; Audience: Cuban government and people; Purpose: establish permanent U.S. rights of intervention and naval basing; Significance: effectively negated Teller and established the protectorate system that would govern U.S.-Cuba relations until 1934. Cross-document synthesis: the evolution from Teller to Platt demonstrates that even when Congress explicitly disclaimed imperial intentions, strategic and economic logic drove imperial outcomes. Outside knowledge: USS Maine, yellow press, Dewey at Manila Bay, Treaty of Paris, Philippine acquisition, Cuba's de facto protectorate status 1901–1934, Roosevelt Corollary as the legal follow-on.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.20, US.21 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Complex thesis addressing both 'turning point' and 'inevitable product' dimensions. SOAPS analysis of at least two documents accurately and specifically. Cross-document synthesis (Teller → Platt contradiction). Extensive outside knowledge. Well-organized argumentative essay.
5 - Advanced: Clear thesis. SOAPS applied to at least two documents accurately. Good outside knowledge. Addresses the Teller/Platt contradiction but may not fully develop the 'turning point vs. inevitable' framework.
4 - Proficient: Clear thesis. Uses all three documents as evidence. SOAPS applied to at least two documents with reasonable accuracy. Some outside knowledge. Coherent argument.
3 - Adequate: Thesis present but simple. Uses two or more documents. Some SOAPS elements. Limited outside knowledge. Some organizational issues.
2 - Developing: Weak or no thesis. Uses one or two documents without SOAPS. Little outside knowledge. Descriptive rather than argumentative.
1 - Beginning: No thesis. Minimal document use. No SOAPS. No outside knowledge.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
— Doc 1: McKinley's economic/commercial framing; distinguish from humanitarian yellow-press justification; note 'enforcing American interests' as the operative phrase.
— Doc 2: Teller's explicit anti-annexation intent; note its unanimous passage alongside the war authorization; significance = set up later contradiction with Platt.
— Doc 3: Platt's intervention rights and naval basing provisions; note this was imposed as a condition of U.S. military withdrawal; Cuba had no real choice; significance = established protectorate in all but name.

items.stem:
Document-Based Question: Big Stick Diplomacy and the Monroe Doctrine, 1823–1904

Directions: Read the two documents below. Then write a well-organized essay addressing the following question: How did the Roosevelt Corollary transform the Monroe Doctrine from a defensive statement into an instrument of American imperial power, and what were the consequences for U.S.–Latin American relations?

Your essay must:
— Apply HIPP analysis to both documents
— Construct a clear argument that evaluates the transformation from Monroe to Roosevelt
— Incorporate outside knowledge of specific U.S. interventions in Latin America
— Address the long-term consequences for U.S.–Latin American relations

---
DOCUMENT 1
President James Monroe, Annual Message to Congress (Monroe Doctrine), December 2, 1823 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"We owe it therefore to candor and to the amicable relations existing between the United States and those [European] powers to declare that we should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety. With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere. But with the Governments who have declared their independence and whose independence we have acknowledged, we could not view any interposition for the purpose of oppressing them, or controlling in any other manner their destiny, by any European power, in any other light than as the manifestation of an unfriendly disposition toward the United States."

---
DOCUMENT 2
President Theodore Roosevelt, Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, Annual Message to Congress, December 6, 1904 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"Chronic wrongdoing, or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may in America, as elsewhere, ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation, and in the Western Hemisphere the adherence of the United States to the Monroe Doctrine may force the United States, however reluctantly, to the exercise of an international police power in cases of such wrongdoing or impotence... We would interfere with them only in the last resort, and then only if it became evident that their inability or unwillingness to do justice at home and abroad had violated the rights of the United States or had invited foreign aggression to the detriment of the entire body of American nations."
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: Diplomacia del Gran Garrote y la Doctrina Monroe, 1823–1904

Instrucciones: Lea los dos documentos a continuación. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿Cómo transformó el Corolario Roosevelt la Doctrina Monroe de una declaración defensiva en un instrumento del poder imperial americano, y cuáles fueron las consecuencias para las relaciones EE. UU.–América Latina?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis HIPP a ambos documentos
— Construir un argumento claro que evalúe la transformación de Monroe a Roosevelt
— Incorporar conocimiento externo de intervenciones específicas de EE. UU. en América Latina
— Abordar las consecuencias a largo plazo para las relaciones EE. UU.–América Latina

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Presidente James Monroe, Mensaje Anual al Congreso (Doctrina Monroe), 2 de diciembre de 1823 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"Se lo debemos por tanto a la franqueza y a las relaciones amistosas existentes entre los Estados Unidos y esas potencias [europeas] declarar que consideraríamos cualquier intento de su parte de extender su sistema a cualquier porción de este hemisferio como peligroso para nuestra paz y seguridad. Con las colonias o dependencias existentes de cualquier potencia europea no hemos interferido y no interferiemos. Pero con los Gobiernos que han declarado su independencia y cuya independencia hemos reconocido, no podríamos ver ninguna interposición con el propósito de oprimirlos, o controlando de cualquier otra manera su destino, por ninguna potencia europea, de otra manera que como la manifestación de una disposición desfavorable hacia los Estados Unidos."

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Presidente Theodore Roosevelt, Corolario Roosevelt a la Doctrina Monroe, Mensaje Anual al Congreso, 6 de diciembre de 1904 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"El mal obrar crónico, o la impotencia que resulta en un aflojamiento general de los lazos de la sociedad civilizada, puede en América, como en otros lugares, requerir en última instancia la intervención de alguna nación civilizada, y en el hemisferio occidental la adhesión de los Estados Unidos a la Doctrina Monroe puede obligar a los Estados Unidos, aunque sea reluctantemente, al ejercicio de un poder policial internacional en casos de tal mal obrar o impotencia... Solo interferiríamos con ellos como último recurso, y entonces solo si se hiciera evidente que su incapacidad o renuncia a hacer justicia en casa y en el exterior había violado los derechos de los Estados Unidos o había invitado a la agresión extranjera en detrimento de toda la comunidad de naciones americanas."
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response argues clearly — such as: 'The Monroe Doctrine (1823) was a passive warning to Europe against recolonization; Roosevelt's Corollary (1904) actively claimed the right of the United States to intervene in Latin American affairs as an "international police power," transforming the doctrine from a defensive to an offensive instrument and establishing the legal framework for decades of U.S. imperialism in the hemisphere.' HIPP analysis of both documents: Document 1 (Monroe) — Historical context: Latin American independence movements (1810s–1820s), Holy Alliance threat of European reintervention; Intended audience: European powers (Great Britain, France, Russia, Spain); Purpose: deter European recolonization and establish U.S. sphere of influence; Point of view: Monroe was defensive — the U.S. explicitly said it would 'not interfere' with existing colonies. Note the key phrase 'not interfered and shall not interfere' — Monroe is promising non-intervention in both directions. Document 2 (Roosevelt Corollary) — Historical context: Venezuela Crisis (1902–03) in which European creditors sent warships to collect debts; Dominican Republic fiscal crisis; Purpose: claim U.S. right to intervene before Europe could; Point of view: paternalistic-imperialist ('chronic wrongdoing,' 'civilized society') — Roosevelt assumes Latin American states are incapable of self-governance. HIPP contrast: Monroe said the U.S. would not interfere; Roosevelt said the U.S. must act as a police power. The Corollary hijacks Monroe's authority while reversing its logic. Outside knowledge: Venezuela Crisis (1902–03), U.S. intervention in Dominican Republic (1905), Cuba, Haiti (1915), Nicaragua (1912–1933), Good Neighbor Policy (FDR, 1933) as eventual correction. Consequences for Latin America: deep anti-American resentment ('Yankee imperialism'); Latin American independence compromised; structural inequality in U.S.–Latin American relations.

items.stem:
Extended Response: American Imperialism and the Ideology of Expansion

Using your knowledge of U.S. history from 1890 to 1914, write an extended essay that evaluates the following question: Was American imperialism in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries primarily driven by economic necessity, strategic ambition, or ideological mission? Construct a well-organized argument that draws on at least three specific examples from this period, integrates multiple motivations, and connects the ideology of American expansion to earlier traditions such as Manifest Destiny and to later foreign policy patterns such as the Roosevelt Corollary and U.S. involvement in World War I. Your essay must present a clear claim, provide specific historical evidence, explain the reasoning that connects your evidence to your claim, and acknowledge and refute a counterargument.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: El Imperialismo Americano y la Ideología de la Expansión

Usando su conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU. desde 1890 hasta 1914, escriba un ensayo extendido que evalúe la siguiente pregunta: ¿Fue el imperialismo americano a finales del siglo XIX y principios del XX impulsado principalmente por la necesidad económica, la ambición estratégica, o la misión ideológica? Construya un argumento bien organizado que se apoye en al menos tres ejemplos específicos de este período, integre múltiples motivaciones, y conecte la ideología de la expansión americana con tradiciones anteriores como el Destino Manifiesto y con patrones posteriores de política exterior como el Corolario Roosevelt y la participación de EE. UU. en la Primera Guerra Mundial. Su ensayo debe presentar una afirmación clara, proporcionar evidencia histórica específica, explicar el razonamiento que conecta su evidencia con su afirmación, y reconocer y refutar un contraargumento.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response makes a complex, defensible claim — such as: 'American imperialism was driven by an interlocking combination of economic, strategic, and ideological forces that reinforced each other and were largely inseparable: Mahan's sea-power thesis united commerce and military strategy; Beveridge and Social Darwinism provided the racial-ideological justification; and the closing of the frontier created the economic pressure that made expansion feel necessary.' The essay uses at least three specific examples: (1) Hawaii annexation (1898) — driven by sugar industry interests (economic), strategic Pacific base for Mahan's navy (strategic), and 1893 illegal overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani supported by U.S. Marines (political/ideological); (2) Spanish-American War and Philippine acquisition (1898–1902) — McKinley's economic framing, Beveridge's racial mission, Dewey's naval victory as strategic proof-of-concept; (3) Panama Canal (1903) — Roosevelt's engineering of Panamanian independence to secure a canal consistent with Mahan's chain-of-bases theory, with 'civilized world' rhetoric masking U.S. self-interest. Connection to Manifest Destiny: imperialism of the 1890s was Manifest Destiny applied oceanic — the same racial and religious justifications (God's chosen people, civilizing mission) moved from continental to global scale. Connection to Roosevelt Corollary and WWI: the Corollary formalized the police-power logic; U.S. entry into WWI was sold as an ideological mission (making the world safe for democracy) but driven by economic entanglement and submarine warfare — showing that the pattern of intertwined motives continued. Counterargument acknowledged and refuted: 'One might argue that humanitarian concerns — freeing Cuba from Spanish oppression — were the primary driver; however, the Platt Amendment's transformation of Cuba into a protectorate immediately after the war demonstrates that humanitarian rhetoric served imperial ends.'

4 - Ejemplar: Afirmación compleja y defendible que integra las motivaciones económicas, estratégicas e ideológicas en lugar de elegir una. Tres o más ejemplos específicos con evidencia precisa. items.stem:
Extended Response: U.S. Foreign Policy and the Limits of Power, 1898–1920

Using your knowledge of U.S. history, write an extended essay that evaluates the following question: How did the acquisition of overseas territories between 1898 and 1920 change the United States' relationship with the rest of the world, and to what extent did those changes create new problems that the United States struggled to manage?

Your essay must draw on at least three specific examples, construct a clear argument about the costs and consequences of territorial expansion, connect your analysis to the principles stated in the Monroe Doctrine and the Fourteen Points, and explain how the tensions created by empire-building shaped U.S. foreign policy decisions during this period. Your response should acknowledge the perspective of people in the acquired territories — in the Philippines, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Cuba, or Panama — and evaluate how those perspectives challenge or complicate traditional narratives of American expansion.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: La Política Exterior de EE. UU. y los Límites del Poder, 1898–1920

Usando su conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU., escriba un ensayo extendido que evalúe la siguiente pregunta: ¿Cómo cambió la adquisición de territorios de ultramar entre 1898 y 1920 la relación de los Estados Unidos con el resto del mundo, y en qué medida crearon esos cambios nuevos problemas que los Estados Unidos tuvo dificultades para manejar?

Su ensayo debe apoyarse en al menos tres ejemplos específicos, construir un argumento claro sobre los costos y consecuencias de la expansión territorial, conectar su análisis con los principios establecidos en la Doctrina Monroe y los Catorce Puntos, y explicar cómo las tensiones creadas por la construcción del imperio moldearon las decisiones de política exterior de EE. UU. durante este período. Su respuesta debe reconocer la perspectiva de las personas en los territorios adquiridos — en las Filipinas, Hawái, Puerto Rico, Cuba o Panamá — y evaluar cómo esas perspectivas desafían o complican las narrativas tradicionales de la expansión americana.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response makes a complex, defensible claim — such as: 'The acquisition of overseas territories between 1898 and 1920 transformed the United States from a continental into a global power, but this transformation generated persistent contradictions — between democratic ideals and imperial practice, between strategic ambition and administrative capability, and between American promises and territorial realities — that left the U.S. managing an empire it was ideologically unprepared to own.' At least three specific examples: (1) Philippines — Philippine-American War (1899–1902) cost the U.S. approximately $400 million and 4,234 U.S. deaths, with Filipino casualties estimated in the hundreds of thousands; Emilio Aguinaldo's resistance revealed that Filipinos did not regard U.S. rule as liberation; Insular Cases (1901) created a legal second-class status for territorial residents. (2) Cuba — Platt Amendment (1901) transformed the promised independence (Teller) into a protectorate; U.S. military occupation lasted until 1902, with re-interventions in 1906 and 1912; this planted the seeds of anti-American nationalism that would eventually produce the Cuban Revolution (1959). (3) Panama — U.S. engineering of independence (1903) and the 10-mile Canal Zone created lasting resentment in Panama (which eventually led to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977). Connection to Monroe Doctrine: Monroe's defensive posture became Roosevelt's 'police power' claim — the acquired territories required active administration and protection, generating the very interventionist pattern Monroe had tried to avoid. Connection to Fourteen Points: Wilson's call for self-determination and open covenants directly contradicted the reality of U.S. territorial governance; colonial peoples noted the hypocrisy. Territory-holder perspectives: Filipino nationalists under Aguinaldo argued the U.S. had betrayed its own Declaration of Independence; Puerto Ricans received Jones Act citizenship (1917) without full representation; Native Hawaiians lost their queen and sovereignty in 1893; Panamanians gained nominal independence but lost sovereignty over the Canal Zone.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph shows FDR delivering a fireside chat, c. 1933.

(Photograph, c. 1933. Public Domain.)

How did Roosevelt's use of radio, as shown in this photograph, change the relationship between the president and the American public?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo cambió el uso de la radio por Roosevelt la relación entre el presidente y el público?

choices.text: Radio had no impact because most Americans could not afford receivers during the Depression
Radio allowed the president to bypass newspapers and speak directly to millions of Americans in their homes, creating a personal connection
Roosevelt used radio only to communicate with Congress, not the general public
Radio broadcasts replaced all other forms of presidential communication permanently

items.explanation: Radio transformed presidential communication. By the 1930s, most American homes had radios. FDR's conversational tone made listeners feel he was speaking directly to them, creating an unprecedented personal bond between president and public. This direct communication helped build support for controversial New Deal programs.
items.explanationEs: La radio permitió a Roosevelt comunicarse directamente con millones de estadounidenses, creando un vínculo personal sin precedentes.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

This 1936 Farm Security Administration photograph by Arthur Rothstein shows a desolate farmstead on the Great Plains. A father and his two sons run toward their small wooden farmhouse as a massive wall of dust approaches from behind. The land around the house is flat and barren, with drifting dust partially burying fences and farm structures.

(Photograph by Arthur Rothstein for the Farm Security Administration, 1936. Library of Congress, Farm Security Administration Collection.)

How did agricultural farming practices of the early twentieth century contribute to the environmental disaster shown in this photograph?

choices.text: Overuse of irrigation diverted river water, causing rivers to dry up and leaving the soil too wet to support crops
Farmers had plowed up native grasses to plant crops, removing the root systems that held the topsoil in place against wind erosion
A government program forced farmers to plant a single crop, which trapped moisture and caused flooding that loosened the soil
Farmers over-planted forests, cutting off wind patterns that normally brought rainfall to the plains region

items.explanation: Farmers on the Great Plains had plowed up the deep-rooted native grasses that held the soil in place, replacing them with wheat and other crops. When the drought of the 1930s killed the crops, there were no root systems left to anchor the topsoil, leaving it vulnerable to the massive wind erosion visible in the photograph. Mechanized farming had also accelerated the scale of this land conversion. Choice A describes a problem in a different region. Choice C reverses the causal relationship. Choice D confuses the water-related Dust Bowl with different agricultural practices.

items.stem: Coolidge's statement most clearly reflects which prevailing political philosophy of the 1920s?

choices.text: Strong federal regulation of private enterprise
Pro-business policies and limited government intervention
Government ownership of major industries
Federal redistribution of wealth through taxation

items.explanation: Coolidge's confidence in business expressed the decade's governing philosophy: low taxes, reduced federal spending, and minimal interference with private enterprise. Choice A is wrong because strong federal regulation was the Progressive approach the 1920s pulled back from. Choice D is wrong because redistribution through taxation was the opposite of the era's tax-cutting policy. That philosophy shaped the federal response when the Depression began.

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the chart?

choices.text: The stock market grew steadily without disruption throughout the late 1920s
The Dow Jones average remained stable throughout 1929
Stock prices rose continuously from 1925 through the end of 1929

items.explanation: The chart shows the Dow reaching its high point in September 1929 and then falling steeply in late October, the collapse remembered as Black Thursday and Black Tuesday. Choice A is wrong because the data show a sharp break, not uninterrupted growth. Choice C is wrong because prices turned down before the year ended. The crash exposed how much of the boom rested on buying stock on margin.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The c.1919 cartoon depicts the conflict between temperance advocates and the liquor industry over Prohibition. Both sides are shown in opposition, reflecting the intense cultural and political divisions of the era.

Which of the following groups was most prominently associated with the push for Prohibition?

choices.text: Industrial labor unions, who saw alcohol consumption as a working-class right
Recent immigrants from Europe, who brought traditions of moderate alcohol use
Protestant women's organizations like the Women's Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League
Urban saloon owners, who sought federal regulation to standardize the liquor industry

items.explanation: C is correct: The temperance movement, led largely by Protestant women's organizations such as the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) and the Anti-Saloon League, was the primary force behind the push for Prohibition. They argued that alcohol destroyed families, led to poverty, and caused social decay. A is incorrect: industrial workers and labor unions generally opposed Prohibition, as it targeted working-class leisure. B is incorrect: immigrants, many of whom came from cultures with traditions of alcohol consumption (Germans, Italians, Irish), tended to oppose Prohibition. D is incorrect: saloon owners were the leading opponents of Prohibition.

items.stem:
Read the excerpt below.

"The Eighteenth Amendment: The manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors within, the importation thereof into, or the exportation thereof from the United States and all territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof for beverage purposes is hereby prohibited." — 18th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, 1919

Which of the following best describes an unintended consequence of Prohibition as established by the 18th Amendment?

choices.text: Alcohol consumption immediately dropped to nearly zero as Americans overwhelmingly complied with the law.
Organized crime expanded dramatically as criminal organizations took control of the illegal alcohol trade and used profits to corrupt law enforcement.
Prohibition strengthened respect for law by demonstrating that the government could successfully regulate personal behavior.
The law dramatically reduced the power of criminal organizations by eliminating their most profitable product.

items.explanation: Prohibition's most significant unintended consequence was the dramatic growth of organized crime. With alcohol production and sale made illegal, criminal organizations like those of Al Capone took control of the illicit alcohol trade, becoming enormously wealthy and powerful. The profits from bootlegging were used to bribe law enforcement and politicians, fueling corruption. Option A is incorrect because alcohol consumption did not immediately drop to zero — illegal speakeasies proliferated. Option C is incorrect because Prohibition actually weakened respect for law, not strengthened it, as millions of Americans openly violated it. Option D is incorrect because Prohibition increased, not decreased, the power and profits of criminal organizations.

items.correctAnswer: Propaganda: Office of War Information produced posters ("Rosie the Riveter"), films, radio programs to build unity and demonize enemies. Rationing: tires, gasoline, sugar, meat, coffee rationed via coupon books; created shared sacrifice. Economic controls: War Production Board converted factories to military production; price controls prevented inflation; war bonds financed the war while reducing consumer spending. Arguments for most effective vary — rationing created tangible shared sacrifice, propaganda shaped attitudes, economic conversion actually won the war.
items.explanation: A strong response should explain that propaganda agencies built support for the war, rationing directed scarce goods such as gasoline and rubber, and economic controls shifted industry toward military production. It should also judge which method most effectively built public support and defend that claim with specific evidence, not just description. This prompt matters because modern wars are won by mobilizing civilians and the economy, not only soldiers on the battlefield.

items.correctAnswer: Strong responses should present multiple perspectives with specific evidence, demonstrate understanding that reasonable people can disagree about this decision, and construct their own argument. Which evidence most strongly supports this argument?
items.stemEs: En la década de 1920, la radiodifusión se extendió rápidamente por los Estados Unidos, llegando a millones de hogares al final de la década. Al mismo tiempo, las películas mudas dieron paso a las películas sonoras, y la asistencia al cine se disparó. Un estudiante argumenta que la radio y el cine juntos crearon la primera verdadera cultura popular nacional en la historia estadounidense. ¿Qué evidencia apoya más fuertemente este argumento?

choices.text: Radio and film were highly profitable industries that sold national advertising to major corporations, generating enormous revenue.
choices.textEs: La radio y el cine eran industrias rentables que vendían publicidad a corporaciones nacionales.

choices.text: By 1929, over 600 radio stations were broadcasting across the United States, making it the most rapidly adopted technology in American history.
choices.textEs: Para 1929, había más de 600 estaciones de radio transmitiendo en los Estados Unidos.

choices.text: A single radio broadcast of a championship boxing match simultaneously reached millions of listeners, creating shared national experience across regional and class lines.
choices.textEs: Una sola transmisión de radio de un combate de boxeo de campeonato llegó a millones de oyentes simultáneamente, creando una experiencia nacional compartida más allá de las líneas regionales y de clase.

choices.text: Religious and community leaders in many rural regions publicly condemned radio and film as serious threats to local cultural traditions and moral standards.
choices.textEs: Líderes religiosos y comunitarios en muchas regiones condenaron la radio y el cine como amenazas a las tradiciones culturales locales.

items.explanation: A single broadcast reaching millions simultaneously — and a single film creating nationally shared references — represents the mechanism by which a unified national culture emerged. This simultaneity and scale was unprecedented before electronic mass media. C directly supports the argument by showing the mechanism. A supports commercialization but not cultural unification. B shows reach but not the shared-culture effect. D describes a reaction against, rather than the creation of, national popular culture.
items.explanationEs: Una sola transmisión que llega a millones simultáneamente, y una sola película creando referencias compartidas a nivel nacional, representa el mecanismo por el cual surgió una cultura nacional unificada. Esta simultaneidad y escala no tenían precedentes antes de los medios de comunicación electrónicos masivos. C apoya directamente el argumento al mostrar el mecanismo. A apoya la comercialización pero no la unificación cultural. B muestra el alcance pero no el efecto de cultura compartida. D describe una reacción en contra, en lugar de la creación, de la cultura popular nacional.

items.stem: Charles Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic solo flight generated extraordinary media coverage and made him an instant international celebrity. Radio broadcasts and newsreel films brought his achievement to audiences worldwide within hours. What does Lindbergh's reception reveal about the relationship between new media technologies and celebrity culture in the 1920s?
items.stemEs: El vuelo transatlántico en solitario de Charles Lindbergh en 1927 generó una cobertura mediática extraordinaria y lo convirtió en una celebridad internacional instantánea. Las transmisiones de radio y los noticieros cinematográficos llevaron su hazaña a audiencias en todo el mundo en cuestión de horas. ¿Qué revela la recepción de Lindbergh sobre la relación entre las nuevas tecnologías de medios y la cultura de la celebridad en la década de 1920?

choices.text: The public admired Lindbergh primarily because his flight demonstrated American technological superiority over European nations.
choices.textEs: El público admiraba a Lindbergh principalmente porque su vuelo demostró la superioridad tecnológica estadounidense sobre las naciones europeas.

choices.text: The invention of radio directly caused public interest in aviation, explaining why air travel expanded rapidly after 1927.
choices.textEs: La invención de la radio causó directamente el interés público en la aviación, explicando por qué los viajes aéreos se expandieron rápidamente después de 1927.

choices.text: Lindbergh used his celebrity to promote commercial radio and film, becoming a spokesman for the entertainment industry.
choices.textEs: Lindbergh usó su celebridad para promover la radio y el cine comerciales, convirtiéndose en vocero de la industria del entretenimiento.

choices.text: Mass media technologies amplified individual achievement into national cultural events, creating a new kind of celebrity that depended on instantaneous mass communication.
choices.textEs: Las tecnologías de medios masivos amplificaron el logro individual en eventos culturales nacionales, creando un nuevo tipo de celebridad que dependía de la comunicación masiva instantánea.

items.explanation: Lindbergh's fame was inseparable from mass media — the same flight in 1907 would have generated far less cultural impact. Radio and film created the infrastructure for instantaneous mass attention, transforming individual achievement into national event. D correctly identifies this media-celebrity interdependence. A is partially true but does not explain the media relationship. B confuses correlation with causation. C misrepresents Lindbergh's primary cultural significance, which was national hero rather than technology promoter.
items.explanationEs: La fama de Lindbergh era inseparable de los medios masivos: el mismo vuelo en 1907 habría generado un impacto cultural mucho menor. La radio y el cine crearon la infraestructura para la atención masiva instantánea, transformando el logro individual en evento nacional. D identifica correctamente esta interdependencia entre medios y celebridad. A es parcialmente verdadero pero no explica la relación mediática. B confunde correlación con causalidad. C malinterpreta el significado cultural primario de Lindbergh, que fue héroe nacional más que promotor de tecnología.

items.stem: Babe Ruth's fame in the 1920s extended far beyond baseball. His image appeared in advertisements, newspapers, and newsreels, making him one of the first athletes to achieve national celebrity status. A historian argues that Ruth's fame would have been impossible without the mass media of the 1920s. Which reasoning best evaluates the strength of this argument?
items.stemEs: La fama de Babe Ruth en la década de 1920 se extendió mucho más allá del béisbol. Su imagen aparecía en anuncios, periódicos y noticieros cinematográficos, convirtiéndolo en uno de los primeros atletas en lograr el estatus de celebridad nacional. Un historiador argumenta que la fama de Ruth habría sido imposible sin los medios masivos de la década de 1920. ¿Qué razonamiento evalúa mejor la solidez de este argumento?

choices.text: The argument is strong because mass media amplified Ruth's reach to a national scale, though his exceptional athletic performance provided the content that media distributed.
