items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze the following three primary sources. For each document, apply the HIPP framework (Historical context, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view). Then construct a written argument that addresses the central question: To what extent did the legal dismantling of 'separate but equal' between 1954 and 1957 translate into actual desegregation on the ground?

---
Document 1: Excerpt from Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954). Source: National Archives, archives.gov.

"We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs... are deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment... We have now announced that such segregation is a denial of the equal protection of the laws."

---
Document 2: Excerpt from the 'Declaration of Constitutional Principles' (Southern Manifesto), signed by 101 members of Congress, March 12, 1956. Source: Congressional Record, 84th Congress, 2nd Session, Vol. 102, Part 4 (March 12, 1956), pp. 4459–4460; National Archives, archives.gov.

"We regard the decision of the Supreme Court in the school cases as a clear abuse of judicial power... The original Constitution does not mention education. Neither does the 14th Amendment nor any other amendment... This unwarranted exercise of power by the Court, contrary to the Constitution, is creating chaos and confusion in the States principally affected... We pledge ourselves to use all lawful means to bring about a reversal of this decision which is contrary to the Constitution and to prevent the use of force in its implementation."

---
Document 3: Excerpt from President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Executive Order 10730, authorizing the use of federal troops to enforce school integration in Little Rock, Arkansas, September 24, 1957. Source: Executive Order 10730, Code of Federal Regulations, Title 3 (1957); National Archives, archives.gov.

"WHEREAS certain persons in the state of Arkansas... have wilfully obstructed the enforcement of orders of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas with regard to matters relating to enrollment and attendance at public schools... NOW, THEREFORE, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and Statutes of the United States... it is hereby ordered as follows: The Secretary of Defense is authorized and directed to use the armed forces of the United States as he may deem necessary to enforce any orders of the United States District Court."

---
Using all three documents and your knowledge of the period, construct a multi-paragraph argument that analyzes: (1) the gap between legal authority (Document 1) and practical resistance (Document 2), (2) what the executive response (Document 3) reveals about the enforcement mechanisms available to translate legal principle into social reality, and (3) what these three documents together suggest about the relationship between judicial, legislative, and executive power in advancing or resisting civil rights.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analice los siguientes tres fuentes primarias. Para cada documento, aplique el marco HIPP (Contexto histórico, Audiencia prevista, Propósito, Punto de vista). Luego construya un argumento escrito que aborde la pregunta central: ¿En qué medida el desmantelamiento legal de 'separado pero igual' entre 1954 y 1957 se tradujo en una desegregación real sobre el terreno?

---
Documento 1: Extracto de Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954). Fuente: Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"Concluimos que, en el campo de la educación pública, la doctrina de 'separado pero igual' no tiene lugar. Las instalaciones educativas separadas son intrínsecamente desiguales. Por lo tanto, sostenemos que los demandantes... están privados de la protección igualitaria de las leyes garantizada por la Decimocuarta Enmienda... Ahora hemos declarado que tal segregación es una denegación de la protección igualitaria de las leyes."

---
Documento 2: Extracto de la 'Declaración de Principios Constitucionales' (Manifiesto del Sur), firmado por 101 miembros del Congreso, 12 de marzo de 1956. Fuente: Registro del Congreso, 84.º Congreso, 2.ª Sesión, Vol. 102, Parte 4 (12 de marzo de 1956), pp. 4459–4460; Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"Consideramos la decisión de la Corte Suprema en los casos escolares como un claro abuso del poder judicial... La Constitución original no menciona la educación. Tampoco lo hace la 14.ª Enmienda ni ninguna otra enmienda... Este ejercicio injustificado del poder por parte de la Corte, contrario a la Constitución, está creando caos y confusión en los Estados principalmente afectados... Nos comprometemos a usar todos los medios legales para lograr la revocación de esta decisión que es contraria a la Constitución y para prevenir el uso de la fuerza en su implementación."

---
Documento 3: Extracto de la Orden Ejecutiva 10730 del Presidente Dwight D. Eisenhower, que autoriza el uso de tropas federales para hacer cumplir la integración escolar en Little Rock, Arkansas, 24 de septiembre de 1957. Fuente: Orden Ejecutiva 10730, Código de Regulaciones Federales, Título 3 (1957); Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"CONSIDERANDO que ciertas personas en el estado de Arkansas... han obstruido deliberadamente el cumplimiento de las órdenes del Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Este de Arkansas con respecto a asuntos relacionados con la inscripción y asistencia a las escuelas públicas... AHORA, POR LO TANTO, en virtud de la autoridad que me confieren la Constitución y los Estatutos de los Estados Unidos... se ordena lo siguiente: El Secretario de Defensa está autorizado y dirigido a usar las fuerzas armadas de los Estados Unidos según lo considere necesario para hacer cumplir cualquier orden del Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos."

---
Usando los tres documentos y su conocimiento del período, construya un argumento de varios párrafos que analice: (1) la brecha entre la autoridad legal (Documento 1) y la resistencia práctica (Documento 2), (2) lo que la respuesta ejecutiva (Documento 3) revela sobre los mecanismos de aplicación disponibles para traducir el principio legal en realidad social, y (3) lo que estos tres documentos en conjunto sugieren sobre la relación entre el poder judicial, legislativo y ejecutivo para avanzar o resistir los derechos civiles.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response would include: ARGUMENT: The three documents reveal that legal authority (judicial) was necessary but not sufficient to produce desegregation — it required executive enforcement against legislative resistance, demonstrating that civil rights progress depended on the alignment of all three branches. DOCUMENT 1 HIPP: Historical context: 1954, Cold War era, U.S. embarrassed by racial segregation in competing with USSR for allegiance of newly decolonized nations. Intended audience: Lower courts, school boards, state governments, and the American public. Purpose: To establish a constitutional ruling that 'separate but equal' (Plessy) violates the Equal Protection Clause. Point of view: The unanimous Court, drawing on sociological evidence (Kenneth Clark doll studies) as well as legal precedent — unusually relying on social science rather than purely legal argument. DOCUMENT 2 HIPP: Historical context: Post-Brown 'massive resistance' movement among Southern Democrats, most vocally after Brown II (1955) implementation decree. Intended audience: Southern state governments, other Southern members of Congress, and Southern voters — a political rallying document. Purpose: To provide political cover for continued resistance to desegregation under the guise of constitutional objection. Point of view: 101 members of Congress from 11 former Confederate states; represents the political power of Southern Democrats who controlled key Congressional committees. DOCUMENT 3 HIPP: Historical context: September 1957, Governor Faubus had used the Arkansas National Guard to block integration of Central High School. Mob violence on Sept. 23 made the federal government's authority appear powerless. Intended audience: The Arkansas governor, state officials, federal military commanders, and the American public (demonstrating federal resolve). Purpose: To use executive power to enforce the judicial order — bypassing state resistance by federalizing military authority. Point of view: Eisenhower, acting from institutional duty rather than personal enthusiasm for desegregation. SYNTHESIS: Students should argue that the three documents together illustrate a structural tension in American federalism: judicial decisions create rights but cannot self-enforce; legislative resistance (Document 2 signatories held committee power that would block civil rights legislation until 1964) created a governance gap; executive action (Document 3) was available only in crisis situations, not as a systematic enforcement tool. This gap explains why the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) were essential — they created statutory enforcement mechanisms.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.71, US.73 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Student applies HIPP analysis accurately and insightfully to all three documents, identifying historical context, audience, purpose, and point of view with specific historical grounding. Constructs a sophisticated, evidence-based argument about the gap between legal authority and practical enforcement. Synthesizes across all three documents (does not treat each in isolation). Accurately explains the structural roles of judicial, legislative, and executive branches in the civil rights context. Uses outside historical knowledge (Brown II, Cold War context, massive resistance, Congressional committee power) to deepen the argument. Writing is analytical, cohesive, and advances a clear, defensible thesis.
5 - Advanced: Student applies HIPP accurately to all three documents with most elements present and mostly accurate. Constructs a clear argument about the legal-enforcement gap with specific evidence from all three documents. Uses some outside knowledge. Synthesis is present but may not fully integrate all three documents into a single coherent argument.
4 - Proficient: Student applies HIPP to all three documents with most elements present, though some may be vague or partially accurate. Argument addresses the central question with evidence from at least two documents. Some outside knowledge used. Synthesis is present but somewhat mechanical (documents analyzed separately rather than as a set).
3 - Adequate: Student applies HIPP to two of three documents with reasonable accuracy. Argument addresses the central question but may rely primarily on one or two documents. Limited outside knowledge. Analysis is descriptive rather than interpretive in places.
2 - Developing: Student attempts HIPP analysis but applies it to only one document or applies it inaccurately. Argument is present but underdeveloped or partially answers the central question. Little outside knowledge. Documents are summarized rather than analyzed.
1 - Beginning: Student provides basic summaries of one or two documents without HIPP analysis. Argument is missing or too vague to address the central question. No meaningful synthesis across documents.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS (HIPP for all three): Doc 1 — Cold War context, unanimous Court, sociological evidence (Clark doll studies), 14th Amendment Equal Protection; Doc 2 — Massive resistance, 101 Southern congressmen, constitutional pretext, political audience, blocking enforcement; Doc 3 — Faubus crisis, Eisenhower's institutional (not ideological) motivation, executive enforcement power, military deployment.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Brown II implementation decree (1955); massive resistance movement; Governor Faubus and Arkansas National Guard; 101st Airborne deployment; Supremacy Clause; Cold War context of desegregation; Southern Democrats' committee power in Congress; gap leading to Civil Rights Act 1964 and VRA 1965.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: El estudiante aplica el análisis HIPP de manera precisa y perspicaz a los tres documentos, identificando el contexto histórico, la audiencia, el propósito y el punto de vista con fundamento histórico específico. Construye un argumento sofisticado y basado en evidencia sobre la brecha entre la autoridad legal y la aplicación práctica. Sintetiza los tres documentos (no los trata de forma aislada). Explica con precisión los roles estructurales de las ramas judicial, legislativa y ejecutiva en el contexto de los derechos civiles. Usa conocimiento histórico externo (Brown II, contexto de la Guerra Fría, resistencia masiva, poder de los comités del Congreso) para profundizar el argumento. La escritura es analítica, cohesiva y avanza una tesis clara y defendible.
5 - Avanzado: El estudiante aplica HIPP con precisión a los tres documentos con la mayoría de los elementos presentes y mayormente precisos. Construye un argumento claro sobre la brecha legal-aplicación con evidencia específica de los tres documentos. Usa algo de conocimiento externo. La síntesis está presente pero puede no integrar completamente los tres documentos en un solo argumento coherente.
4 - Competente: El estudiante aplica HIPP a los tres documentos con la mayoría de los elementos presentes, aunque algunos pueden ser vagos o parcialmente precisos. El argumento aborda la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos documentos. Se usa algo de conocimiento externo. La síntesis está presente pero algo mecánica (los documentos se analizan por separado en lugar de como un conjunto).
3 - Adecuado: El estudiante aplica HIPP a dos de los tres documentos con razonable precisión. El argumento aborda la pregunta central pero puede depender principalmente de uno o dos documentos. Conocimiento externo limitado. El análisis es descriptivo en lugar de interpretativo en algunos lugares.
2 - En desarrollo: El estudiante intenta el análisis HIPP pero lo aplica solo a un documento o lo aplica de manera incorrecta. El argumento está presente pero poco desarrollado o responde parcialmente la pregunta central. Poco conocimiento externo. Los documentos se resumen en lugar de analizarse.
1 - Inicial: El estudiante proporciona resúmenes básicos de uno o dos documentos sin análisis HIPP. El argumento está ausente o es demasiado vago para abordar la pregunta central. No hay síntesis significativa entre documentos.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EXPECTATIVAS DE ANÁLISIS DE DOCUMENTOS (HIPP para los tres): Doc 1 — Contexto de la Guerra Fría, Corte unánime, evidencia sociológica (estudios de muñecas de Clark), Protección Igualitaria de la 14.ª Enmienda; Doc 2 — Resistencia masiva, 101 congresistas sureños, pretexto constitucional, audiencia política, bloqueo de la aplicación; Doc 3 — Crisis de Faubus, motivación institucional (no ideológica) de Eisenhower, poder ejecutivo de aplicación, despliegue militar.
EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Decreto de implementación de Brown II (1955); movimiento de resistencia masiva; gobernador Faubus y Guardia Nacional de Arkansas; despliegue de la 101.ª División Aerotransportada; Cláusula de Supremacía; contexto de la Guerra Fría de la desegregación; poder de los comités del Congreso de los Demócratas del Sur; brecha que llevó a la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la LDV de 1965.

choices.textEs: Viajes en autobús interraciales por el Sur para probar la desegregación del transporte interestatal

choices.text: Bus tours organized by the Freedom Riders to register voters across the South
choices.textEs: Giras en autobús organizadas por los Freedom Riders para registrar votantes en todo el sur

choices.text: Federal bus subsidies that enabled poor African Americans to travel between cities
choices.textEs: Subsidios federales para autobuses que permitieron a afroamericanos pobres viajar entre ciudades

choices.text: Caravans of teachers who traveled to integrate southern public schools
choices.textEs: Caravanas de maestros que viajaron para integrar las escuelas públicas del sur

items.explanation: Freedom Riders traveled on interstate buses to see whether Southern states would obey federal rulings banning segregation in travel. Choices about registering voters are wrong because the rides focused on terminals, waiting rooms, and buses. The campaign exposed the gap between Supreme Court decisions and local enforcement.
items.explanationEs: Los Viajes de la Libertad de 1961, organizados por el Congreso de Igualdad Racial (CORE), pusieron a prueba el cumplimiento de Boynton v. Virginia (1960), que prohibió la segregación en los autobuses interestatales y las terminales. Los viajeros afroamericanos y blancos viajaron juntos a través del Sur enfrentando violencia para forzar al gobierno federal a hacer cumplir la ley. Las opciones que confunden los Viajes con sentadas o boicots son incorrectas.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical context that made the Brown v. Board decision possible?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál de las siguientes opciones best describes the historical context that made the Brown v. Board decision possible?

choices.text: Cold War pressure from the Soviet Union forced the U.S. government to address racial inequality
choices.textEs: Guerra Fría pressure from the Soviet Union forced the U.S. government to address racial inigualdad

choices.text: Decades of NAACP legal strategy and growing civil rights activism challenged segregation through the courts
choices.textEs: Decades of NAACP legal strategy and growing derechos civiles activism challenged segregación through the courts

choices.text: Congress passed legislation requiring school desegregation before the Supreme Court ruled
choices.textEs: Congreso passed legislación requiring school desegregación before the Corte Suprema ruled

choices.text: President Eisenhower ordered federal agencies to desegregate before the Court acted
choices.textEs: President Eisenhower ordered federal agencies to desegregate before the Court acted

items.explanation: Brown became possible after decades of NAACP legal work that first challenged inequality in graduate and professional schools before taking on K-12 segregation. Choices that treat Brown as a sudden change are wrong because the ruling grew out of a long courtroom strategy. That gradual buildup shows how social movements often combine activism with patient legal planning.
items.explanationEs: Brown became possible after decades of NAACP legal work that first challenged inigualdad in graduate and professional schools before taking on K-12 segregación. Choices that treat Brown as a sudden change are wrong because the ruling grew out of a long courtroom strategy. That gradual buildup shows how social movements often combine activism with patient legal planning.

items.stem: The 'Southern Manifesto' of 1956, signed by 101 members of Congress, was a declaration opposing —
items.stemEs: The 'Southern Manifesto' of 1956, signed by 101 members of Congreso, was a declaration opposing —

choices.text: Eisenhower's use of federal troops in the Korean War
choices.textEs: Eisenhower's use of federal troops in the Guerra de Corea

choices.text: The Montgomery Bus Boycott and MLK's leadership
choices.textEs: The Montgomery Bus Boycott and MLK's leadership

choices.text: The Supreme Court's Brown v. Board decision on school desegregation
choices.textEs: The Corte Suprema's Brown v. Board decision on school desegregación

choices.text: Federal legislation to establish a permanent Civil Rights Commission
choices.textEs: Federal legislación to establish a permanent derechos civiles Commission

items.explanation: The Southern Manifesto was a 1956 statement signed by members of Congress condemning Brown v. Board and urging resistance to desegregation. Choices about supporting civil rights are wrong because the document defended segregation, not equality. It gave segregationist resistance a national political voice.
items.explanationEs: The Southern Manifesto was a 1956 statement signed by members of Congreso condemning Brown v. Board and urging resistance to desegregación. Choices about supporting derechos civiles are wrong because the document defended segregación, not igualdad. It gave segregaciónist resistance a national political voice.

items.stem: What was the "all deliberate speed" phrase in Brown II criticized for?
items.stemEs: ¿Por qué fue criticada la frase "toda velocidad deliberada" en Brown II?

choices.text: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which established "separate but equal"
choices.textEs: Requerir que la integración ocurriera demasiado rápido

choices.text: The separate but equal doctrine established in Plessy v. Ferguson
choices.textEs: Crear plazos estrictos que eran imposibles de cumplir

choices.text: Declared school segregation unconstitutional and overturned Plessy
choices.textEs: Dar demasiado poder al gobierno federal

choices.text: Being too vague and allowing Southern states to delay integration
choices.textEs: Ser demasiado vaga y permitir que estados del Sur retrasaran la integración

items.explanation: Brown II ordered desegregation to proceed with "all deliberate speed" in 1955, but that vague phrase gave many Southern districts room to stall. Choices suggesting immediate integration are wrong because school systems used the wording to delay for years. The case shows that Supreme Court victories still depended on enforcement and political will.
items.explanationEs: Brown II ordered desegregación to proceed with "all deliberate speed" in 1955, but that vague phrase gave many Southern districts room to stall. Choices suggesting immediate integración are wrong because school systems used the wording to delay for years. The case shows that Corte Suprema victories still depended on enforcement and political will.

items.stem: What was the philosophy of nonviolent direct action?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál era la filosofía de la acción directa no violenta?

choices.text: A Birmingham official who ordered attacks on protesters with dogs and hoses
choices.textEs: Usar violencia solo como último recurso cuando métodos pacíficos fallaron

choices.text: A movement emphasizing Black pride, self-determination, and political power
choices.textEs: Evitar toda confrontación y esperar un cambio gradual

choices.text: Using peaceful protests to create tension that forces negotiation and change
choices.textEs: Usar protestas pacíficas para crear tensión que fuerce negociación y cambio

choices.text: A violent riot erupted when James Meredith enrolled, requiring federal troops
choices.textEs: Trabajar exclusivamente a través del sistema judicial para lograr derechos civiles

items.explanation: King believed nonviolent direct action should create public tension that exposed injustice and forced negotiation without using violence. Choices calling for armed retaliation are wrong because King grounded his strategy in peaceful civil disobedience. That approach helped the movement win moral credibility and national attention.
items.explanationEs: King believed nonviolent direct action should create public tension that exposed injustice and forced negotiation without using violence. Choices calling for armed retaliation are wrong because King grounded his strategy in peaceful civil disobedience. That approach helped the movement win moral credibility and national attention.

items.stem: What was the significance of Linda Brown in the Brown v. Board case?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia de Linda Brown en el caso Brown v. Board?

choices.text: Segregation psychologically harmed Black children and violated equal protection
choices.textEs: Fue la abogada que argumentó el caso ante la Corte Suprema

choices.text: She was the plaintiff whose case challenged school segregation in Topeka, Kansas
choices.textEs: Fue la demandante cuyo caso desafió la segregación escolar en Topeka, Kansas

choices.text: To protect nine Black students integrating Central High School against mob violence
choices.textEs: Fue la primera estudiante afroamericana en integrar una escuela del Sur

choices.text: They organized "respectable" resistance through economic pressure and political action
choices.textEs: Fue una jueza de la Corte Suprema que falló sobre el caso

items.explanation: Linda Brown was the Kansas student whose family joined the lawsuit challenging segregated schools in Topeka. Other choices are wrong if they describe lawyers or judges, because Brown was the child plaintiff at the center of the case. Her case gave a human face to the constitutional fight over equal education.
items.explanationEs: Linda Brown was the Kansas student whose family joined the lawsuit challenging segregated schools in Topeka. Other choices are wrong if they describe lawyers or judges, because Brown was the child plaintiff at the center of the case. Her case gave a human face to the constitucional fight over equal education.

items.stem: What was the significance of the "I Have a Dream" speech?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia del discurso "Tengo un Sueño"?

choices.text: It shocked the nation and helped build support for federal civil rights legislation
choices.textEs: Fue pronunciado para anunciar la aprobación de la Ley de Derechos Civiles

choices.text: They served as meeting places, organizing centers, and sources of moral leadership
choices.textEs: Pidió resistencia armada inmediata contra la segregación

choices.text: It articulated the vision of racial harmony and became an iconic civil rights moment
choices.textEs: Articuló la visión de armonía racial y se convirtió en un momento icónico de derechos civiles

choices.text: Interracial bus rides through the South to test desegregation of interstate transportation
choices.textEs: Se enfocó exclusivamente en asuntos económicos en lugar de derechos civiles

items.explanation: King's "I Have a Dream" speech gave powerful language to the movement's vision of racial equality, citizenship, and moral urgency. Choices treating it as a law or court ruling are wrong because its force came from persuasion and symbolism, not legal power. The speech became one of the defining public statements of the civil rights era.
items.explanationEs: King's "I Have a Dream" speech gave powerful language to the movement's vision of racial igualdad, ciudadanía, and moral urgency. Choices treating it as a law or court ruling are wrong because its force came from persuasion and symbolism, not legal power. The speech became one of the defining public statements of the derechos civiles era.

items.stem: What was significant about the integration of Clinton High School in Tennessee?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fue significativo sobre la integración de Clinton High School en Tennessee?

choices.text: A voter registration campaign in Mississippi facing violent opposition
choices.textEs: Fue la primera escuela con fondos federales en integrarse en la región

choices.text: Her refusal to give up her bus seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
choices.textEs: Fue la última escuela pública en integrarse en la antigua Confederación

choices.text: It was the first state-supported high school in the South to integrate
choices.textEs: Fue la primera escuela secundaria estatal del Sur en integrarse

choices.text: It established federal authority to enforce constitutional protections
choices.textEs: Se integró pacíficamente sin resistencia ni protesta de la comunidad

items.explanation: Clinton High School in Tennessee became the first state-supported high school in the South to integrate after Brown. Choices about Little Rock or Ole Miss are wrong because those conflicts happened later in Arkansas and Mississippi, not in Tennessee. The episode showed that desegregation battles were not limited to one state but spread across the South.
items.explanationEs: Clinton High School in Tennessee became the first state-supported high school in the South to integrate after Brown. Choices about Little Rock or Ole Miss are wrong because those conflicts happened later in Arkansas and Mississippi, not in Tennessee. The episode showed that desegregación battles were not limited to one state but spread across the South.

items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue el enfoque principal del Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. para lograr derechos civiles?

choices.text: Nonviolent resistance and peaceful civil disobedience tactics
choices.textEs: Resistencia no violenta y tácticas pacíficas de desobediencia civil

choices.text: Economic boycotts combined with organized armed self-defense
choices.textEs: Boicots económicos combinados con autodefensa armada organizada

choices.text: Legal challenges filed exclusively through the federal court system
choices.textEs: Desafíos legales presentados exclusivamente en el sistema de tribunales federales

choices.text: Black nationalism and advocacy for complete racial separation
choices.textEs: Nacionalismo negro y defensa de la separación racial completa

items.explanation: King believed nonviolent direct action should create public tension that exposed injustice and forced negotiation without using violence. Choices calling for armed retaliation are wrong because King grounded his strategy in peaceful civil disobedience. That approach helped the movement win moral credibility and national attention.

items.stem: What was Strom Thurmond's stance on civil rights legislation?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la postura de Strom Thurmond sobre la legislación de derechos civiles?

choices.text: He drafted and proposed compromise versions of civil rights bills
choices.textEs: Redactó y propuso versiones de compromiso de proyectos de derechos civiles

choices.text: He publicly supported it as a moderate bipartisan Southern Democrat
choices.textEs: La apoyó públicamente como demócrata moderado bipartidista del Sur

choices.text: He strategically abstained from voting on all civil rights measures
choices.textEs: Se abstuvo estratégicamente de votar en todas las medidas de derechos civiles

choices.text: He fiercely opposed it and conducted a record 24-hour filibuster
choices.textEs: Se opuso ferozmente y realizó un filibusterismo récord de 24 horas

items.explanation: Strom Thurmond fiercely opposed civil rights legislation and became famous for his 24-hour filibuster against an earlier civil rights bill. Choices describing him as a civil rights supporter are wrong because he was one of the movement's most visible Senate opponents. His resistance showed how deeply segregation was defended in national politics.
items.explanationEs: Strom Thurmond fiercely opposed derechos civiles legislación and became famous for his 24-hour filibuster against an earlier derechos civiles bill. Choices describing him as a derechos civiles supporter are wrong because he was one of the movement's most visible Senado opponents. His resistance showed how deeply segregación was defended in national politics.

items.stem: What was the outcome of the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue el resultado del Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery?

choices.text: The boycott collapsed after city officials arrested leaders
choices.textEs: El boicot colapsó después de que funcionarios arrestaron a los líderes

choices.text: Protesters accepted a compromise for seating in the rear
choices.textEs: Los manifestantes aceptaron un compromiso para asientos en la parte trasera

choices.text: The city agreed to hire African American bus drivers
choices.textEs: La ciudad acordó contratar conductores de autobús afroamericanos

choices.text: The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
choices.textEs: La Corte Suprema declaró inconstitucional la segregación en autobuses

items.explanation: The boycott ended after the courts ruled in Browder v. Gayle that segregated buses were unconstitutional and the Supreme Court let that ruling stand. Choices claiming the city voluntarily changed first are wrong because legal action was essential to the victory. The result proved that protest, community discipline, and court challenges could work together.
items.explanationEs: The boycott ended after the courts ruled in Browder v. Gayle that segregated buses were unconstitucional and the Corte Suprema let that ruling stand. Choices claiming the city voluntarily changed first are wrong because legal action was essential to the victory. The result proved that protest, community discipline, and court challenges could work together.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia de la Escuela Popular Highlander en Tennessee?

choices.text: It trained civil rights leaders in nonviolent organizing tactics
choices.textEs: Entrenó líderes de derechos civiles en tácticas de organización no violenta

choices.text: Shocked audiences and built support for civil rights legislation
choices.textEs: Fue la primera escuela pública integrada en Tennessee

choices.text: A voting rights march where marchers were beaten on Bloody Sunday
choices.textEs: Sirvió como sede del Fondo de Defensa Legal de la NAACP

choices.text: Fired workers, evicted tenants, and denied credit to supporters
choices.textEs: Fue el sitio donde se presentó por primera vez Brown v. Board

items.explanation: The Highlander Folk School in Tennessee trained activists such as Rosa Parks and others in citizenship education and nonviolent organizing. Choices that describe it as a protest site itself are wrong because its main role was training and preparation. It became an important behind-the-scenes institution in the movement.
items.explanationEs: The Highlander Folk School in Tennessee trained activists such as Rosa Parks and others in ciudadanía education and nonviolent organizing. Choices that describe it as a protest site itself are wrong because its main role was training and preparation. It became an important behind-the-scenes institution in the movement.

items.stem: What was Tent City in Fayette County, Tennessee?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fue Tent City en el Condado de Fayette, Tennessee?

choices.text: Protests at segregated lunch counters requesting service
choices.textEs: Un cuartel temporal para organizadores del Verano de la Libertad

choices.text: The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
choices.textEs: Un área de preparación para la huelga de trabajadores sanitarios de Memphis

choices.text: April 1968 in Memphis while supporting sanitation workers
choices.textEs: Un campo de entrenamiento para tácticas de resistencia no violenta

choices.text: A settlement for those evicted after registering to vote
choices.textEs: Un asentamiento para quienes fueron desalojados después de registrarse para votar

items.explanation: Tent City in Fayette County sheltered Black families who were evicted by white landowners after trying to register and vote. Choices about buses or lunch counters are wrong because this was a housing response to voter intimidation. The settlement showed the economic risks civil rights activists faced in rural communities.
items.explanationEs: Tent City in Fayette County sheltered Black families who were evicted by white landowners after trying to register and vote. Choices about buses or lunch counters are wrong because this was a housing response to voter intimidation. The settlement showed the economic risks derechos civiles activists faced in rural communities.

items.stem: What happened during the Birmingham bombings of 1963?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué sucedió durante los bombardeos de Birmingham de 1963?

choices.text: Nonviolent resistance and peaceful civil disobedience tactics
choices.textEs: Un autobús de los Viajeros de la Libertad fue incendiado fuera de la ciudad

choices.text: A 1963 protest where students faced fire hoses and police dogs
choices.textEs: Los vehículos de los alguaciles federales fueron destruidos con explosivos

choices.text: An MLK-led organization that coordinated nonviolent protests
choices.textEs: La sede de la SCLC fue atacada por segregacionistas

choices.text: The 16th Street Baptist Church was bombed, killing four girls
choices.textEs: La Iglesia Bautista de la Calle 16 fue bombardeada, matando a cuatro niñas

items.explanation: In September 1963, white supremacists bombed Birmingham's 16th Street Baptist Church, killing four African American girls. Choices about bus rides or voting drives are wrong because this was a terrorist attack on a church tied to the movement. The bombing deepened national outrage over violent resistance to civil rights.
items.explanationEs: In September 1963, white supremacists bombed Birmingham's 16th Street Baptist Church, killing four African American girls. Choices about bus rides or voting drives are wrong because this was a terrorist attack on a church tied to the movement. The bombing deepened national outrage over violent resistance to derechos civiles.

items.stem: How did President Eisenhower respond to the Little Rock Nine crisis?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo respondió el Presidente Eisenhower a la crisis de los Nueve de Little Rock?

choices.text: He publicly supported Governor Faubus' defiance of federal law
choices.textEs: Apoyó públicamente el desafío del Gobernador Faubus a la ley federal

choices.text: He declined to intervene in what he called a state matter
choices.textEs: Se negó a intervenir en lo que llamó un asunto estatal

choices.text: He sent federal troops to enforce the desegregation order
choices.textEs: Envió tropas federales para hacer cumplir la orden de desegregación

choices.text: He negotiated a gradual integration plan with Arkansas officials
choices.textEs: Negoció un plan de integración gradual con funcionarios de Arkansas

items.explanation: President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne and federalized the Arkansas National Guard to enforce desegregation at Little Rock Central High in 1957. A choice about negotiation alone is wrong because Eisenhower used military power to carry out a federal court order. The crisis showed that the federal government could step in when states defied constitutional rights.
items.explanationEs: President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne and federalized the Arkansas National Guard to enforce desegregación at Little Rock Central High in 1957. A choice about negotiation alone is wrong because Eisenhower used military power to carry out a federal court order. The crisis showed that the gobierno federal could step in when states defied constitucional rights.

items.stem: What role did the NAACP play in the Civil Rights Movement?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué papel jugó la NAACP en el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles?

choices.text: Used the National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine entry
choices.textEs: Organizar protestas de acción directa como sentadas y marchas

choices.text: Legal battles including Brown v. Board and activist defense
choices.textEs: Batallas legales incluyendo Brown v. Board y defensa de activistas

choices.text: A document signed by Southern congressmen denouncing Brown
choices.textEs: Entrenar activistas en técnicas de resistencia no violenta

choices.text: Advocated for Black separation and economic self-sufficiency
choices.textEs: Coordinar boicots económicos de negocios segregados

items.explanation: The NAACP fought segregation largely through legal cases, including Brown v. Board, while also supporting activists on the ground. Choices that portray it mainly as an armed group are wrong because its central strength was courtroom strategy and organized advocacy. Its work laid the legal groundwork for many later movement victories.
items.explanationEs: The NAACP fought segregación largely through legal cases, including Brown v. Board, while also supporting activists on the ground. items.stem: What was "massive resistance"?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fue la "resistencia masiva"?

choices.text: A theory that states could nullify federal rulings they opposed
choices.textEs: Una estrategia coordinada de protesta de derechos civiles en el Sur

choices.text: Being too vague and allowing Southern states to delay integration
choices.textEs: La estrategia legal integral de la NAACP contra la segregación

choices.text: It ordered desegregation to proceed with "all deliberate speed"
choices.textEs: Los esfuerzos del gobierno federal para hacer cumplir órdenes de integración

choices.text: Southern states' policy of defying Brown through school closures
choices.textEs: Política de estados del Sur de desafiar Brown mediante cierres de escuelas

items.explanation: Massive resistance was the Southern campaign to block Brown through school closures, delay tactics, and political defiance. Choices that describe peaceful acceptance are wrong because many Southern leaders openly organized against integration. This resistance explains why Brown did not quickly desegregate most Southern schools.

This resistance explains why Brown did not quickly desegregate most Southern schools.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Nashville sit-ins?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia de las sentadas de Nashville?

choices.text: A voting rights march where marchers were beaten on Bloody Sunday
choices.textEs: Fueron las primeras sentadas en resultar en arrestos masivos

choices.text: They became a model for nonviolent protest and integrated counters
choices.textEs: Se convirtieron en modelo de protesta no violenta e integraron mostradores

choices.text: Four college students sat at a segregated Woolworth lunch counter
choices.textEs: Terminaron sin lograr victorias de integración

choices.text: SCLC protests using children marchers that faced violent response
choices.textEs: Inspiraron la fundación del Fondo de Defensa Legal de la NAACP

items.explanation: The Nashville sit-ins trained students in disciplined nonviolence and helped force downtown lunch counters to desegregate. Choices that focus only on speeches are wrong because Nashville became important as an organizing model for direct action. Many future movement leaders, including John Lewis and Diane Nash, sharpened their skills there.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Poor People's Campaign?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia de la Campaña de los Pobres?

choices.text: MLK's 1968 campaign addressing economic injustice for all races
choices.textEs: La campaña de MLK de 1968 abordando injusticia económica para todas las razas

choices.text: Fired workers, evicted tenants, and denied credit to supporters
choices.textEs: Un esfuerzo para fortalecer el cumplimiento de la Ley de Derechos Civiles

choices.text: Their bus was firebombed and riders were beaten by an angry mob
choices.textEs: Una campaña enfocada exclusivamente en derechos de voto del Sur

choices.text: A 1963 protest where students faced fire hoses and police dogs
choices.textEs: Una campaña para expandir programas de acción afirmativa nacionalmente

items.explanation: The Poor People's Campaign was King's 1968 effort to push the nation beyond legal equality toward jobs, housing, and anti-poverty measures for people of all races. Choices that define it only as a school campaign are wrong because it focused on economic justice in Washington, D.C. It reflected King's belief that civil rights without economic security was incomplete.

It reflected King's belief that derechos civiles without economic security was incomplete.

items.stem: What was "Letter from Birmingham Jail"?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fue la "Carta desde la Cárcel de Birmingham"?

choices.text: A voter registration campaign in Mississippi facing violent opposition
choices.textEs: Una declaración pública de funcionarios de Birmingham defendiendo segregación

choices.text: Her refusal to give up her bus seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
choices.textEs: Un escrito legal presentado como parte de un caso federal de desegregación

choices.text: It was the first state-supported high school in the South to integrate
choices.textEs: Un manifiesto del SNCC pidiendo tácticas más agresivas

choices.text: MLK's letter defending nonviolent resistance and criticizing moderates
choices.textEs: Carta de MLK defendiendo resistencia no violenta y criticando a moderados

items.explanation: In "Letter from Birmingham Jail," King argued that unjust laws violate moral law and therefore should be disobeyed through nonviolent civil disobedience. Choices saying he rejected law completely are wrong because he insisted protesters accept legal penalties to expose injustice. The letter became one of the movement's clearest statements about law, conscience, and democracy.

items.stem: What legal doctrine did Brown v. Board of Education overturn?

choices.text: Being too vague and allowing Southern states to delay integration
choices.textEs: La doctrina de revisión judicial de Marbury v. Madison

choices.text: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which established "separate but equal"
choices.textEs: La doctrina de derechos de los estados de la era de la Guerra Civil

choices.text: The separate but equal doctrine established in Plessy v. Ferguson

choices.text: Declared school segregation unconstitutional and overturned Plessy

items.explanation: Brown v. Board overturned Plessy v. Ferguson, the 1896 case that had approved the "separate but equal" doctrine. Other options are wrong if they name later civil rights cases, because Plessy was the ruling that originally gave segregation constitutional cover. Ending Plessy's logic weakened Jim Crow far beyond the schoolhouse.

items.stem: What happened to the Freedom Riders when they arrived in Anniston, Alabama?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué les pasó a los Viajeros de la Libertad cuando llegaron a Anniston, Alabama?

choices.text: Fired workers, evicted tenants, and denied credit to supporters
choices.textEs: Fueron recibidos por simpatizantes locales de derechos civiles

choices.text: Their bus was firebombed and riders were beaten by an angry mob
choices.textEs: Su autobús fue incendiado y los viajeros fueron golpeados por una turba furiosa

Las opciones que sugieren que Eisenhower envió tropas por otras razones son incorrectas.

items.explanation: King drew from Mahatma Gandhi's example of civil disobedience, which meant resisting unjust laws peacefully and accepting punishment to reveal injustice. Choices about violent revolution are wrong because Gandhi influenced King toward disciplined nonviolence. This global connection shows that the civil rights movement borrowed tactics from other freedom struggles.
items.explanationEs: Martin Luther King Jr. estudió la filosofía no violenta de Mahatma Gandhi (satyagraha o "fuerza de la verdad") y la adaptó al movimiento de derechos civiles, viajando a la India en 1959 para estudiar las técnicas no violentas. King aplicó la resistencia no violenta a Montgomery, Birmingham y Selma. Las opciones que sugieren que King favorecía la confrontación armada son incorrectas.

items.stem: Which earlier Supreme Court doctrine did Brown v. Board of Education overturn in public education?

choices.text: Judicial review established in Marbury v. Madison
The exclusionary rule established in Mapp v. Ohio
The 'clear and present danger' test established in Schenck v. United States
The 'separate but equal' doctrine established in Plessy v. Ferguson

items.explanation: Brown v. Board of Education (347 U.S. 483, 1954) unanimously overturned the 'separate but equal' doctrine that the Court had established in Plessy v. Ferguson (163 U.S. 537, 1896). The Brown Court held that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,' violating the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. Marbury (judicial review), Mapp (exclusionary rule), and Schenck (clear and present danger) involve unrelated constitutional doctrines.
items.explanationEs: Brown v. Board of Education (347 U.S. 483, 1954) anuló por unanimidad la doctrina de 'separados pero iguales' que la Corte había establecido en Plessy v. Ferguson (163 U.S. 537, 1896). La Corte de Brown sostuvo que 'las instalaciones educativas separadas son inherentemente desiguales,' violando la Cláusula de Igual Protección de la Decimocuarta Enmienda. Marbury (revisión judicial), Mapp (regla de exclusión) y Schenck (peligro claro y presente) involucran doctrinas constitucionales no relacionadas.

This aerial photograph shows the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August 28, 1963. An estimated 250,000 people are gathered along the National Mall and around the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., facing the Lincoln Memorial. The massive crowd stretches from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial far down the length of the Mall. It was at this event that Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech.

(Photograph of the March on Washington, August 28, 1963. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.)

What was the primary purpose of the March on Washington in 1963?

choices.text: To demand that the federal government end the military draft and reduce defense spending
To protest U.S. involvement in the Korean War and call for withdrawal of troops
To demand federal civil rights legislation and draw national attention to racial inequality in jobs and public life

items.explanation: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom was organized to pressure Congress and President Kennedy to pass comprehensive civil rights legislation and to draw national attention to racial inequality in employment and public life. Choice B confuses the march's domestic focus with a foreign policy objective. Choice D gets the chronology wrong — the Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964, after the march.

items.explanationEs: Malcolm X defendió el nacionalismo negro, la autodefensa y la autodeterminación, rechazando inicialmente la integración como meta y argumentando que los afroamericanos deberían lograr la libertad "por cualquier medio necesario". Después de su peregrinación de 1964 a La Meca, las opiniones de Malcolm X evolucionaron hacia una mayor cooperación interracial.

items.explanation: The murders of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner during Freedom Summer shocked the nation because the men were killed for helping register Black voters. Choices that treat the killings as a local issue are wrong because they intensified national demands for federal civil rights action. The case revealed the deadly alliance of racism and political exclusion in Mississippi.

choices.text: It trained civil rights leaders in nonviolent organizing tactics

items.explanation: Television brought scenes of peaceful protesters being attacked into millions of homes, especially during Birmingham and Selma. Choices about reducing attention are wrong because the images increased public sympathy and pressure on national leaders. Mass media turned local civil rights struggles into national political crises.

items.explanation: Rosa Parks refused to surrender her seat on a Montgomery bus in December 1955, and her arrest helped launch the 381-day Montgomery Bus Boycott. A choice about organizing Nashville sit-ins is wrong because that work is associated with Diane Nash, not Parks. Her action helped turn a local protest into a national civil rights breakthrough.

items.stem: What were sit-ins and how did they advance the civil rights movement?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fueron las sentadas y cómo avanzaron el movimiento de derechos civiles?

choices.text: Protesters sat at segregated lunch counters until served, forcing businesses to desegregate
choices.textEs: Los manifestantes se sentaban en mostradores de almuerzo segregados hasta ser servidos, forzando a los negocios a desegregarse

choices.text: Workers refusing to leave factories until employers granted desegregated workspaces
choices.textEs: Trabajadores que se negaban a salir de las fábricas hasta que los empleadores otorgaran espacios laborales desegregados

choices.text: Silent vigils held outside southern courthouses during civil rights trials
choices.textEs: Vigilias silenciosas frente a tribunales del sur durante juicios de derechos civiles

choices.text: Boycotts of department stores in the North to pressure southern affiliates
choices.textEs: Boicots de grandes almacenes en el norte para presionar a las filiales del sur

items.explanation: Sit-ins were nonviolent protests in which students sat at segregated lunch counters and asked to be served, forcing businesses to confront segregation publicly. A choice about bus boycotts is wrong because sit-ins targeted lunch counters and stores, not transportation. They helped launch a new phase of youth-led direct action in 1960.
items.explanationEs: Las sentadas comenzaron el 1 de febrero de 1960 cuando cuatro estudiantes afroamericanos de Carolina del Norte A&T se sentaron en el mostrador del almuerzo "solo para blancos" de Woolworth en Greensboro, Carolina del Norte. Las sentadas se extendieron a aproximadamente sesenta ciudades del Sur a finales de marzo de 1960 y llevaron a la fundación del SNCC. Las opciones que las describen como violentas o limitadas a una ciudad son incorrectas.

choices.text: Over 250,000 people gathered and King delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech
choices.textEs: Más de 250,000 personas se reunieron y King pronunció su discurso "Tengo un Sueño"

choices.text: About 25,000 people gathered to demand immediate withdrawal from the Vietnam War
choices.textEs: Alrededor de 25,000 personas se reunieron para exigir la retirada inmediata de la Guerra de Vietnam

choices.text: A march of veterans demanding earlier payment of the World War II GI Bill bonus
choices.textEs: Una marcha de veteranos exigiendo el pago anticipado del bono de la Ley GI de la Segunda Guerra Mundial

choices.text: A women's suffrage parade that influenced the 19th Amendment's passage
choices.textEs: Un desfile por el sufragio femenino que influyó en la aprobación de la Enmienda 19

items.explanation: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom was the massive 1963 rally where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech. A is wrong because anti-draft protests were about Vietnam, not this civil rights demonstration in Washington. The march showed the movement could unite moral protest with demands for jobs and federal legislation.
items.explanationEs: La Marcha sobre Washington del 28 de agosto de 1963 reunió a unas 250,000 personas en el National Mall y presentó el discurso "I Have a Dream" de Martin Luther King Jr. Construyó apoyo nacional para la legislación pendiente que se convirtió en la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964. Las opciones que la confunden con Selma o con un evento posterior son incorrectas.

It showed the strength of organized nonviolent protest and launched Martin Luther King Jr. to national prominence.

items.explanation: Malcolm X argued for Black nationalism, self-defense, and self-determination, which contrasted sharply with King's strategy of nonviolent integration. Choices that make him the founder of nonviolent protest are wrong because he criticized that approach for much of his public life. His ideas shaped the rise of Black Power and broadened debate within the freedom struggle.

Choices that describe it as a court case are wrong because Birmingham was a street protest campaign. Its televised brutality helped push the Kennedy administration toward stronger civil rights legislation.

items.stemEs: La "Carta desde la Cárcel de Birmingham" de Martin Luther King Jr. (1963) respondió a clérigos blancos que llamaron a sus protestas "imprudentes e inoportunas." ¿Cuál fue el argumento central de King?

items.explanation: In "Letter from Birmingham Jail," King argued that unjust laws violate moral law and therefore should be disobeyed through nonviolent civil disobedience. Choices saying he rejected law completely are wrong because he insisted protesters accept legal penalties to expose injustice. The letter became one of the movement's clearest statements about law, conscience, and democracy.
items.explanationEs: King distinguía entre leyes justas e injustas, argumentando que desobedecer leyes injustas aceptando las consecuencias demuestra el más alto respeto por la ley.

choices.text: Federal stimulus spending inevitably produces inflation regardless of economic context

choices.textEs: The service sector of the economy was more resilient than manufacturing to pandemic disruption

choices.text: The United States needed to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity that had been lost to globalization
choices.textEs: The United States needed to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity that had been lost to globalización

Choices saying the problem was only domestic are wrong because the disruption spread through international networks. The pandemic made economic interdependence visible to ordinary consumers.

items.stem: The qualified immunity doctrine — which shields police officers from civil liability unless they violated 'clearly established' law — has been criticized by police reform advocates because —
items.stemEs: The qualified immunity doctrine — which shields police officers from civil liability unless they violated 'clearly established' law — has been criticized by police reform advocates because —

choices.text: Courts interpret 'clearly established' so narrowly that almost any use of force is immune from civil lawsuits
choices.textEs: Courts interpret 'clearly established' so narrowly that almost any use of force is immune from civil lawsuits

choices.text: It prevents criminal prosecution of officers who use excessive force
choices.textEs: It prevents criminal prosecution of officers who use excessive force

choices.text: The Supreme Court created it without constitutional authority in a series of decisions beginning in the 1960s

choices.text: It applies only to sworn officers, creating unequal treatment between police and private security
choices.textEs: It applies only to sworn officers, creating unequal treatment between police and private security

items.explanation: Qualified immunity has been criticized because courts often require a nearly identical previous case before allowing civil suits against officers, which makes accountability difficult. Choices saying the doctrine guarantees every victim a remedy are wrong because critics argue it blocks many claims. The debate shows how legal doctrine can shape the practical limits of civil-rights enforcement.
