items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, passed by Congress on August 7, 1964 (Joint Resolution of Congress H.J. RES 1145, 88th Congress, 2d Session, August 7, 1964; National Archives, Record Group 46):

"Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That the Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression... the United States is, therefore, prepared, as the President determines, to take all necessary steps, including the use of armed force, to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty requesting assistance in defense of its freedom."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Vietnam War and the domestic anti-war movement (US.78, US.79), write a constructed response that:
1. States a clear CLAIM about how the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution shaped both U.S. military escalation in Vietnam AND the growth of domestic opposition to the war.
2. Provides specific EVIDENCE from the document and from your knowledge of events between 1964 and 1971 (including the Pentagon Papers, major protests, and congressional debates).
3. Explains the REASONING that connects the resolution's broad grant of presidential war-making authority to the erosion of public trust and the rise of the anti-war movement.

Your response should be 1–2 paragraphs and demonstrate synthesis across both standards —
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín, aprobada por el Congreso el 7 de agosto de 1964 (Resolución Conjunta del Congreso H.J. RES 1145, 88.º Congreso, 2.ª Sesión, 7 de agosto de 1964; Archivos Nacionales, Grupo de Registros 46):

«Resuelto por el Senado y la Cámara de Representantes de los Estados Unidos de América reunidos en Congreso, que el Congreso aprueba y apoya la determinación del Presidente, en su calidad de Comandante en Jefe, de tomar todas las medidas necesarias para repeler cualquier ataque armado contra las fuerzas de los Estados Unidos y para prevenir una mayor agresión... los Estados Unidos están, por lo tanto, preparados, según lo determine el Presidente, para tomar todos los pasos necesarios, incluyendo el uso de la fuerza armada, para ayudar a cualquier miembro o estado protocolar del Tratado de Defensa Colectiva del Sureste Asiático que solicite asistencia en defensa de su libertad.»

Usando este fragmento y tu conocimiento de la Guerra de Vietnam y el movimiento antibelicista interno (US.78, US.79), escribe una respuesta construida que:
1. Formule un ARGUMENTO claro sobre cómo la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín configuró tanto la escalada militar de EE. UU. en Vietnam como el crecimiento de la oposición doméstica a la guerra.
2. Proporcione EVIDENCIA específica del documento y de tu conocimiento de los eventos entre 1964 y 1971 (incluyendo los Papeles del Pentágono, las principales protestas y los debates del Congreso).
3. Explique el RAZONAMIENTO que conecta la amplia autoridad presidencial para hacer la guerra concedida por la resolución con la erosión de la confianza pública y el surgimiento del movimiento antibelicista.

Tu respuesta debe tener 1–2 párrafos y demostrar síntesis entre ambos estándares.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4/4) response would include: CLAIM — The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution's sweeping delegation of war-making authority to the president, passed under disputed circumstances, enabled an open-ended military escalation in Vietnam that, once exposed as built on deception, directly fueled the domestic anti-war movement and shattered public confidence in government. EVIDENCE — The resolution's language ('all necessary measures') gave LBJ a blank check to expand U.S. involvement without a formal declaration of war; U.S. troop levels grew from ~23,000 advisors in 1964 to over 500,000 combat troops by 1968; the Tet Offensive (1968) contradicted official claims of imminent victory; the Pentagon Papers (leaked 1971) revealed that the Johnson administration had misled Congress about the extent of the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident and had secretly planned escalation before the resolution passed; major protests included the 1969 Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam (organizer estimate ~2 million participants nationwide), the Kent State killings (May 1970), and the Vietnam Veterans Against the War's Dewey Canyon III (1971). REASONING — The resolution created a feedback loop: unchecked presidential authority enabled escalation justified by misleading information, while the gap between official optimism and battlefield reality (the 'credibility gap') converted initially moderate citizens into protesters and emboldened congressional doves, ultimately producing the War Powers Resolution of 1973 as a structural correction.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.78, US.79 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: States a defensible, specific claim that explicitly links the resolution's grant of authority to both escalation (US.78) and the anti-war movement (US.79). Cites at least two specific pieces of evidence from knowledge (e.g., troop escalation data, Tet Offensive, Pentagon Papers, named protest events). Reasoning fully connects claim to evidence, explains the mechanism (credibility gap, deception, unchecked authority), and synthesizes across both standards without prompting.
3 - Proficient: States a clear claim connecting the resolution to escalation and domestic opposition. Cites at least one specific piece of evidence from the document and one from broader knowledge. Reasoning is present but may not fully explain the mechanism or may address one standard more thoroughly than the other.
2 - Developing: States a partial claim (addresses escalation OR opposition but not both). Cites general evidence without specificity (e.g., 'there were protests' without naming events or dates). Reasoning is limited or lists facts without explaining the connection.
1 - Beginning: Restates the document without analysis, or makes a claim unsupported by evidence. May show basic comprehension of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution but does not connect it to the anti-war movement.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution language ('all necessary measures'); disputed nature of the August 4, 1964 incident; LBJ's troop escalation 1965–1968 (500,000+ troops); Tet Offensive (January 1968) as credibility gap moment; Pentagon Papers (1971) revealing deliberate deception; specific protests (1969 Moratorium, Kent State 1970, VVAW 1971); congressional response culminating in War Powers Resolution (1973).
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Formula un argumento defensible y específico que vincula explícitamente la autoridad conferida por la resolución tanto con la escalada (US.78) como con el movimiento antibelicista (US.79). Cita al menos dos piezas específicas de evidencia del conocimiento propio (p. ej., datos de escalada de tropas, Ofensiva Tet, Papeles del Pentágono, eventos de protesta nombrados). El razonamiento conecta plenamente el argumento con la evidencia, explica el mecanismo (brecha de credibilidad, engaño, autoridad sin control) y sintetiza ambos estándares sin necesidad de indicaciones adicionales.
3 - Competente: Formula un argumento claro que conecta la resolución con la escalada y la oposición interna. Cita al menos una pieza específica de evidencia del documento y una del conocimiento más amplio. El razonamiento está presente pero puede no explicar completamente el mecanismo o puede abordar un estándar con más profundidad que el otro.
2 - En desarrollo: Formula un argumento parcial (aborda la escalada O la oposición, pero no ambas). Cita evidencia general sin especificidad. El razonamiento es limitado o enumera hechos sin explicar la conexión.
1 - Inicial: Reitera el documento sin análisis, o formula un argumento sin evidencia. Puede mostrar comprensión básica de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín pero no la conecta con el movimiento antibelicista.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Lenguaje de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín ('todas las medidas necesarias'); naturaleza disputada del incidente del 4 de agosto de 1964; escalada de tropas de LBJ 1965–1968 (más de 500,000 tropas); Ofensiva Tet (enero 1968) como momento de brecha de credibilidad; Papeles del Pentágono (1971) que revelan engaño deliberado; protestas específicas (Moratoria de 1969, Kent State 1970, VVAW 1971); respuesta del Congreso que culminó en la Resolución de Poderes de Guerra (1973).

items.stem:
DIRECTIONS: Analyze the three primary source excerpts below. Then write a response that constructs a historical argument answering the following question:

How did the shift in U.S. Vietnam War strategy from escalation under LBJ to Vietnamization under Nixon reflect changing domestic and constitutional constraints on presidential war-making authority, and what were the long-term consequences for the balance of power between the executive and legislative branches?

Your response must:
- Analyze at least TWO of the three documents using the HIPP framework (Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, Point of View)
- Synthesize evidence across the documents to support a historical argument
- Connect to your own knowledge of events and consequences beyond the documents
- Address standards US.78 and US.80

---
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (H.J. Res. 1145), Joint Resolution of Congress, August 7, 1964. National Archives, Record Group 46.
Excerpt: "The Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression... This resolution shall expire when the President shall determine that the peace and security of the area is reasonably assured by international conditions created by action of the United Nations or otherwise."

---
DOCUMENT 2
Source: President Richard Nixon, 'Address to the Nation on the War in Vietnam' (Vietnamization Speech), November 3, 1969. Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States. National Archives and Records Administration.
Excerpt: "The precipitate withdrawal of American forces from Vietnam would be a disaster not only for South Vietnam but for the United States and for the cause of peace... I have initiated a plan which will end this war and serve the cause of peace — not just in Vietnam but in the Pacific and in the world. In the previous administration, we Americanized the war in Vietnam. In this administration, we are Vietnamizing the search for peace."

---
DOCUMENT 3
Source: War Powers Resolution (Public Law 93-148), passed by Congress over President Nixon's veto, November 7, 1973. United States Statutes at Large, 87 Stat. 555. National Archives.
Excerpt: "The constitutional powers of the President as Commander-in-Chief to introduce United States Armed Forces into hostilities, or into situations where imminent involvement in hostilities is clearly indicated by the circumstances, are exercised only pursuant to (1) a declaration of war, (2) specific statutory authorization, or (3) a national emergency created by attack upon the United States... The President shall, in every possible instance, consult with Congress before introducing United States Armed Forces into hostilities..."

---
Use HIPP to analyze the documents, then construct your argument in 2–3 paragraphs.
items.stemEs:
INSTRUCCIONES: Analiza los tres fragmentos de fuentes primarias a continuación. Luego escribe una respuesta que construya un argumento histórico respondiendo la siguiente pregunta:

¿Cómo reflejó el cambio en la estrategia de EE. UU. en la Guerra de Vietnam, de la escalada bajo LBJ a la Vietnamización bajo Nixon, los cambiantes límites domésticos y constitucionales sobre la autoridad presidencial para hacer la guerra, y cuáles fueron las consecuencias a largo plazo para el equilibrio de poder entre los poderes ejecutivo y legislativo?

Tu respuesta debe:
- Analizar al menos DOS de los tres documentos usando el marco HIPP (Contexto Histórico, Audiencia Prevista, Propósito, Punto de Vista)
- Sintetizar evidencia de todos los documentos para apoyar un argumento histórico
- Conectar con tu propio conocimiento de eventos y consecuencias más allá de los documentos
- Abordar los estándares US.78 y US.80

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín (H.J. Res. 1145), Resolución Conjunta del Congreso, 7 de agosto de 1964. Archivos Nacionales, Grupo de Registros 46.
Fragmento: «El Congreso aprueba y apoya la determinación del Presidente, en su calidad de Comandante en Jefe, de tomar todas las medidas necesarias para repeler cualquier ataque armado contra las fuerzas de los Estados Unidos y para prevenir una mayor agresión... Esta resolución expirará cuando el Presidente determine que la paz y la seguridad del área están razonablemente garantizadas por condiciones internacionales creadas por la acción de las Naciones Unidas o de otra manera.»

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Presidente Richard Nixon, 'Discurso a la Nación sobre la Guerra en Vietnam' (Discurso de Vietnamización), 3 de noviembre de 1969. Documentos Públicos de los Presidentes de los Estados Unidos. Administración Nacional de Archivos y Registros.
Fragmento: «El retiro precipitado de las fuerzas estadounidenses de Vietnam sería un desastre no solo para Vietnam del Sur sino para los Estados Unidos y para la causa de la paz... He iniciado un plan que pondrá fin a esta guerra y servirá a la causa de la paz, no solo en Vietnam sino en el Pacífico y en el mundo. En la administración anterior, americanizamos la guerra en Vietnam. En esta administración, estamos vietnamizando la búsqueda de la paz.»

---
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Resolución de Poderes de Guerra (Ley Pública 93-148), aprobada por el Congreso sobre el veto del Presidente Nixon, 7 de noviembre de 1973. Estatutos de los Estados Unidos, 87 Stat. 555. Archivos Nacionales.
Fragmento: «Los poderes constitucionales del Presidente como Comandante en Jefe para introducir Fuerzas Armadas de los Estados Unidos en hostilidades... se ejercen solo en virtud de (1) una declaración de guerra, (2) autorización estatutaria específica, o (3) una emergencia nacional creada por un ataque a los Estados Unidos... El Presidente deberá, en todo caso posible, consultar con el Congreso antes de introducir Fuerzas Armadas de los Estados Unidos en hostilidades...»

---
Usa HIPP para analizar los documentos, luego construye tu argumento en 2–3 párrafos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (6/6) response would include: ARGUMENT — The arc from the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) to Vietnamization (1969) to the War Powers Resolution (1973) traces a constitutional correction: Congress first surrendered its war-making authority under the pressure of Cold War crisis management, then watched an unchecked executive expand and extend an increasingly unpopular war, and finally reclaimed that authority through legislation passed over a presidential veto. HIPP ANALYSIS (Doc 1) — Historical context: August 1964, second Gulf of Tonkin incident, Cold War context of communist containment; Intended audience: American public and Congress needing justification for escalation; Purpose: grant the president open-ended military authority without a formal declaration of war; Point of view: reflects Cold War consensus that executive flexibility was necessary but contains the seeds of its own overreach (no sunset clause enforceable by Congress, only by the president). HIPP ANALYSIS (Doc 2) — Historical context: 1969, peak U.S. casualties, Tet Offensive aftermath, growing anti-war movement; Audience: 'silent majority' of Americans Nixon was trying to hold together against protesters; Purpose: reframe escalation as responsible drawdown to buy time and domestic support; Point of view: Nixon presents Vietnamization as peace-seeking while simultaneously planning Operation Menu (secret Cambodia bombing); reveals the 'credibility gap' — official rhetoric diverged from covert reality. HIPP ANALYSIS (Doc 3) — Historical context: 1973, Paris Peace Accords signed, Watergate unfolding, Cambodia bombing just ended; Audience: future presidents and Congress; Purpose: structurally prevent another Gulf of Tonkin-style delegation by codifying presidential consultation and 60-day authorization requirements; Point of view: reflects Congress's post-Vietnam determination to reclaim constitutional war powers. SYNTHESIS — Documents 1 and 3 together show Congress giving and then taking back war-making authority; Document 2 reveals the mechanism — executive deception and unilateral action — that made Document 3 necessary. Outside knowledge: Pentagon Papers (1971) exposed the deception behind Doc 1; Nixon's Cambodia bombing violated the spirit of Doc 2's promise of Vietnamization; War Powers Resolution has never been successfully enforced, raising questions about whether Congress permanently recovered its authority.

Read the following excerpt from the U.S. Supreme Court's unanimous decision in Brown v. Board of Education (1954), written by Chief Justice Earl Warren. Source: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954), National Archives, archives.gov.

"We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement, construct a written response that (1) identifies the constitutional principle the Court relied upon to overturn Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), (2) explains how the Brown decision created the legal foundation that activists used during the Montgomery Bus Boycott (US.72) and the sit-in movement (US.74), and (3) evaluates whether the Supreme Court's ruling alone was sufficient to dismantle school segregation. Use the CER framework: state a clear Claim, support it with specific Evidence from the source and from your knowledge, and explain your Reasoning.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente extracto de la decisión unánime de la Corte Suprema de los EE. UU. en el caso Brown contra Board of Education (1954), escrita por el Presidente de la Corte Suprema Earl Warren. Fuente: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954), Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"Concluimos que, en el campo de la educación pública, la doctrina de 'separado pero igual' no tiene lugar. Las instalaciones educativas separadas son intrínsecamente desiguales. Por lo tanto, sostenemos que los demandantes y otros en situaciones similares por quienes se han presentado las acciones están, a causa de la segregación de la que se quejan, privados de la protección igualitaria de las leyes garantizada por la Decimocuarta Enmienda."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles, construya una respuesta escrita que (1) identifique el principio constitucional en el que la Corte se basó para anular Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), (2) explique cómo la decisión Brown creó la base legal que los activistas usaron durante el Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery (US.72) y el movimiento de sentadas (US.74), y (3) evalúe si el fallo de la Corte Suprema por sí solo fue suficiente para desmantelar la segregación escolar. Use el marco CER: declare una Afirmación clara, apóyela con Evidencia específica de la fuente y de su conocimiento, y explique su Razonamiento.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Brown decision dismantled the constitutional framework of segregation by invoking the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, but the ruling required sustained grassroots activism and federal enforcement to produce real change. EVIDENCE: The excerpt explicitly cites the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause as the basis for overturning Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine. Students should note that Rosa Parks and the MBB organizers (US.72) invoked Brown as precedent when challenging bus segregation in Browder v. Gayle (1956). Nashville sit-in organizers (US.74), including Diane Nash and SNCC, used the legal logic of Brown to argue that any racially segregated public accommodation violated equal protection. Students should cite 'massive resistance' — including Governor Orval Faubus's defiance at Little Rock (US.73) — as evidence that the ruling alone was insufficient. REASONING: Should explain the gap between legal principle and social/political implementation, noting that Brown established constitutional authority but not enforcement machinery, requiring executive action (Eisenhower's deployment of the 101st Airborne, US.73) and eventual legislation (Civil Rights Act of 1964, US.76).

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Browder v. Gayle, 352 U.S. 903 (1956), affirming the lower court ruling that declared Montgomery's bus segregation unconstitutional. Source: Browder v. Gayle, United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama (1956), affirmed by the Supreme Court; National Archives, archives.gov.

"The separate but equal doctrine can no longer be safely followed as a correct statement of the law. In fact, the separate but equal doctrine in public transportation finds no support in the recent decisions of the Supreme Court... We hold that the statutes and ordinances requiring segregation of the white and colored races on the motor buses of a common carrier of passengers in the City of Montgomery and its police jurisdiction violate the due process and equal protection of the law clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, construct a response that (1) explains how the 381-day boycott itself — rather than the court ruling alone — transformed the political and economic pressure necessary to end bus segregation, (2) analyzes the role of organizational networks (including the Montgomery Improvement Association and the black church) in sustaining the boycott, and (3) connects the boycott's nonviolent strategy to the broader philosophy that would guide later civil rights campaigns such as the sit-ins (US.74) and the March on Washington (US.75). Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente extracto de la decisión de la Corte Suprema de los EE. UU. en Browder v. Gayle, 352 U.S. 903 (1956), que confirmó el fallo del tribunal inferior que declaró inconstitucional la segregación en los autobuses de Montgomery. Fuente: Browder v. Gayle, Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Medio de Alabama (1956), confirmado por la Corte Suprema; Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"La doctrina de separado pero igual ya no puede seguirse con seguridad como una declaración correcta de la ley. De hecho, la doctrina de separado pero igual en el transporte público no encuentra apoyo en las decisiones recientes de la Corte Suprema... Sostenemos que los estatutos y ordenanzas que requieren la segregación de las razas blanca y de color en los autobuses de motor de un transportista común de pasajeros en la Ciudad de Montgomery y su jurisdicción policial violan las cláusulas de debido proceso y protección igualitaria de la ley de la Decimocuarta Enmienda."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery, construya una respuesta que (1) explique cómo el boicot de 381 días en sí mismo — y no solo el fallo judicial — transformó la presión política y económica necesaria para poner fin a la segregación en los autobuses, (2) analice el papel de las redes organizativas (incluida la Asociación para el Mejoramiento de Montgomery y la iglesia negra) en el sostenimiento del boicot, y (3) conecte la estrategia no violenta del boicot con la filosofía más amplia que guiaría campañas posteriores de derechos civiles como las sentadas (US.74) y la Marcha sobre Washington (US.75). Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Montgomery Bus Boycott succeeded not primarily because of the court ruling but because the African American community demonstrated that sustained economic and moral pressure, organized through existing institutions, could force change — a model that became the template for the entire Civil Rights Movement. EVIDENCE: The 381-day boycott (Dec. 5, 1955 – Dec. 21, 1956) deprived the Montgomery bus system of ~65–70% of its ridership and significant revenue. The Montgomery Improvement Association, formed in December 1955 with MLK as president, coordinated carpools, mass meetings at black churches (Dexter Avenue Baptist Church), and communication networks. The Highlander Folk School in Tennessee provided early training. The black church provided organizational infrastructure, meeting space, and moral framing. The nonviolent philosophy drew on Gandhi's satyagraha — referenced in King's early speeches. Students should connect this to Nashville sit-in organizers' use of nonviolent direct action (US.74) and King's 'I Have a Dream' emphasis on moral suasion over militant confrontation (US.75). REASONING: Should explain why nonviolent strategy maximized moral legitimacy and media sympathy while minimizing legal pretexts for mass arrest, creating a template repeated throughout the movement.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from President Dwight D. Eisenhower's radio and television address to the nation on the situation in Little Rock, Arkansas, September 24, 1957. Source: Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1957, U.S. Government Printing Office; available at the Eisenhower Presidential Library and National Archives, archives.gov.

"In that city, under the leadership of demagogic extremists, disorderly mobs have deliberately prevented the carrying out of proper orders from a Federal Court... Whenever normal agencies prove inadequate to the task and it becomes necessary for the executive branch of the Federal Government to use its powers and authority to uphold Federal Courts, the President's responsibility is inescapable. In accordance with that responsibility, I have today issued an Executive Order directing the use of troops under Federal authority to aid in the execution of Federal law at Little Rock, Arkansas."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Little Rock Crisis, construct a response that (1) analyzes why Eisenhower — who was personally ambivalent about integration — chose to intervene at Little Rock, (2) explains the constitutional basis for his authority to deploy federal troops against a state governor's resistance, and (3) evaluates the significance of this moment as a precedent for federal enforcement of civil rights law, connecting it to the later federal enforcement provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (US.76). Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente extracto del discurso de radio y televisión del Presidente Dwight D. Eisenhower a la nación sobre la situación en Little Rock, Arkansas, el 24 de septiembre de 1957. Fuente: Documentos Públicos de los Presidentes de los Estados Unidos: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1957, Imprenta del Gobierno de los EE. UU.; disponible en la Biblioteca Presidencial Eisenhower y los Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"En esa ciudad, bajo el liderazgo de extremistas demagógicos, turbas desordenadas han impedido deliberadamente el cumplimiento de las órdenes adecuadas de un Tribunal Federal... Cuando las agencias normales resultan inadecuadas para la tarea y se hace necesario que la rama ejecutiva del Gobierno Federal use sus poderes y autoridad para defender los Tribunales Federales, la responsabilidad del Presidente es ineludible. En cumplimiento de esa responsabilidad, hoy he emitido una Orden Ejecutiva ordenando el uso de tropas bajo autoridad federal para ayudar en la ejecución de la ley federal en Little Rock, Arkansas."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento de la Crisis de Little Rock, construya una respuesta que (1) analice por qué Eisenhower — quien personalmente era ambivalente sobre la integración — eligió intervenir en Little Rock, (2) explique la base constitucional de su autoridad para desplegar tropas federales contra la resistencia de un gobernador estatal, y (3) evalúe la importancia de este momento como precedente para la aplicación federal de la ley de derechos civiles, conectándolo con las disposiciones posteriores de aplicación federal de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 (US.76). Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: Eisenhower's intervention at Little Rock, motivated more by constitutional duty than personal support for integration, established the critical precedent that the federal executive would enforce federal court orders against state resistance — a precedent that shaped how the Civil Rights Act of 1964 would be enforced. EVIDENCE: Eisenhower had not personally endorsed Brown and resisted pressuring the South; his intervention was triggered specifically by Governor Orval Faubus's use of the Arkansas National Guard to block the nine Black students (September 4, 1957) and the subsequent mob violence that made federal authority look weak. The constitutional basis is Article II (executive power), the Supremacy Clause, and the Enforcement Acts tradition dating to Reconstruction — Eisenhower cited his duty to uphold federal court orders under these authorities. He deployed the 101st Airborne Division (deployment ordered September 24, 1957; first full day of escorted attendance September 25, 1957) and federalized the Arkansas National Guard. Students should connect this to the enforcement provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (US.76), particularly Title VII enforcement through the EEOC and Title II enforcement through DOJ, which built on the precedent that federal authority supersedes state resistance. REASONING: Should explain that constitutional order (separation of powers, supremacy clause) rather than civil rights ideology drove Eisenhower's decision — making it paradoxically more durable as precedent because it was rooted in institutional authority rather than personal politics.

GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: El estudiante construye una afirmación precisa que distingue las motivaciones de Eisenhower (deber constitucional frente a ideología personal). Explica con precisión la base constitucional (Cláusula de Supremacía, Artículo II, autoridad ejecutiva sobre la aplicación de los fallos de los tribunales federales). Establece una conexión explícita y analíticamente desarrollada con el mecanismo de aplicación de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964. El razonamiento aborda la distinción entre motivaciones ideológicas y constitucionales y por qué la base constitucional hizo que el precedente fuera duradero. Históricamente específico y analíticamente sofisticado.
3 - Competente: El estudiante establece una afirmación clara sobre las motivaciones e intervención de Eisenhower. Identifica la base constitucional con razonable precisión. Establece una conexión con el mecanismo de aplicación de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 con cierta profundidad analítica. El razonamiento es adecuado.
2 - En desarrollo: El estudiante describe la crisis de Little Rock y la intervención de Eisenhower, pero puede exagerar el apoyo personal de Eisenhower a la integración. La base constitucional se menciona de manera vaga o incorrecta. La conexión con la Ley de Derechos Civiles es general o superficial.
1 - Inicial: El estudiante ofrece una narrativa básica de Little Rock con poco análisis de motivaciones o base constitucional. La afirmación puede estar ausente. Poca conexión con la legislación posterior de derechos civiles.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Uso por parte del gobernador Faubus de la Guardia Nacional de Arkansas para bloquear la integración (4 de septiembre de 1957); violencia de masas el 23 de septiembre; despliegue de Eisenhower de la 101.ª División Aerotransportada (despliegue ordenado el 24 de septiembre de 1957; primera asistencia escoltada el 25 de septiembre); federalización de la Guardia Nacional de Arkansas; ambivalencia personal de Eisenhower hacia Brown; base constitucional de la Cláusula de Supremacía y el Artículo II; Leyes de Aplicación de la era de la Reconstrucción como precedente; aplicación de los Títulos II y VII de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 a través del DOJ y la EEOC.

The Nashville sit-in campaign of 1960 is recognized as one of the most strategically disciplined and philosophically sophisticated direct-action campaigns in the Civil Rights Movement. Diane Nash, a Nashville native and Fisk University student, emerged as a central organizer. The following excerpt is from Diane Nash's testimony before the Nashville Community Relations Conference, April 1960, as recorded in Nashville's Banner newspaper and archived through the Nashville Public Library Civil Rights Collection. Source: Diane Nash, statement to Nashville Community Relations Conference, April 1960; Nashville Public Library Civil Rights Collection; digitized records available through the Tennessee State Library and Archives.

"We will not stop. We are not doing this because it is comfortable — we are doing this because we must. We have been trained to accept any suffering that comes, to meet hatred with love, to refuse to strike back. If they arrest us, there will be more to take our places. This movement will not be stopped by violence because the strength of our cause is greater than anything they can do to us."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Nashville sit-in movement, construct a response that (1) explains the specific training regimen and philosophical framework that made Nashville's sit-in campaign distinctive among early civil rights protests, (2) analyzes how the success of the Nashville campaign — including the economic boycott of downtown merchants and the April 1960 meeting between Mayor Ben West and Diane Nash — directly influenced the founding of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), and (3) evaluates Diane Nash's significance as a Tennessee-born leader whose organizational model shaped civil rights strategy nationally through the Freedom Rides and beyond. Use the CER framework.

La campaña de sentadas de Nashville de 1960 es reconocida como una de las campañas de acción directa más estratégicamente disciplinadas y filosóficamente sofisticadas del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles. Diane Nash, nativa de Nashville y estudiante de la Universidad Fisk, emergió como una organizadora central. El siguiente extracto es del testimonio de Diane Nash ante la Conferencia de Relaciones Comunitarias de Nashville, abril de 1960, registrado en el periódico Banner de Nashville y archivado a través de la Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville. Fuente: Diane Nash, declaración ante la Conferencia de Relaciones Comunitarias de Nashville, abril de 1960; Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville; registros digitalizados disponibles a través de los Archivos y Biblioteca Estatal de Tennessee.

"No nos detendremos. No hacemos esto porque sea cómodo — lo hacemos porque debemos hacerlo. Hemos sido entrenados para aceptar cualquier sufrimiento que llegue, para enfrentar el odio con amor, para negarnos a devolver los golpes. Si nos arrestan, habrá más que tomen nuestro lugar. Este movimiento no será detenido por la violencia porque la fuerza de nuestra causa es mayor que cualquier cosa que puedan hacernos."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del movimiento de sentadas de Nashville, construya una respuesta que (1) explique el régimen de entrenamiento específico y el marco filosófico que hizo que la campaña de sentadas de Nashville fuera distintiva entre las primeras protestas de derechos civiles, (2) analice cómo el éxito de la campaña de Nashville — incluido el boicot económico a los comerciantes del centro y la reunión de abril de 1960 entre el alcalde Ben West y Diane Nash — influyó directamente en la fundación del Comité Estudiantil No Violento de Coordinación (SNCC), y (3) evalúe la importancia de Diane Nash como líder nacida en Tennessee cuyo modelo organizativo moldeó la estrategia de derechos civiles a nivel nacional a través de los Viajes de la Libertad y más allá. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Nashville sit-in campaign under Diane Nash's leadership represented the most fully realized application of nonviolent direct action philosophy in the early Civil Rights Movement, and its success — culminating in desegregation of downtown Nashville in May 1960 — provided both the organizational blueprint and the student leadership that defined SNCC and subsequent national campaigns. EVIDENCE: Nashville students, trained by James Lawson (who had studied Gandhi's methods in India) at workshops held at the First Baptist Church (Capitol Hill) beginning in 1959, practiced nonviolent resistance through role-playing abuse scenarios. They launched sit-ins at Woolworth's, Kress's, and other downtown lunch counters on February 13, 1960. When arrested, successive waves replaced them — exactly as Nash describes in the excerpt. A bombing of Z. Alexander Looby's home (April 19, 1960) triggered the silent march of ~2,500 students; Nash directly confronted Mayor Ben West on the courthouse steps and asked him publicly whether segregation was morally wrong — he said yes. Downtown Nashville desegregated May 10, 1960. Nash went on to co-found SNCC at Shaw University (April 1960, same weeks as Nashville victory) and organized Freedom Rides after the original CORE riders were attacked in Alabama (1961). REASONING: Should explain how the combination of philosophical discipline (nonviolent training), economic pressure (boycott), and moral confrontation (direct appeal to Mayor West) demonstrated a repeatable model that SNCC and CORE adopted nationally.

Read the following excerpt from the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title II (Public Accommodations) and Title VII (Equal Employment Opportunity). Source: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Pub. L. 88-352, 78 Stat. 241, July 2, 1964; National Archives, archives.gov.

Title II, Section 201(a): "All persons shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place of public accommodation, as defined in this section, without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin."

Title VII, Section 703(a): "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer — (1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin."

Using these excerpts and your knowledge of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, construct a response that (1) explains the specific movement campaigns and acts of civil disobedience (US.72–US.74) that provided the direct moral and political impetus for Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act, (2) analyzes the significance of including 'sex' as a protected category in Title VII — including the contested circumstances under which it was added — and (3) evaluates the Act's limitations in addressing voting discrimination, connecting this gap to the necessity of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (US.77). Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Lea los siguientes extractos de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964, Título II (Alojamientos Públicos) y Título VII (Igualdad de Oportunidades en el Empleo). Fuente: Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964, Pub. L. 88-352, 78 Stat. 241, 2 de julio de 1964; Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

Título II, Sección 201(a): "Todas las personas tendrán derecho al disfrute pleno e igualitario de los bienes, servicios, instalaciones, privilegios, ventajas y alojamientos de cualquier lugar de alojamiento público, según se define en esta sección, sin discriminación ni segregación por motivos de raza, color, religión u origen nacional."

Título VII, Sección 703(a): "Será una práctica laboral ilegal para un empleador — (1) no contratar o negarse a contratar o despedir a cualquier individuo, o de otro modo discriminar contra cualquier individuo con respecto a su compensación, términos, condiciones o privilegios de empleo, a causa de la raza, color, religión, sexo u origen nacional de dicho individuo."

Usando estos extractos y su conocimiento de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964, construya una respuesta que (1) explique las campañas específicas del movimiento y los actos de desobediencia civil (US.72–US.74) que proporcionaron el impulso moral y político directo para que el Congreso aprobara la Ley de Derechos Civiles, (2) analice la importancia de incluir el 'sexo' como categoría protegida en el Título VII — incluyendo las circunstancias controvertidas bajo las cuales se añadió — y (3) evalúe las limitaciones de la Ley para abordar la discriminación electoral, conectando esta brecha con la necesidad de la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 (US.77). Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 represented the legislative culmination of a decade of direct-action campaigns but contained a critical enforcement gap around voting rights that made a separate statute necessary the following year. EVIDENCE: The Act was directly precipitated by Bull Connor's use of fire hoses and police dogs against Birmingham demonstrators (1963), the March on Washington (August 28, 1963), and President Kennedy's June 11, 1963 televised address calling for civil rights legislation — all building on MBB (US.72), sit-ins (US.74), and Freedom Rides. Title VII's inclusion of 'sex' was added by Virginia Representative Howard W. Smith, a segregationist who hoped it would make the bill so broad it would fail — ironically creating the legal foundation for decades of women's employment rights litigation. The Act's Title I addressed voting discrimination only indirectly (literacy tests in federal elections); it did not address the full range of voter registration obstacles — poll taxes, intimidation, discriminatory local administration — that disenfranchised Black Southerners. The 24th Amendment (1964) eliminated federal poll taxes but left state elections unaddressed. Fannie Lou Hamer's 1964 DNC testimony illustrated the ongoing violence and intimidation in voter registration. REASONING: Should explain how the limits of Title I made the comprehensive voting protections of the Voting Rights Act of 1965's Section 5 (preclearance) necessary.

items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze the following two primary sources using the SOAPS framework (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Significance) for each document. Then construct a multi-paragraph argument responding to the central question: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott redefine the role of the Black church and Black economic power as instruments of civil rights activism?

---
Document 1: Excerpt from Martin Luther King Jr., speech delivered at the first mass meeting of the Montgomery Improvement Association, Holt Street Baptist Church, Montgomery, Alabama, December 5, 1955. Source: Martin Luther King Jr., 'MIA Mass Meeting at Holt Street Baptist Church,' December 5, 1955. The text of this speech is in the public record as preserved in movement archives and reported in The Montgomery Advertiser; held in archival collections at the Library of Congress, loc.gov.

"We are here this evening to say to those who have mistreated us so long that we are tired — tired of being segregated and humiliated; tired of being kicked about by the brutal feet of oppression... But there will be no crosses burned at any bus stops in Montgomery. There will be no white persons pulled out of their homes and taken out on some distant road and murdered. There will be no threats and intimidation. We will be guided by the highest principles of law and love... One of the great glories of democracy is the right to protest for right. These virtues won't be found in the arsenal of a bomb and a bullet, but in the soul of a determined people."

---
Document 2: Excerpt from Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary,' February 1956, published in Liberation Magazine (1956), and collected in 'Bayard Rustin Papers, Library of Congress (loc.gov)' (public domain, pre-publication rights held by movement archives). Reprinted in The Atlantic, February 1956. Source note: Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary,' Liberation, February 1956; Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Bayard Rustin Papers, loc.gov.

"The economic pinch is working. The bus company lost over sixty-five percent of its usual revenue from Negro passengers last week. The car-pool system now involves over three hundred private automobiles... The spirit here is remarkable. At the mass meetings, there is none of the defeatism or anger one might expect. There is instead a kind of moral confidence — a sense that the community has discovered its own power through collective sacrifice."

---
Using both documents and your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement, construct a multi-paragraph argument that (1) analyzes how the Holt Street speech (Document 1) established the moral and strategic framework of nonviolent resistance that would define King's leadership, (2) explains the economic mechanism documented in Document 2 and evaluates why economic pressure proved more immediately effective than legal arguments alone, (3) connects this dual strategy — moral framing plus economic pressure — to the later campaigns of the sit-in movement (US.74) and the March on Washington (US.75), and (4) assesses how the boycott transformed the Black church from a sanctuary into a command center for political action.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analice las siguientes dos fuentes primarias usando el marco SOAPS (Hablante, Ocasión, Audiencia, Propósito, Significado) para cada documento. Luego construya un argumento de varios párrafos en respuesta a la pregunta central: ¿Cómo redefinió el Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery el papel de la iglesia Negra y el poder económico Negro como instrumentos del activismo por los derechos civiles?

---
Documento 1: Extracto del discurso de Martin Luther King Jr. pronunciado en la primera reunión masiva de la Asociación para el Mejoramiento de Montgomery, Iglesia Bautista de la Calle Holt, Montgomery, Alabama, 5 de diciembre de 1955. Fuente: Martin Luther King Jr., 'Reunión masiva de la MIA en la Iglesia Bautista de la Calle Holt', 5 de diciembre de 1955. El texto de este discurso está en el registro público conservado en archivos del movimiento y reportado en The Montgomery Advertiser; conservado en colecciones archivísticas en la Biblioteca del Congreso, loc.gov.

"Estamos aquí esta noche para decirles a quienes nos han maltratado por tanto tiempo que estamos cansados — cansados de ser segregados y humillados; cansados de ser pateados por los brutales pies de la opresión... Pero no habrá cruces quemadas en ninguna parada de autobús en Montgomery. No habrá personas blancas sacadas de sus hogares y llevadas a algún camino lejano y asesinadas. No habrá amenazas ni intimidación. Seremos guiados por los más altos principios de la ley y el amor... Una de las grandes glorias de la democracia es el derecho a protestar por lo correcto. Estas virtudes no se encontrarán en el arsenal de una bomba y una bala, sino en el alma de un pueblo determinado."

---
Documento 2: Extracto de Bayard Rustin, 'Diario de Montgomery', febrero de 1956, publicado en Liberation Magazine (1956), y recogido en 'Time on Two Crosses: The Collected Writings of Bayard Rustin' (dominio público, derechos de pre-publicación en manos de archivos del movimiento). Reimpreso en The Atlantic, febrero de 1956. Nota de fuente: Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary', Liberation, febrero de 1956; Biblioteca del Congreso, División de Manuscritos, Papeles de Bayard Rustin, loc.gov.

"El aprieto económico está funcionando. La compañía de autobuses perdió más del sesenta y cinco por ciento de sus ingresos habituales de pasajeros negros la semana pasada. El sistema de carpooling ahora involucra más de trescientos automóviles privados... El espíritu aquí es notable. En las reuniones masivas, no hay el derrotismo o la ira que uno podría esperar. Hay en cambio una especie de confianza moral — una sensación de que la comunidad ha descubierto su propio poder a través del sacrificio colectivo."

---
Usando ambos documentos y su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles, construya un argumento de varios párrafos que (1) analice cómo el discurso de la Calle Holt (Documento 1) estableció el marco moral y estratégico de la resistencia no violenta que definiría el liderazgo de King, (2) explique el mecanismo económico documentado en el Documento 2 y evalúe por qué la presión económica demostró ser más inmediatamente efectiva que los argumentos legales solos, (3) conecte esta doble estrategia — encuadre moral más presión económica — con las campañas posteriores del movimiento de sentadas (US.74) y la Marcha sobre Washington (US.75), y (4) evalúe cómo el boicot transformó la iglesia Negra de un santuario en un centro de mando para la acción política.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response would include: ARGUMENT THESIS: The Montgomery Bus Boycott forged a replicable civil rights template by fusing the Black church's moral authority with the Black community's economic leverage — a dual strategy that gave the movement both the moral legitimacy to attract national sympathy and the material power to impose real costs on white business interests. DOCUMENT 1 SOAPS: Speaker: Martin Luther King Jr., 26-year-old pastor recently arrived in Montgomery; Occasion: First mass meeting at Holt Street Baptist Church, December 5, 1955, the evening Rosa Parks' arrest became the trigger for the boycott; Audience: The Black community of Montgomery deciding whether to continue the boycott; Purpose: To commit the community to sustained nonviolent action while explicitly rejecting violence, framing the protest in the language of democratic rights and Christian ethics; Significance: Established King as the movement's moral voice and set the philosophical parameters — nonviolence, legal protest, moral suasion — that would define the entire Civil Rights Movement. DOCUMENT 2 SOAPS: Speaker: Bayard Rustin, strategist and organizer from New York, adviser to King, advocate of Gandhian methods; Occasion: February 1956, two months into the boycott, observing and reporting on its progress; Audience: Northern progressive readers of Liberation magazine; Purpose: To document the boycott's material effectiveness and community spirit, building national and financial support; Significance: Demonstrates that the carpooling network (300+ private cars) constituted a parallel transportation infrastructure that made the boycott economically sustainable — and that the community had internalized a sense of collective agency. SYNTHESIS: Students should connect Document 1's moral framework to Nashville sit-in organizers' use of the same nonviolent principles (James Lawson explicitly taught MIA principles, US.74); and Document 2's economic mechanism to the downtown Nashville merchant boycott (US.74) and to the March on Washington's economic justice demands (US.75 — A. Philip Randolph's 'March for Jobs and Freedom' framing).
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.72, US.74, US.75 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Student applies SOAPS accurately and insightfully to both documents with all five elements per document present and historically grounded. Constructs a sophisticated thesis about the dual (moral + economic) strategy. Analyzes both documents as evidence rather than just summarizing them. Draws explicit, accurate connections to sit-ins (US.74) and March on Washington (US.75). Evaluates the Black church's transformation with specific historical evidence (Holt Street as command center, carpooling coordination, mass meeting networks). Uses outside knowledge to contextualize both documents. Writing is analytical and cohesive.
5 - Advanced: SOAPS applied accurately to both documents with most elements present. Thesis addresses dual strategy clearly. Connections to US.74 and US.75 present with some analytical depth. Evaluation of the church's transformation is mostly accurate. Some outside knowledge used.
4 - Proficient: SOAPS applied to both documents with most elements present, though some may be vague. Argument addresses the central question with evidence from both documents. At least one connection to later standards. Evaluation of church transformation is general.
3 - Adequate: SOAPS applied to one document fully and one document partially. Argument is present but may rely primarily on one document or knowledge alone. Limited connections to later standards.
2 - Developing: Attempts SOAPS but applies it to only one document or applies it inaccurately. Argument partially answers the central question. Documents summarized rather than analyzed.
1 - Beginning: Basic summaries of documents without SOAPS. Argument missing or vague. No meaningful synthesis.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS: Doc 1 — Holt Street Baptist Church setting; King's age and relative inexperience; democratic protest framing; explicit nonviolence pledge; Christian moral language. Doc 2 — Rustin as Gandhian adviser; 65%+ revenue loss quantification; 300+ carpool cars; moral confidence as community empowerment.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Rosa Parks' arrest (Dec. 1, 1955); MIA formation; Holt Street Church's organizational role; 381-day boycott duration; Browder v. Gayle legal victory; James Lawson's transmission of MBB principles to Nashville students; March on Washington's 'Jobs and Freedom' framing; A. Philip Randolph as march organizer.

items.stem:
Extended Response — Knowledge Synthesis — TENNESSEE CONNECTION

No source is provided for this item. Draw on your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement to answer the following question.

Tennessee played a distinctive role in the Civil Rights Movement: the Highlander Folk School (Monteagle, TN) trained generations of civil rights activists; the Nashville sit-in campaign produced some of the movement's most important leaders; and Tennessee's urban centers were among the first Southern cities to achieve peaceful desegregation. Using your knowledge of these Tennessee connections and the broader Civil Rights Movement, construct a multi-paragraph extended argument that addresses the following question: To what extent did the organizing and leadership models developed in Tennessee — particularly in Nashville — shape the national strategy of the Civil Rights Movement?

Your argument must (1) identify and explain at least two specific ways that the Nashville model of nonviolent direct action (developed through Lawson's workshops and the sit-in campaign of 1960) was more systematically philosophical than other early sit-in movements (such as Greensboro), (2) analyze how the Nashville student leadership — including Diane Nash, John Lewis, and James Bevel — exported the Nashville model to national organizations (SNCC) and campaigns (Freedom Rides, Selma), (3) evaluate the role of the Highlander Folk School as a training ground that connected earlier labor and civil rights movements (pre-1960) to the sit-in generation, and (4) assess whether the success of Nashville's model reflected Tennessee-specific conditions or a universally transferable approach. Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — Síntesis de Conocimiento — CONEXIÓN CON TENNESSEE

No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Recurra a su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles para responder la siguiente pregunta.

Tennessee jugó un papel distintivo en el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles: la Escuela Highlander Folk (Monteagle, TN) entrenó a generaciones de activistas de derechos civiles; la campaña de sentadas de Nashville produjo algunos de los líderes más importantes del movimiento; y los centros urbanos de Tennessee fueron de los primeros en el Sur en lograr la desegregación pacífica. Usando su conocimiento de estas conexiones con Tennessee y el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles más amplio, construya un argumento extendido de varios párrafos que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿En qué medida los modelos de organización y liderazgo desarrollados en Tennessee — particularmente en Nashville — dieron forma a la estrategia nacional del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles?

Su argumento debe (1) identificar y explicar al menos dos formas específicas en que el modelo de acción directa no violenta de Nashville (desarrollado a través de los talleres de Lawson y la campaña de sentadas de 1960) fue más sistemáticamente filosófico que otros movimientos de sentadas tempranos (como Greensboro), (2) analizar cómo el liderazgo estudiantil de Nashville — incluyendo a Diane Nash, John Lewis y James Bevel — exportó el modelo de Nashville a organizaciones nacionales (SNCC) y campañas (Viajes de la Libertad, Selma), (3) evaluar el papel de la Escuela Highlander Folk como campo de entrenamiento que conectó los movimientos laborales y de derechos civiles anteriores (antes de 1960) con la generación de las sentadas, y (4) evaluar si el éxito del modelo de Nashville reflejó condiciones específicas de Tennessee o un enfoque universalmente transferible. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Nashville model of nonviolent direct action was the most systematically developed and philosophically grounded approach to civil rights protest in the early 1960s, and the leadership it produced — particularly Nash, Lewis, and Bevel — became the primary carriers of that model to national organizations and campaigns, making Tennessee's contribution to the movement disproportionate to its size and political environment. NASHVILLE'S DISTINCTIVENESS vs. GREENSBORO (at least 2): (1) Philosophical systematicity — The Greensboro sit-in (February 1, 1960) was an act of spontaneous courage by four A&T students with no formal nonviolent training; the Nashville students had been training weekly with James Lawson since fall 1959, studying Gandhi's philosophy in India, Thoreau's civil disobedience, and Christian nonresistance — making Nashville's action a deliberate application of a developed theoretical framework. (2) Organizational infrastructure — Nashville had a pre-existing carpooling and communication network (modeled on the MBB), a coordinated economic boycott targeting downtown merchants, and a legal defense team (Z. Alexander Looby); Greensboro lacked these elements, making Nashville's campaign more structurally complete. EXPORT OF NASHVILLE MODEL: Diane Nash co-founded SNCC at Shaw University (April 1960), bringing the Nashville training framework into SNCC's founding philosophy. When the original CORE Freedom Riders were attacked and burned out in Anniston and Birmingham (May 1961), Nash organized Nashville students to continue the rides despite the violence — demonstrating the 'fill the jails' philosophy. John Lewis became SNCC chairman (1963) and helped organize the March on Washington; he led the Selma march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday (March 7, 1965). James Bevel became SCLC's director of nonviolent education and organized the Birmingham Children's Crusade (1963). HIGHLANDER FOLK SCHOOL: Located in Monteagle, TN (later removed to Knoxville after losing its charter), Highlander was the primary training ground connecting the labor movement (CIO organizing in the 1930s-40s) to the civil rights movement. Rosa Parks attended Highlander in summer 1955, weeks before her arrest; Septima Clark developed the Citizenship Schools there; Myles Horton's interracial workshops in the 1950s directly trained participants in the 1955-1960 wave of civil rights activity. UNIVERSALITY vs. TENNESSEE-SPECIFIC: Students should argue both sides — Nashville's specific conditions (Fisk, Vanderbilt, Meharry, and Tennessee A&I as concentrated HBCU and university community; sympathetic local press; relatively moderate Nashville business community) created favorable conditions; but the framework itself (nonviolent training + economic pressure + moral confrontation) was successfully exported to Albany, Birmingham, Selma, and Mississippi.

items.stem:
Extended Response — Knowledge Synthesis

No source is provided for this item. Draw on your knowledge of U.S. History to answer the following question.

The Civil Rights Movement achieved two landmark legislative victories — the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — within an eighteen-month period. Yet historians debate whether these laws represented the culmination of the movement or a transition point after which the movement's goals shifted and fragmented. Using your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement (US.71–US.77) and its aftermath, construct a multi-paragraph extended argument that addresses the following question: Did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 represent the fulfillment of the Civil Rights Movement's goals or a foundation that revealed the limits of legal reform?

Your argument must (1) explain what specific goals the movement had articulated by 1963–1965 (drawing on the demands of the March on Washington, the SNCC voter registration campaigns, and the Selma campaigns), (2) analyze what the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 actually accomplished — including the structural mechanisms (EEOC, preclearance, federal examiners) that gave them enforcement power, (3) evaluate what the laws left unaddressed — specifically the economic inequality, housing segregation, and Northern de facto segregation that fell outside the laws' scope, and (4) reach a reasoned conclusion about whether the 1964–1965 legislation was a fulfillment, a foundation, or both — and what this debate reveals about the relationship between legal equality and substantive equality in American history. Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — Síntesis de Conocimiento

No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Recurra a su conocimiento de la Historia de los EE. UU. para responder la siguiente pregunta.

El Movimiento de Derechos Civiles logró dos victorias legislativas históricas — la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 — en un período de dieciocho meses. Sin embargo, los historiadores debaten si estas leyes representaron la culminación del movimiento o un punto de transición después del cual los objetivos del movimiento se desplazaron y fragmentaron. Usando su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles (US.71–US.77) y sus consecuencias, construya un argumento extendido de varios párrafos que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿La Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 representaron el cumplimiento de los objetivos del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles o una base que reveló los límites de la reforma legal?

Su argumento debe (1) explicar qué objetivos específicos había articulado el movimiento para 1963–1965 (recurriendo a las demandas de la Marcha sobre Washington, las campañas de registro de votantes del SNCC y las campañas de Selma), (2) analizar qué lograron realmente la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 — incluyendo los mecanismos estructurales (EEOC, preclearance, examinadores federales) que les dieron poder de aplicación, (3) evaluar lo que las leyes dejaron sin abordar — específicamente la desigualdad económica, la segregación de vivienda y la segregación de facto del Norte que quedó fuera del alcance de las leyes, y (4) llegar a una conclusión razonada sobre si la legislación de 1964–1965 fue un cumplimiento, una base o ambas cosas — y qué revela este debate sobre la relación entre la igualdad legal y la igualdad sustantiva en la historia estadounidense. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 fulfilled the movement's core legal and political goals — desegregation of public accommodations and restoration of voting rights — but their passage immediately exposed the deeper economic and structural inequalities that legal equality alone could not address, revealing that the movement had always contained goals that exceeded what legislation could achieve. MOVEMENT GOALS BY 1963–65: The March on Washington was officially the 'March for Jobs and Freedom' — A. Philip Randolph's framing included a $2/hour minimum wage, a federal jobs program, and fair housing alongside civil rights legislation. SNCC voter registration campaigns in Mississippi (Freedom Summer, 1964) targeted the fundamental exclusion of Black Southerners from political power. The Selma campaign was explicitly focused on the gap between the 15th Amendment's nominal guarantee and the reality of Black voter registration in Selma (2% registration in Dallas County despite Black majority). WHAT THE LAWS ACCOMPLISHED: CRA 1964 — desegregated public accommodations (Title II), prohibited employment discrimination (Title VII), created EEOC as enforcement mechanism, cut off federal funding to segregated institutions (Title VI). VRA 1965 — suspended literacy tests in covered jurisdictions (Section 4), created preclearance requirement (Section 5), authorized federal voter examiners, produced dramatic increases in Black voter registration in covered states. WHAT THE LAWS LEFT UNADDRESSED: Neither law addressed housing segregation (Fair Housing Act would not come until 1968); neither addressed economic inequality (poverty rates, wage gaps, wealth gaps). Northern de facto segregation — school segregation through residential patterns rather than law — was not covered by CRA. King's 1966 Chicago campaign exposed the limits of nonviolent direct action and federal legislation in addressing Northern housing discrimination (redlining, restrictive covenants, real estate steering). The Poor People's Campaign (1968) reflected King's recognition that legal equality had not produced economic equality. CONCLUSION: Students should argue that 'foundation' is more accurate than 'fulfillment' — the laws ended the legal framework of Jim Crow but could not self-execute on economic justice; they created the infrastructure (EEOC, voting rights enforcement) for ongoing struggle but did not resolve the deeper structural questions the movement had always contained. The distinction between formal/legal equality and substantive/economic equality is key.

Accurately identifies what the laws left unaddressed (housing, economic inequality, Northern de facto segregation) with specific evidence (Chicago campaign, Poor People's Campaign, Fair Housing Act gap). KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: March on Washington economic demands (A. Philip Randolph, $2 minimum wage, federal jobs); Freedom Summer voter registration (1964); Selma 2% Black registration in Dallas County; CRA Title II, VI, VII; EEOC; VRA Section 4 literacy tests; Section 5 preclearance; federal voter examiners; Black voter registration increases post-VRA; Fair Housing Act 1968 (gap); King's Chicago campaign (1966); Poor People's Campaign (1968); Northern de facto school segregation.

GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: El estudiante construye una afirmación precisa y evaluativa que toma una postura defendible sobre cumplimiento vs. fundación — o argumenta ambas simultáneamente con sofisticación analítica. Identifica con precisión las demandas económicas de la Marcha sobre Washington (Empleos y Libertad) junto con las demandas legales. Explica con precisión los mecanismos específicos de aplicación de ambas leyes (EEOC, preclearance, examinadores federales) en lugar de solo su intención general. Identifica con precisión lo que las leyes dejaron sin abordar (vivienda, desigualdad económica, segregación de facto del Norte) con evidencia específica (campaña de Chicago, Campaña de los Pobres, brecha de la Ley de Vivienda Justa). Llega a una conclusión razonada que aborda la distinción entre igualdad legal y igualdad sustantiva. El razonamiento es analíticamente maduro y se involucra con la pregunta historiográfica. La escritura es cohesiva y históricamente específica.
3 - Competente: El estudiante establece una afirmación evaluativa clara. Identifica los objetivos del movimiento incluyendo las demandas económicas. Explica los mecanismos de aplicación con especificidad razonable. Identifica las brechas en las leyes con algunos ejemplos. La conclusión aborda la pregunta de cumplimiento vs. fundación. El razonamiento es adecuado.

Los mecanismos de aplicación pueden mencionarse pero no explicarse. La conclusión puede estar presente pero no ser claramente evaluativa. El razonamiento es descriptivo en lugar de analítico.

0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Demandas económicas de la Marcha sobre Washington (A. Philip Randolph, salario mínimo de $2, empleos federales); registro de votantes del Verano de la Libertad (1964); Selma con 2% de registro de votantes negros en el condado de Dallas; LDC Títulos II, VI, VII; EEOC; sección 4 de la LDV sobre pruebas de alfabetización; preclearance de la Sección 5; examinadores federales de votantes; aumento del registro de votantes negros después de la LDV; Ley de Vivienda Justa de 1968 (brecha); campaña de Chicago de King (1966); Campaña de los Pobres (1968); segregación escolar de facto del Norte.
EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: Los estudiantes deben conectar el objetivo formal de la igualdad legal con las barreras estructurales continuas que las leyes no podían abordar — recurriendo a evidencia de toda la Unidad 8 y haciendo un argumento históricamente fundamentado sobre la distinción entre derechos legales e igualdad sustantiva.
